Benjamin Jowett's translation, first published in 1871 in his Dialogues of Plato, is used here. Read [Gorgias](/book/1879?lang=en) and [Meno](/book/81?lang=en).

about: In Hippolytus, the goddess Aphrodite, offended because the young hunter Hippolytus worships only the virgin goddess Artemis, makes his stepmother Phaedra fall in love with him, with tragic results for them all. In The Bacchae, the god Dionysus returns to his birthplace, Thebes, disguised as a young man, to punish the city for refusing his worship; the women of Thebes rush to the mountains in ecstasy, and the young king Pentheus, who tries to stop them, is lured to a terrible fate.
context: Euripides wrote Hippolytus in 428 BC and The Bacchae near the end of his life, in Macedonia, and The Bacchae is often thought his greatest play. These translations are by Gilbert Murray, whose versions brought Greek tragedy back to the modern stage. Compare Racine's [Phaedra](/book/2172?lang=en).

about: Troy has fallen. Its men are dead, and in the ruins the women wait to be shared out as slaves among the Greek victors: the old queen Hecuba, her daughter Cassandra, who foresees the doom of the Greeks, her daughter-in-law Andromache, and Helen, whose beauty caused the war. One terrible decision follows another, above all the order to kill Andromache's little son, so that no heir of Troy will grow up to take revenge.
context: Euripides staged the play in 415 BC, months after Athens had destroyed the island of Melos, killing its men and enslaving its women and children, and it is one of the most powerful protests against war ever written. This translation is by Gilbert Murray. Read [Thucydides](/book/7136?lang=en), who tells the story of Melos.

about: Strepsiades, an old farmer ruined by his son's passion for horse racing, decides to send the young man to the 'Thinkery' of Socrates, where students are said to learn how to win any argument, right or wrong, and so escape their debts. When his son refuses, he goes himself, and finds Socrates suspended in a basket in the air, worshipping the Clouds. The comedy ends with the son beating his father and justifying it by the new logic, and the father setting fire to the school.
context: Aristophanes staged the comedy in 423 BC, and its mocking portrait of Socrates as a sophist was recalled by Socrates himself at his trial, in Plato's [Apology](/book/75?lang=en). This translation is by W. J. Hickie. Read Aristophanes's [The Frogs](/book/7978?lang=en).

about: Two Athenians, tired of lawsuits and taxes, leave their city in search of a quieter life and persuade the birds to build a great city in the sky, Cloudcuckooland, between heaven and earth. The new city cuts off the smoke of the sacrifices rising to the gods, who begin to starve, while a parade of busybodies from Athens, a poet, a prophet, a surveyor, an inspector and an informer, tries to move in and is chased away.
context: Aristophanes staged the comedy in 414 BC, and it is often considered his most imaginative play; 'cloud-cuckoo-land' has become an expression for a world of fantasy. Read [The Clouds](/book/2708?lang=en) and [Lysistrata](/book/7685?lang=en).

about: This history tells the story of Muslim Spain, al-Andalus, from the conquest led by Tariq ibn Ziyad in 711 to the fall of Granada in 1492: the Umayyad emirate and caliphate of Cordoba under Abd al-Rahman I and Abd al-Rahman III, the splendour of Cordoba with its great mosque, libraries and scholars, the breakup into rival taifa kingdoms, the coming of the Almoravids and Almohads, and the last kingdom of the Nasrids with its Alhambra.
context: Stanley Lane-Poole (1854–1931), a British historian of the Islamic world, published the book in 1886 in the Story of the Nations series, with additions by Arthur Gilman, and it celebrates the civilisation of al-Andalus in a way that was unusual for a European writer of his day. Read Washington Irving's [The Alhambra](/book/45043?lang=en) and [Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada](/book/3414?lang=en).

about: Abu al-Ala al-Maarri, the blind poet of Maarrat al-Numan in Syria, was one of the boldest thinkers in Arabic literature: sceptical of dogma and inherited tradition, a vegetarian who refused all food from animals, and a pessimist who believed it better not to bring children into the world. This small book offers English verse renderings, in quatrains, of thoughts from his poetry on reason, death, injustice and the vanity of human pride.
context: Al-Maarri (973–1057), who lost his sight as a child and lived for decades in seclusion as 'the prisoner of two prisons', his blindness and his house, is the author of the Luzumiyyat and the Epistle of Forgiveness. This version, by Henry Baerlein, was published in 1908 in the Wisdom of the East series, and it is a free adaptation rather than a literal translation. Compare al-Ghazali's [Deliverance from Error](/book/53565?lang=en).

about: Nur al-Din Abd al-Rahman Jami, the last great classical poet of Persia, was also a Sufi master of the Naqshbandi order. This small book introduces his life and thought and offers selections from his poetry, above all from Yusuf and Zulaikha, part of his cycle of seven poems, the Haft Awrang, which retells the story of the prophet Joseph and the wife of his Egyptian master as an allegory of the soul's love for God, together with short poems on divine beauty and love.
context: Jami (1414–1492) lived at the court of Herat, in today's Afghanistan, and wrote in both Persian and Arabic. This edition, by F. Hadland Davis, was published in 1908 in the Wisdom of the East series. Compare [The Diwan of Abu'l-Ala](/book/11755?lang=en) and [Poems from the Divan of Hafiz](/book/68368?lang=en).

about: Hafiz of Shiraz is the best-loved poet of Persia, whose ghazals, short lyrics of love, wine and longing, can be read both as songs of earthly pleasure and as mystical poems about the love of God; in Iran his divan is still opened at random to tell one's fortune. This book offers a selection of his poems in English verse, with a long introduction on his life, his city and the Sufi ideas behind his imagery.
context: Hafiz (about 1315–1390) spent nearly his whole life in Shiraz. His translator, Gertrude Bell (1868–1926), was then a young traveller who had just visited Persia; she later became an archaeologist and British official in Iraq, played a leading part in the making of the modern Iraqi state, and founded the Iraq Museum in Baghdad. This first edition appeared in 1897. Compare [The Persian Mystics: Jami](/book/40774?lang=en).

about: In eight books of blank verse, Sir Edwin Arnold tells the life of Prince Siddhartha, the Buddha, as an Indian Buddhist might tell it: his sheltered youth in a palace of pleasures, his marriage to the beautiful Yasodhara, the four sights of an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a holy man that awaken him to suffering, his flight from the palace, his years of searching, his enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, and his teaching of the path to freedom from suffering.
context: Published in 1879, the poem sold hundreds of thousands of copies and introduced Buddhism to a generation of Western readers; the young Gandhi read it in London. Arnold (1832–1904) also translated the Bhagavad Gita as [The Song Celestial](/book/2540?lang=en). Compare [The Dhammapada](/book/2208?lang=en) and Hesse's [Siddhartha](/book/2649?lang=en).

about: A Genoese sea captain, returning from a voyage round the world, tells a Knight Hospitaller about an ideal city he found on an island near the equator. Built on a hill within seven circles of walls painted with all the knowledge of the world, the City of the Sun is ruled by a priest-king called Sun, or Metaphysician, with three ministers, Power, Wisdom and Love. Its citizens hold all things in common, work only four hours a day, and are educated by walking among the pictures on their walls.
context: Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639), a Dominican friar and philosopher, wrote the book around 1602 while imprisoned in Naples for leading a conspiracy against Spanish rule; he spent twenty-seven years in prison. It is one of the classic utopias of the Renaissance. Compare More's [Utopia](/book/2317?lang=en) and Bacon's [New Atlantis](/book/2585?lang=en).

about: Taking the first ten books of Livy's history of Rome as his starting point, Niccolò Machiavelli asks why the Roman Republic grew so great and lasted so long, and what modern states could learn from it. He argues that a republic in which nobles and people struggle within the law is stronger and freer than a monarchy, that good laws and good armies go together, that religion can hold a state together, and that states must be renewed from time to time by a return to their first principles.
context: Machiavelli wrote the Discourses between about 1513 and 1519, alongside [The Prince](/book/259?lang=en), and many readers think they show his true republican convictions; they were published in 1531, after his death. This translation is by Ninian Hill Thomson. For more in the same vein, read his [History of Florence](/book/2614?lang=en).

about: When Edmund Burke attacked the French Revolution in 1790, Thomas Paine answered him in Rights of Man, the centrepiece of this volume of his collected writings. He defends the Revolution, argues that every generation has the right to govern itself, that governments exist only by the consent of the people and that hereditary monarchy and aristocracy are absurd, and in the second part proposes taxes on the rich to pay for public education, pensions for the old and help for the poor.
context: Published in 1791 and 1792, Rights of Man sold in enormous numbers and was banned in Britain, where Paine was tried and outlawed for seditious libel; he fled to France and was elected to its National Convention. This volume of The Writings of Thomas Paine, edited by Moncure Daniel Conway, also contains his other writings of 1779 to 1792. Read [Common Sense](/book/491?lang=en).

about: 'My own mind is my own church.' Written partly while he was imprisoned in Paris during the Terror, The Age of Reason, the centrepiece of this volume, is Thomas Paine's argument for deism: belief in one God, the creator, known through reason and nature rather than through revelation. He examines the Bible book by book, rejecting the authority of priests and miracles, while insisting that he is no atheist and that true religion lies in doing justice and loving mercy.
context: Published between 1794 and 1796, the book was attacked as blasphemous, cost Paine many friends in America, and sold widely among working people in Britain despite the prosecution of its sellers. This volume of The Writings of Thomas Paine, edited by Moncure Daniel Conway, also contains his other writings of 1794 to 1796. Read [Common Sense](/book/491?lang=en) and [Rights of Man](/book/3831?lang=en).

about: Stephen Gordon, the only child of a wealthy English family, is given a boy's name by her father, who longed for a son, and grows up feeling different from other girls, loving riding, fencing and books. As a young woman she falls in love with women, is rejected by her mother and driven from her home, becomes a successful novelist, serves as an ambulance driver in the First World War and, in Paris, loves a young Welsh woman, Mary, while longing for a world that will accept people like her.
context: Radclyffe Hall (1880–1943) published the novel in 1928 as a plea for tolerance, and although it contains nothing explicit, it was tried for obscenity in London and banned in Britain for twenty years. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2024. Compare Virginia Woolf's [Night and Day](/book/1479?lang=en).

about: Denis Stone, a shy young poet, spends a summer at Crome, an English country house full of eccentric guests: the host, who is writing a history of the house; his wife, who studies horoscopes and the stock market; a painter, a mystic, a cynic who predicts a future in which babies will be bred in bottles, and Anne, the cool, amused young woman Denis loves but cannot bring himself to tell. Little happens except talk, endless, brilliant and absurd.
context: Aldous Huxley (1894–1963) published his first novel in 1921, at twenty-seven, satirising guests he had met at Garsington Manor, the home of Lady Ottoline Morrell. Its talk of babies bred in bottles already looks forward to Brave New World. Read also his [Antic Hay](/book/54951?lang=en).

about: In London just after the First World War, Theodore Gumbril, a bored young schoolmaster, gives up teaching to sell his invention, trousers with an inflatable seat, and, disguised with a false beard as a 'Complete Man', throws himself into the restless, cynical world of the city's artists and intellectuals: a failed painter of huge historical canvases, a scientist who neglects his wife for his experiments, and the fascinating, unhappy Myra Viveash, who drifts through every party in search of a feeling she has lost.
context: Aldous Huxley published the satire in 1923, and it was condemned by some as immoral and admired by others as the truest picture of the 'lost generation' in London. Read his [Crome Yellow](/book/2191?lang=en), and compare Fitzgerald's [This Side of Paradise](/book/1085?lang=en).

about: On the Cotton Blossom, a floating theatre that travels the Mississippi, Magnolia Hawks, the daughter of the boat's kindly captain, Andy, and his stern wife, Parthy, grows up among actors and river people. She falls in love with the handsome gambler Gaylord Ravenal and follows him to Chicago, where his luck rises and falls, while her friend Julie, the boat's leading lady, is driven off the river when it is discovered that she has Black ancestry and is married to a white man, in a state where such marriages are forbidden.
context: Edna Ferber published the novel in 1926, and the next year it became the musical Show Boat by Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein, with the song 'Ol' Man River', a landmark of American theatre. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2022. Read Ferber's [So Big](/book/56092?lang=en).

about: Selina Peake, the daughter of a gambler, becomes a schoolteacher in a Dutch farming community near Chicago, marries a stolid farmer and, after his death, works the poor land herself, growing vegetables and selling them at the Chicago market, to give her son Dirk, whom she calls 'So Big', a better life. Dirk grows up to be a rich, successful bond salesman, but his mother wonders whether he has lost the beauty and meaning she found in her own hard life.
context: Edna Ferber (1885–1968) published the novel in 1924, and it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1925; it entered the public domain in the United States in 2020. Read her [Show Boat](/book/61218?lang=en), and compare Cather's [O Pioneers!](/book/404?lang=en).

about: Tommy Stubbins, a cobbler's son in Puddleby, becomes the assistant of Doctor Dolittle, learns animal languages from the parrot Polynesia and sets sail with him in search of a famous lost naturalist, Long Arrow. Their voyage takes them to Spain, where the Doctor wins a bet that he can stop bullfighting, and to Spidermonkey Island, a floating island in the Atlantic, where he helps end a war, is crowned king, and finally comes home inside a giant sea snail.
context: Hugh Lofting published the book in 1922, and it won the Newbery Medal for American children's literature the following year. Read [The Story of Doctor Dolittle](/book/801?lang=en).

about: Emil Tischbein, a schoolboy from a small German town, is sent by train to Berlin with money for his grandmother pinned inside his jacket. When he wakes up on the train the money has gone, and he is sure the thief is the man in a bowler hat who shared his compartment. In the big city Emil follows the man, and a band of Berlin boys, led by the clever Gustav with his motor horn, joins him in a great hunt across the city to catch the thief.
context: Erich Kästner (1899–1974) published the novel in 1929, one of the first children's books set in a real modern city, and its realism and humour made it a classic; when the Nazis burned Kästner's books in 1933, this one was at first spared. This is the first American translation, by May Massee, with Walter Trier's drawings. Compare [The Railway Children](/book/2073?lang=en).

about: In this first collection of his critical essays, T. S. Eliot sets out ideas that shaped modern literary criticism. In 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' he argues that a poet must write with the whole of past literature in his bones, and that poetry 'is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion'; in 'Hamlet and His Problems' he calls Hamlet an artistic failure and introduces the idea of the 'objective correlative'; and he writes on Marlowe, Jonson, Dante and the critics of his day.
context: Eliot published the book in 1920, two years before [The Waste Land](/book/1549?lang=en), and its essays became foundations of the 'New Criticism' taught in universities for decades. Read his [Prufrock](/book/1682?lang=en).

about: In six lectures, Thomas Carlyle argues that history is shaped by great men and that admiring them, 'hero-worship', is a deep human need. He moves from the hero as divinity, the Norse god Odin, to the hero as prophet, the Prophet Muhammad, whom he defends against the prejudices of European writers as a sincere man and a great soul; then the hero as poet, Dante and Shakespeare; as priest, Luther and Knox; as man of letters, Johnson, Rousseau and Burns; and as king, Cromwell and Napoleon.
context: Carlyle gave the lectures in London in 1840 and published them in 1841. His lecture on Muhammad, unusual for its respect for Islam in the Europe of his time, was widely discussed and has often been translated into Arabic. Read Carlyle's [The French Revolution](/book/1529?lang=en) and [Sartor Resartus](/book/1308?lang=en).

about: This is the English version of the Qur'an, the holy book of Islam, made by George Sale and first published in 1734: all one hundred and fourteen suras, rendered from the Arabic with notes drawn largely from the classical commentators such as al-Baydawi and the two Jalals, and a long 'Preliminary Discourse' in which Sale describes pre-Islamic Arabia, the life of the Prophet and the beliefs and practices of Muslims. For Muslims, any translation is an interpretation of the meanings of the Qur'an, not the Qur'an itself.
context: Sale (about 1697–1736), an English lawyer and orientalist who learned Arabic in London, produced the standard English version for nearly two centuries; it was read by Voltaire and Gibbon, and Thomas Jefferson's copy was used in 2007 when the first Muslim member of the United States Congress took his oath. Compare T. W. Arnold's [The Preaching of Islam](/book/61067?lang=en).

about: The Gesta Romanorum, 'Deeds of the Romans', is a medieval collection of tales in Latin, each followed by a Christian moral: stories of emperors, knights, princesses and saints, many set in an imaginary Rome, of clever tricks, magic rings, faithful animals and wicked stepmothers. Among them are early versions of the story of the three caskets that Shakespeare used in The Merchant of Venice and of the tale of a king and his three daughters behind King Lear.
context: Compiled, probably in England, around 1300 to give preachers examples for their sermons, the collection was one of the most popular books of the Middle Ages and a storehouse of plots for Chaucer, Boccaccio, Shakespeare and later writers. This translation is by Charles Swan. Read [The Merchant of Venice](/book/8?lang=en) and [King Lear](/book/5?lang=en).

about: This book reproduces twenty drawings by Kahlil Gibran, the Lebanese poet and painter: dreamlike figures of men and women, mothers and children, centaurs and souls rising towards the sky, drawn in soft, flowing lines that recall William Blake and the sculptor Rodin, whom Gibran admired. An introductory essay discusses his art and his search, in image as in word, for the unity of the human and the divine.
context: Gibran (1883–1931), who studied art in Paris and lived in New York, published the book in 1919, between [The Madman](/book/101?lang=en) and [The Forerunner](/book/49482?lang=en). Many of his drawings illustrate his own books, above all [The Prophet](/book/98?lang=en).

about: King Henry V has died young, leaving a baby son, Henry VI, and England's conquests in France begin to slip away. While the brave English general Lord Talbot fights on, the French are inspired by Joan of Arc, shown here as a witch called Joan la Pucelle, and at home the nobles quarrel; in a famous scene in the Temple Garden, the Duke of Somerset and Richard Plantagenet pick red and white roses to show their sides, beginning the Wars of the Roses.
context: Probably among Shakespeare's earliest plays, written around 1591, perhaps with other writers, it begins the four-play sequence that ends with [Richard III](/book/1352?lang=en). Its picture of Joan reflects the English propaganda of its time; compare Shaw's [Saint Joan](/book/69758?lang=en). The play's only early text is the First Folio of 1623, which this edition follows.

about: The gentle, pious King Henry VI marries the proud Margaret of Anjou, who soon rules him, and the lords around the throne destroy one another: the good Duke Humphrey of Gloucester is murdered, the Duke of Suffolk is killed by pirates, and Richard, Duke of York, secretly encourages a popular rebellion led by Jack Cade, whose follower Dick the Butcher cries, 'The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers.' At the end York openly claims the crown and the Wars of the Roses begin.
context: Written around 1591, the play is a vivid study of a weak king and a kingdom falling into chaos. A shorter version was printed in 1594 as The First Part of the Contention; this is the fuller First Folio text of 1623. Read [Henry VI, Part 1](/book/1349?lang=en) and [Part 3](/book/1351?lang=en).

about: The Wars of the Roses rage. Richard, Duke of York, is captured at Wakefield, mocked with a paper crown by Queen Margaret and killed; his sons, led by Edward, take revenge and seize the throne, while the helpless King Henry sits on a molehill in the middle of a battle and longs for the simple life of a shepherd. Among York's sons is the hunchbacked Richard of Gloucester, who reveals in a great soliloquy his ambition to hack his way through blood to the crown.
context: Written around 1591, the play completes the story of Henry VI and leads straight into [Richard III](/book/1352?lang=en). A shorter version appeared in 1595 as The True Tragedy of Richard Duke of York; the text here is the First Folio's of 1623. Read [Henry VI, Part 2](/book/1350?lang=en).

about: At the court of King Henry VIII, the proud and powerful Cardinal Wolsey destroys the Duke of Buckingham, and the king, longing for a male heir, sets out to divorce his loyal Spanish queen, Katherine of Aragon, after falling in love with Anne Boleyn. Katherine defends herself with great dignity at her trial, Wolsey himself falls from favour and bids 'a long farewell to all my greatness', and the play ends with the christening of the baby Elizabeth and a prophecy of her glorious reign.
context: Written around 1613, probably with John Fletcher, it was one of Shakespeare's last plays, and at a performance in June 1613 a cannon fired on stage set the thatch of the Globe Theatre alight, and the theatre burned to the ground. It was first printed in the First Folio of 1623, and this text follows it. Compare [Richard III](/book/1352?lang=en).

about: AD 69 was the 'Year of the Four Emperors'. After the death of Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius and finally Vespasian seized power one after another, as Roman armies marched against each other, Rome itself was fought over and the great temple on the Capitol burned. Tacitus tells this year of civil war, and the revolts in Gaul and Germany and the war in Judea that followed, in his concentrated, ironic style, showing, as he puts it, that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome.
context: Tacitus wrote the Histories in the first decade of the second century, and only the first books survive, covering the years 69 and 70. This translation, in two volumes, is by W. Hamilton Fyfe. Read his [Germania and Agricola](/book/7510?lang=en) and Josephus's [Wars of the Jews](/book/2982?lang=en).

about: Lady Susan Vernon, a beautiful, clever and entirely unscrupulous widow of thirty-five, the most accomplished flirt in England, has to leave a house where she has caused a scandal and takes refuge with her brother-in-law's family. There she sets out to captivate her sister-in-law's handsome younger brother, Reginald De Courcy, while trying to force her own shy sixteen-year-old daughter, Frederica, into marriage with a rich fool, all told in a series of letters.
context: Jane Austen wrote this short novel in letters around 1794, when she was about nineteen, but it was published only in 1871, long after her death. Its witty, wicked heroine is unlike any other in her work, and the 2016 film Love & Friendship was based on it. Read [Pride and Prejudice](/book/38?lang=en) and [Emma](/book/39?lang=en).

about: Bert Smallways, a cheerful, ignorant young bicycle mechanic from a London suburb, comes by accident into possession of the secret plans of a new flying machine and is carried off in a runaway balloon to Germany, just as a great German fleet of airships sets out to attack the United States. Bert, a small man in a vast war, witnesses the bombing of New York, the collapse of world finance and a global war in the air that destroys civilisation itself.
context: H. G. Wells published the novel in 1908, only five years after the Wright brothers' first flight, and it predicted the bombing of cities from the air and a world war in which no one wins. Read [The War of the Worlds](/book/180?lang=en) and [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en).

about: Two scientists, the clumsy Mr Bensington and the pompous Professor Redwood, invent a substance, Herakleophorbia, that makes living things grow to giant size. Carelessly handled at an experimental farm, it produces chickens as big as ostriches, enormous wasps and rats, and then children who grow forty feet tall. As the giant children grow up, the ordinary world fears and persecutes them, and a struggle begins between the old, small humanity and the new.
context: H. G. Wells published the novel in 1904, a fable about scientific progress and the fear of change, and it was loosely filmed in 1976. Read [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en) and [The War in the Air](/book/1062?lang=en).

about: Ann Veronica Stanley, a bright, restless biology student of twenty-one, rebels against her strict father's order not to go to a fancy-dress ball, leaves home for London and tries to live on her own. She joins the suffragettes, is arrested in a raid on the House of Commons and spends a month in prison, and falls in love with Capes, her married biology lecturer, with whom she runs away to the Alps.
context: H. G. Wells published the novel in 1909, and its frank picture of a young woman choosing her own life and lover caused a scandal; it drew on his own affair with the young Amber Reeves. Read [Kipps](/book/35192?lang=en) and [Tono-Bungay](/book/1005?lang=en).

about: At a house party in an English country house, the witty, cynical Lord Illingworth offers to make young Gerald Arbuthnot his secretary, a chance that would launch the young man's career. Gerald's mother, Mrs Arbuthnot, a quiet, devout woman, is horrified, for Lord Illingworth is the man who seduced and abandoned her twenty years before and is Gerald's father, a secret she has kept from her son. Around them flows a stream of brilliant, heartless conversation.
context: Oscar Wilde's play was first performed in 1893, and it mixes melodrama with some of his most dazzling epigrams, such as 'The youth of America is their oldest tradition.' Read Wilde's [The Importance of Being Earnest](/book/63?lang=en) and [An Ideal Husband](/book/64?lang=en).

about: These stories of Thomas Hardy's Wessex include 'The Three Strangers', in which an escaped convict, the hangman come to execute him and the convict's brother all take shelter in the same shepherd's cottage on a stormy night; 'The Withered Arm', in which a young farmer's wife's arm withers after a jealous milkmaid dreams of attacking her, and the only cure is to touch the neck of a hanged man; and tales of smugglers, soldiers and village loves.
context: Hardy published the collection in 1888, drawing on the folklore, superstitions and true stories of the Dorset of his childhood. Read Hardy's [The Mayor of Casterbridge](/book/488?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/hardy?lang=en).

about: In the kingdoms of Paflagonia and Crim Tartary, a magic rose and a magic ring make whoever owns them seem beautiful and lovable to everyone, whatever they are really like. The objects pass from hand to hand among a cast of comic royals: the greedy usurping King Valoroso, his vain daughter Angelica, the lazy Prince Bulbo, the true heir Prince Giglio, who must learn to be good, and Betsinda, a little servant girl who turns out to be a lost princess, all watched over by the Fairy Blackstick, who gives the gift of 'a little misfortune'.
context: William Makepeace Thackeray wrote this comic fairy tale for children in 1854, with his own illustrations, as a gentle parody of pantomime and royal pomp. Read Thackeray's [Vanity Fair](/book/896?lang=en).

about: In London, the beautiful, mysterious Countess Narona, a woman with a doubtful reputation, marries Lord Montbarry, who has broken off his engagement to a gentle Irish girl, Agnes, for her sake. Months later Montbarry dies in an old palace in Venice, insured for a large sum, and his English servant vanishes. When the palace becomes a hotel, members of the Montbarry family who stay there suffer strange nightmares, and Agnes is drawn to Venice to discover the truth.
context: Wilkie Collins published the short novel in 1878, mixing a ghost story with a detective puzzle. Read Collins's [The Woman in White](/book/880?lang=en) and [The Moonstone](/book/497?lang=en).

about: During the French and Indian War, around Lake Ontario, Natty Bumppo, now known as the Pathfinder, a scout in his thirties, guides Mabel Dunham, the daughter of a British sergeant, to her father at a frontier fort, together with Chingachgook and the young sailor Jasper Western. Mabel's father hopes she will marry the Pathfinder, who falls deeply in love with her, but a traitor in the garrison and an attack on a lonely island blockhouse test them all.
context: James Fenimore Cooper published the novel in 1840; it is the only Leatherstocking tale in which Natty falls in love, and one of the first American novels set on the Great Lakes. Read [The Last of the Mohicans](/book/1204?lang=en) and [The Deerslayer](/book/3407?lang=en).

about: In 1804, just after the Louisiana Purchase, the old trapper Natty Bumppo, now in his eighties, lives alone on the Great Plains beyond the Mississippi. He meets a family of rough squatters led by the giant Ishmael Bush, who are heading west with a kidnapped young woman hidden in a covered wagon, and helps a young army officer and an absent-minded naturalist to rescue her, amid prairie fires, buffalo stampedes and battles between the Pawnee and the Sioux, before he dies among the Pawnee who have adopted him.
context: Published in 1827, The Prairie was the third of James Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales and tells of Natty's last days. Read [The Pioneers](/book/2431?lang=en) and [The Last of the Mohicans](/book/1204?lang=en).

about: A young college student, Eustace Bright, retells the old Greek myths for children: how Theseus slew the Minotaur in the labyrinth of Crete; how the Pygmies fought the giant Antaeus; how the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus sprang up as armed men; how Persephone was carried off to the underworld; how Jason won the Golden Fleece; and how Circe turned the companions of Ulysses into pigs. Hawthorne tells them in a warm, romantic style, changing details to suit young readers.
context: Nathaniel Hawthorne published the book in 1853 as a sequel to his A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys. Read Homer's [Odyssey](/book/173?lang=en), and Hawthorne's [The Scarlet Letter](/book/411?lang=en).

about: Elam Harnish, known as Burning Daylight, is the most famous man of the Klondike gold rush, a tireless adventurer who races dogsleds across the frozen North and makes a fortune in gold. Taking his millions to San Francisco, he beats the financiers at their own game in ruthless speculation, until he falls in love with his secretary, Dede Mason, who refuses to marry a man so hardened by money, and he must choose between his fortune and a simple life in the hills of California.
context: Jack London published the novel in 1910, and it was one of his most popular books in his lifetime, joining the adventure of the North with a critique of capitalism. Read [The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en) and [Martin Eden](/book/312?lang=en).

about: Polly Milton, a simple, cheerful country girl, comes to visit her rich friend Fanny Shaw in Boston and finds a fashionable family where the children are spoiled, the parents distant and the girls care only for clothes and flirting. Her kindness slowly wins them over, and years later, when Polly returns to the city to earn her living as a music teacher, the Shaws lose their fortune and discover how much they need her old-fashioned values.
context: Louisa May Alcott published the novel in 1870, two years after [Little Women](/book/313?lang=en), and it was one of her most popular books. Read also [Eight Cousins](/book/2863?lang=en), and see [her life](/author/alcott?lang=en).

about: Orphaned at thirteen, Rose Campbell, a pale, delicate girl, goes to live among her many aunts and her seven boy cousins on the 'Aunt Hill' in New England. When her guardian, the kind and sensible Uncle Alec, a doctor and sailor, returns from abroad, he takes charge of her upbringing with modern ideas: fresh air, exercise, simple clothes and good food instead of medicines, and a practical education, and Rose grows strong, cheerful and independent among her lively cousins.
context: Louisa May Alcott published the book in 1875, with a sequel, Rose in Bloom, and its views on healthy living for girls were progressive for their time. Read [Little Women](/book/313?lang=en), and see [her life](/author/alcott?lang=en).

about: Emily Byrd Starr, a dreamy, imaginative girl who wants to be a writer, is orphaned when her beloved father dies and is taken in by her proud, stern aunts, Elizabeth and Laura Murray, at the old family farm of New Moon on Prince Edward Island. There she makes friends with wild Ilse, the artist Teddy and the farm boy Perry, writes letters to her dead father in secret, and knows strange moments she calls 'the flash', glimpses of a beauty beyond everyday things.
context: L. M. Montgomery published the novel in 1923, and she said Emily was more like herself than Anne was. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2019. Read [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en).

about: An unnamed narrator remembers his childhood in the English countryside, where he and his brothers and sisters, orphans brought up by aunts and uncles, the grown-ups they call 'the Olympians', live in a world of their own. In short, funny, wistful chapters they play at knights and pirates, plan adventures, fall in love, and see through the dull, incomprehensible adults who rule them.
context: Kenneth Grahame published the book in 1895, thirteen years before [The Wind in the Willows](/book/595?lang=en), and it was admired by readers from Swinburne to Theodore Roosevelt. Many of its chapters first appeared in magazines, among them the National Observer edited by W. E. Henley, and its sequel is Dream Days.

about: After their mother has died and their father's business has failed, the six Bastable children decide to restore the family fortunes by hunting for treasure. Narrated by Oswald, who pretends not to be Oswald, their schemes include digging for buried gold in the garden, becoming detectives, writing poetry to sell to newspapers, rescuing a princess and holding a gentleman to ransom, each going comically wrong.
context: E. Nesbit published the book in 1899, and Oswald's boastful, self-deceiving voice made it a new kind of children's book, told by a child as children really talk. Read [Five Children and It](/book/1060?lang=en) and [The Railway Children](/book/2073?lang=en).

about: On his twenty-first birthday a young man named Anodos wakes to find his bedroom turning into a forest, and wanders into Fairy Land, a dreamlike world of talking trees, tiny fairies, a palace with a magical library and a marble lady whom he wakes with a song. He is followed everywhere by a dark shadow that withers whatever it touches, and his journey becomes a search for ideal beauty and, at last, the discovery of selfless love.
context: George MacDonald published the novel in 1858, and C. S. Lewis said that reading it as a young man 'baptised' his imagination. Read MacDonald's [The Princess and the Goblin](/book/995?lang=en) and [Lilith](/book/1854?lang=en).

about: Mr Vane, a young man living in his ancestral house, follows the ghostly old librarian, Mr Raven, through a mirror into a strange other world, a region of the dead and the not-yet-born, where he meets the Little Ones, wild children who never grow up, and the beautiful, terrible Lilith, Adam's first wife, who rules the city of Bulika as a vampire princess. Vane must find the way back, and learn what it means to die into true life.
context: George MacDonald published this dark, dreamlike fantasy in 1895, near the end of his life, and it influenced C. S. Lewis, Tolkien and many later writers of fantasy. Read [Phantastes](/book/629?lang=en) and [At the Back of the North Wind](/book/538?lang=en).

about: The second of Andrew Lang's coloured fairy books gathers thirty-seven tales from many lands: from Norway, Soria Moria Castle and The Master Thief; from France, The Twelve Dancing Princesses; from the Grimms, Rapunzel and Snow-White and Rose-Red; from England, Jack and the Beanstalk; from the Norse sagas, the story of Sigurd and the dragon; and many more.
context: Andrew Lang published the book in 1890, a year after [The Blue Fairy Book](/book/803?lang=en), and his series did much to make the world's fairy tales known to English-speaking children; much of the translating and retelling was done by his wife, Leonora Blanche Alleyne, and other collaborators. Read his [Arabian Nights Entertainments](/book/479?lang=en).

about: Sixteen years after the death of Ayesha in the flames of the Pillar of Life, Horace Holly and Leo Vincey travel into Central Asia, following a vision that promised she would return. Crossing the mountains of Tibet, they reach a hidden kingdom ruled by a jealous Khania, who desires Leo, and at last a temple on a fiery mountain, where a mysterious veiled priestess waits for him, in a story of love stronger than death.
context: H. Rider Haggard published this sequel to [She](/book/3281?lang=en) in 1905; like the first book, it is presented as Holly's own manuscript, sent before his death to the editor who had published the earlier story. Readers who enjoy it often go on to [King Solomon's Mines](/book/2351?lang=en) and [Allan Quatermain](/book/998?lang=en).

about: A young lawyer, Malcolm Ross, is summoned at night by Margaret Trelawny, whose father, the Egyptologist Abel Trelawny, has been found unconscious in his room, attacked by something unseen. The house is filled with treasures from the tomb of an ancient Egyptian queen, Tera, whose mummy and magical jewel, a ruby carved with the seven stars of the Plough, her father plans to use in a great experiment to bring her back to life.
context: Bram Stoker, the author of [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en), published the novel in 1903; it is one of the first stories of a mummy's curse, and its original ending was so grim that it was softened in a later edition. Compare Poe's [The Fall of the House of Usher](/book/128?lang=en).

about: Young Adam Salton comes from Australia to visit his great-uncle in the English Midlands, and discovers that the beautiful, cold Lady Arabella March is in fact the human form of an ancient giant white serpent that lives in a deep pit beneath her house, while the half-mad landowner Edgar Caswall tries to dominate a young woman, Lilla, through mesmerism, and flies a huge kite over the countryside.
context: Bram Stoker published his last novel in 1911, a year before his death; strange and disordered, it has become a cult classic and was filmed by Ken Russell in 1988. Read [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en) and [The Jewel of Seven Stars](/book/3870?lang=en).

about: In twenty essays, G. K. Chesterton takes on the famous writers and thinkers of his day, Rudyard Kipling, Bernard Shaw, H. G. Wells and others, arguing that each of them, for all their brilliance, lacks a coherent view of the world, and he includes an essay on the fashionable cult of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. With his usual paradoxes he defends the ordinary man, the family and dogma itself: the real danger, he says, is not people with fixed beliefs but people with none.
context: Chesterton published the book in 1905, and when critics complained that he had attacked others without stating his own philosophy, he replied with [Orthodoxy](/book/480?lang=en). It pairs well with [The Everlasting Man](/book/59884?lang=en).

about: In these short stories, Saki's hero Clovis Sangrail, a languid, sharp-tongued young man about town, punctures the pretensions of Edwardian society with practical jokes and cutting remarks. They include 'Tobermory', in which a cat taught to speak reveals the guests' secrets at a country-house party; 'The Unrest-Cure', in which Clovis cures a dull couple of their boredom with an alarming hoax; and 'Sredni Vashtar', in which a lonely, sickly boy worships a polecat-ferret as a god against his cruel guardian.
context: Saki, the pen name of Hector Hugh Munro (1870–1916), born in Burma, published the collection in 1911; his elegant, macabre humour influenced writers from P. G. Wodehouse to Roald Dahl. He was killed in the First World War. It pairs well with [Beasts and Super-Beasts](/book/575?lang=en).

about: In these short, wicked comic stories, animals often take their revenge on humans and children outwit adults: 'The Open Window', in which a self-possessed girl of fifteen tells a nervous visitor a ghost story about the family's missing men; 'The Lumber-Room', about a boy who escapes his aunt's punishment; and tales of a boar-pig that besieges a garden party and of a supposed werewolf at a country house.
context: Saki published the collection in 1914, two years before he was killed in the war, and 'The Open Window' is one of the most anthologised short stories in English. Read [The Chronicles of Clovis](/book/3781?lang=en).

about: In fourteen comic essays, Jerome K. Jerome offers his idle thoughts on being hard up, on being in love, on vanity, on the weather, on memory, on cats and dogs, on babies, on being shy, on eating and drinking and on getting on in the world, mixing humour with moments of real feeling. 'It is impossible to enjoy idling thoroughly,' he writes, 'unless one has plenty of work to do.'
context: Jerome published the book in 1886, three years before [Three Men in a Boat](/book/613?lang=en), and it sold so well that it made his name. Worth reading alongside it: his [Three Men on the Bummel](/book/2368?lang=en).

about: Years after Three Men in a Boat, J., George and Harris, now middle-aged and two of them married, escape their families for a cycling tour through the Black Forest in Germany. Harris's tandem goes wrong, they get lost, they struggle with German grammar and German regulations and climb mountains they have no need to climb, and the narrator makes sharp, affectionate observations on the orderly German character.
context: Jerome K. Jerome published the book in 1900; a 'bummel', he explains, is a journey with no particular aim. Read [Three Men in a Boat](/book/613?lang=en) and [The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow](/book/1120?lang=en).

about: In the pretty English village of Riseholme, Mrs Emmeline Lucas, known as Lucia, reigns over local society, organising musical evenings and Elizabethan revels, sprinkling her talk with Italian phrases she barely understands and playing the first movement of the Moonlight Sonata to her admiring friends. Her loyal courtier is Georgie Pillson, a fussy, gossipy bachelor who does embroidery. When a famous opera singer and an Indian guru arrive in the village, Lucia's throne is threatened.
context: E. F. Benson (1867–1940) published the novel in 1920, the first of his Mapp and Lucia books, gentle, malicious comedies of snobbery and one-upmanship that have kept a devoted following ever since. Compare Gaskell's [Cranford](/book/697?lang=en).

about: Dickson McCunn, a retired Glasgow grocer with a romantic heart, sets out on a walking holiday in Galloway in search of adventure. He finds it when he meets a band of tough slum boys from Glasgow, the Gorbals Die-Hards, and learns that a beautiful Russian princess is held prisoner in a lonely house, Huntingtower, by Bolshevik agents who want her jewels. With the boys and a young poet, the elderly grocer defends her in a siege.
context: John Buchan published the novel in 1922, the first of his books about Dickson McCunn, a gently comic adventure. Read Buchan's [The Thirty-Nine Steps](/book/857?lang=en) and [Mr Standfast](/book/859?lang=en).

about: In this short collection of experimental stories and sketches, Virginia Woolf tries new ways of catching the flow of the mind: 'The Mark on the Wall', in which a woman's thoughts wander from a mark on her wall to history, nature and war before she discovers what it is; 'Kew Gardens', where scraps of talk from people passing a flower bed mingle with the life of a snail; and 'An Unwritten Novel', in which a passenger on a train invents the life of the woman sitting opposite.
context: Woolf published the book in 1921 through the Hogarth Press, with woodcuts by her sister Vanessa Bell, and these pieces prepared the way for the method of [Mrs Dalloway](/book/348?lang=en). See [her life](/author/woolf?lang=en).

about: In the title story, Bertha Young, a happy young wife in London, is filled one evening with an inexplicable feeling of bliss as she prepares a dinner party, and sees in a pear tree in flower in her garden a symbol of her own life, until the evening reveals a truth she had not suspected. The collection also includes 'Prelude', a portrait of a family moving house in New Zealand seen through the eyes of a child, 'Je ne parle pas français' and 'The Little Governess'.
context: Katherine Mansfield published the book in 1920, two years before [The Garden Party](/book/1652?lang=en); 'Prelude' had first been printed by Virginia and Leonard Woolf's Hogarth Press. Compare Chekhov's [The Darling](/book/12036?lang=en).

about: On Christmas Eve, just after the First World War, Aaron Sisson, a checkweighman at a Nottinghamshire colliery and a gifted amateur flute player, walks out on his wife and children without explanation. He plays in an orchestra in London, falls in with bohemian artists, is befriended by the writer Rawdon Lilly, who nurses him through an illness, and then drifts to Italy, to Florence, in search of a freedom and a friendship he cannot define.
context: D. H. Lawrence published the novel in 1922, and Lilly is a portrait of Lawrence himself; the title refers both to Aaron's flute and to the rod of Aaron in the Bible that blossomed. Read Lawrence's [Sons and Lovers](/book/354?lang=en) and [Women in Love](/book/4324?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/lawrence?lang=en).

about: Alvina Houghton, the only daughter of a draper in a Midlands mining town, refuses the dull life expected of her, trains as a midwife, and then helps with her father's failing business schemes, among them a cinema with a troupe of travelling performers, the Natcha-Kee-Tawaras, who perform an act as 'Red Indians'. Among them is Ciccio, a handsome, silent Italian, and Alvina falls in love with him and follows him to a poor mountain village in Italy.
context: D. H. Lawrence published the novel in 1920, and it won the James Tait Black Prize, the only literary prize he received in his lifetime. Read [The Rainbow](/book/25763?lang=en) and [Sea and Sardinia](/book/33409?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/lawrence?lang=en).

about: In January 1921, D. H. Lawrence and his wife Frieda, whom he calls the 'q-b', the queen bee, left their home in Sicily for a short, impulsive journey to Sardinia. In this travel book he describes their crossing by steamer, the cold, poor inns and buses, the peasants in their costumes, the markets and the mountain villages, with a mixture of irritation, comedy and delight in a land he feels still lies outside the modern world.
context: Lawrence published the book in 1921, and it is one of his liveliest works, written in a rush of vivid impressions. Read his [The Lost Girl](/book/21093?lang=en) and [Sons and Lovers](/book/354?lang=en), and see [his life](/author/lawrence?lang=en).

about: Rickie Elliot, a sensitive, lame young man who loves Cambridge, his friends and the stories he writes, marries the conventional Agnes Pembroke and becomes a master at a dull public school run by her ambitious brother. His life narrows into compromise, until he learns that the wild, careless young countryman Stephen Wonham, whom he has despised, is his own half-brother, and he must decide whether to face the truth.
context: E. M. Forster published the novel in 1907, and he later said it was the book he was most glad to have written. Read [A Room with a View](/book/2780?lang=en) and [Where Angels Fear to Tread](/book/3076?lang=en).

about: Anna Tellwright, the daughter of a rich, miserly Methodist in the pottery town of Bursley, comes into a fortune at twenty-one, but her father still controls her money and her life. As a landlord she is made to press a poor tenant, the struggling manufacturer Titus Price, for his rent, with tragic results, and she is courted by the successful Henry Mynors while she is secretly drawn to Price's gentle, ruined son, Willie.
context: Arnold Bennett published his first novel of the Potteries in 1902, writing with affection and irony about the narrow, chapel-going world he had left for London, and it created the 'Five Towns' of his later masterpiece, [The Old Wives' Tale](/book/5299?lang=en).

about: In the title story, four men, a captain injured in a shipwreck, a cook, an oiler and a newspaper correspondent, struggle for thirty hours in a tiny dinghy off the coast of Florida, within sight of the shore but unable to land through the surf. The collection includes other stories of the sea, the American West and Mexico, among them 'The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky'.
context: Stephen Crane based 'The Open Boat' on his own experience, when the steamer Commodore, carrying arms to Cuban rebels, sank in January 1897 and he survived in a small boat. Published in 1898, it is often called one of the finest short stories in English. Read [The Red Badge of Courage](/book/442?lang=en) and [Maggie](/book/747?lang=en).

about: Penrod Schofield, an imaginative, mischievous eleven-year-old boy in a Midwestern town, is forced to play the Child Sir Lancelot in a school pageant in a costume made from his sister's stockings, and takes his revenge. He dreams of being a famous outlaw, runs a show in his barn with his friend Sam and two brothers from the neighbourhood, fights a bully, and wages a constant war with grown-ups, dancing school and the girl next door.
context: Booth Tarkington published the comic stories in 1914, and they were among the most popular books about American boyhood, though they contain racial attitudes of their time. Read Tarkington's [The Magnificent Ambersons](/book/8549?lang=en), and compare Twain's [The Adventures of Tom Sawyer](/book/48?lang=en).

about: Bartley Alexander, a famous, energetic American engineer at the height of his career, is building the longest cantilever bridge in the world across the St Lawrence River in Canada. Happily married in Boston, he meets again in London the Irish actress Hilda Burgoyne, whom he loved in his youth, and is torn between his two lives, while the great bridge, designed with too thin a margin of safety, rises over the river.
context: Willa Cather published her first novel in 1912, inspired partly by the real collapse of the Quebec Bridge in 1907. It is a short, elegant tragedy, very different from her later prairie novels, [O Pioneers!](/book/404?lang=en) and [My Ántonia](/book/553?lang=en).

about: Robert Frost's first book of poems, arranged like the story of a young man's inner life through the seasons, contains lyrics of love, solitude and the New England countryside: 'Into My Own'; 'Mowing', in which a scythe whispers in the hay; 'The Tuft of Flowers', about flowers a mower has spared for others to enjoy; 'Storm Fear'; and 'Reluctance'.
context: Frost published the book in London in 1913, at thirty-nine, after years of farming and teaching in New Hampshire, and its title comes from Longfellow's poem 'My Lost Youth': 'A boy's will is the wind's will.' Read his [North of Boston](/book/3152?lang=en).

about: In 1284 the town of Hamelin in Germany is overrun by rats. A strange piper in a coat of red and yellow offers to rid the town of them for a thousand guilders, and plays a tune that draws every rat into the river Weser to drown. But when the mayor and council refuse to pay, the piper plays a new tune, and all the children of Hamelin follow him out of the town and into a mountain, never to be seen again, except one lame boy who could not keep up.
context: Robert Browning (1812–1889) wrote the poem in 1842 for a sick child, the son of his friend the actor William Macready, retelling an old German legend. Compare [Sonnets from the Portuguese](/book/2193?lang=en) by his wife, Elizabeth Barrett Browning.

about: Vivie Warren, a brilliant, independent young woman who has just finished studying mathematics at Cambridge, has hardly ever seen her mother, who has paid for her expensive education from abroad. When at last they spend time together, Vivie learns where the money comes from: her mother rose from poverty through prostitution and now manages a chain of brothels across Europe. Mrs Warren defends herself as a woman who had no other way out of poverty, but Vivie must decide what she owes her.
context: Bernard Shaw wrote the play in 1893, but it was banned by the censor in Britain for years, and its first New York production in 1905 was raided by the police. It is a sharp attack on the economic forces that drove women into prostitution. Read [Pygmalion](/book/3914?lang=en) and [Candida](/book/4110?lang=en).

about: The Reverend James Morell, a popular, energetic Christian socialist clergyman in London, is sure of everything, above all of his wife Candida's love. Then Eugene Marchbanks, a young, shy, aristocratic poet whom the couple have befriended, declares that he loves Candida and that Morell does not deserve her. The two men demand that she choose between them, and Candida's choice, and her reason for it, turn the play's ideas about strength and weakness upside down.
context: Bernard Shaw wrote the comedy in 1894, and it became one of his most often performed plays. Read [Arms and the Man](/book/3712?lang=en) and [Man and Superman](/book/3449?lang=en).

about: In this short treatise, George Berkeley sets out the startling theory that material objects do not exist outside the mind: everything we know of a table or a tree is a collection of ideas, colours, shapes and sensations, and 'to be is to be perceived'. What keeps the world in being when no human is looking is the constant perception of God, and the belief in matter, he argues, is not only unnecessary but the root of scepticism and atheism.
context: Berkeley published the Treatise in 1710, at twenty-five, and three years later presented the same ideas in more popular form in his [Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous](/book/4796?lang=en). Compare [Hume's Enquiry](/book/277?lang=en).

about: 'I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness.' In this essay Henry David Thoreau praises the art of walking, of 'sauntering', a word he playfully traces to pilgrims bound for the Holy Land, for hours each day through woods and fields without any purpose, and argues that true freedom and health, for individuals and for a nation, depend on contact with the wild. It contains the famous line 'in Wildness is the preservation of the World'.
context: Thoreau delivered the essay as a lecture several times, and it was published in 1862, a month after his death; it became a founding text of the American conservation movement. Read Thoreau's [Walden](/book/287?lang=en) and [Civil Disobedience](/book/440?lang=en).

about: In Plato's longest and last dialogue, an unnamed Athenian stranger walks with an old Cretan and a Spartan to the cave of Zeus on Crete and, on the way, discusses how to frame the laws of a new city they imagine founding. They consider education, music and drinking parties, marriage, property, crime and punishment, the duties of officials and a council to watch over the laws, and the Athenian's arguments that the gods exist and care for human beings.
context: Plato was still working on the Laws when he died in 347 BC, and it is far more practical than his idealistic [Republic](/book/74?lang=en). Benjamin Jowett's translation makes this long, practical work easy to follow. Read Aristotle's [Politics](/book/84?lang=en).

about: Chitra, the warrior princess of Manipur, raised as a son and trained in hunting and war, falls in love with the great hero Arjuna, who has taken a vow of chastity and rejects her because she is plain and boyish. She begs the god of love to give her perfect beauty for a single year, and Arjuna falls in love with her. But as the year passes, Chitra longs to be loved for herself, the strong woman she really is.
context: Rabindranath Tagore based this lyrical play on an episode of the Mahabharata, wrote it in Bengali in 1892 and published his own English version in 1913. Read Tagore's [The Gardener](/book/6690?lang=en) and [The Song Celestial](/book/2540?lang=en), also taken from the Mahabharata.

about: In three lectures, Rabindranath Tagore warns against the spirit of the modern nation-state, which he calls 'the organised self-interest of a whole people', a machine of commerce and politics that crushes the human spirit, breeds war and justifies empire. He speaks to the West; to Japan, which he fears is copying Western militarism; and to India, which he hopes will find its unity not in nationalism but in the meeting of cultures and in social reform.
context: Tagore delivered the lectures in Japan and the United States in 1916 and 1917, during the First World War, and published them in 1917; they made him unpopular in both countries but now seem prophetic. Read his [Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en) and [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en).

about: Before the gods were, there were Fate and Chance, and one of them set MANA-YOOD-SUSHAI, the greatest of the gods, to sleep; when he wakes, the worlds will end. Meanwhile Skarl the drummer beats his drum without ceasing to keep him asleep, and the lesser gods play with the worlds. In short prose poems, Lord Dunsany invents a complete mythology of gods, prophets and doomed worlds, written in a grave, biblical style.
context: Dunsany published this, his first book, in 1905 at his own expense, with drawings by Sidney Sime, and it was a great influence on H. P. Lovecraft and later fantasy writers. Read his [The King of Elfland's Daughter](/book/55511?lang=en).

about: Ralph, the youngest of four princes of the small kingdom of Upmeads, sets out in search of adventure and hears of the Well at the World's End, whose water gives long life and good fortune to those who drink it. His long quest leads him through strange cities, forests and wastelands, into love with a mysterious lady who has already drunk from the well, and finally, with the brave Ursula, to the well itself beyond the mountains, and home again to defend his own land.
context: William Morris published this long romance in 1896, the year of his death, in a deliberately archaic English, and it greatly influenced Tolkien and C. S. Lewis. Read Morris's [News from Nowhere](/book/3383?lang=en).

about: Philip Nolan, a young American army officer, is caught up in the conspiracy of Aaron Burr and, at his court-martial in 1807, cries out that he wishes never to hear of the United States again. The court grants his wish: for the rest of his life he is kept at sea, passed from one navy ship to another, and no one is ever allowed to speak to him of his country or show him its news. Over the long decades he comes to understand what he has lost.
context: Edward Everett Hale (1822–1909), a Boston clergyman, published the story in 1863, during the Civil War, to strengthen loyalty to the Union, and many readers took it for a true story. The volume adds other tales. Compare Washington Irving's [Rip Van Winkle](/book/55419?lang=en).

about: On the last day of the year, Toby 'Trotty' Veck, a poor, kind old ticket-porter who carries messages in the London streets, hears gentlemen and politicians declare that the poor have no right to exist and that his daughter Meg should not marry. Disheartened, he climbs the church tower, where the goblins of the bells show him a terrible vision of the future that awaits his daughter and her friends if he loses faith, before the New Year's chimes ring out.
context: Charles Dickens wrote this second Christmas book in Genoa in 1844, the year after [A Christmas Carol](/book/33?lang=en), as an angry attack on the economists and magistrates who blamed the poor for their own poverty. See [his life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: Before he wrote any novels, the young Charles Dickens wandered the streets of London as a journalist and described what he saw: crowded streets and markets, pawnshops, gin shops and pubs, Newgate Prison, the courts, the theatres and Greenwich Fair, together with portraits of ordinary people, clerks, cab drivers and shabby-genteel families, and comic tales of middle-class life.
context: The sketches appeared in newspapers and magazines from 1833 and were collected as a book in 1836 under the pen name Boz, the family nickname of Dickens's youngest brother, with illustrations by George Cruikshank, and their success led directly to [The Pickwick Papers](/book/37?lang=en). See [Dickens's life](/author/dickens?lang=en).

about: In his second collection of stories, F. Scott Fitzgerald captures the restless, glittering world of young Americans after the First World War. It includes 'The Curious Case of Benjamin Button', about a man who is born old and grows younger every year; 'The Diamond as Big as the Ritz', a fantasy about a family that owns a mountain made of a single diamond; and 'May Day', a darker story of drunken soldiers and rich young people in New York.
context: Fitzgerald published the collection in 1922, the same year as [The Beautiful and Damned](/book/9179?lang=en), and its title gave a name to the era; Benjamin Button was filmed in 2008. Read [The Great Gatsby](/book/351?lang=en).

about: In the title story, a young lawyer accepts a banker's bet of two million roubles that he cannot endure fifteen years of solitary confinement. Locked in a lodge in the banker's garden with books, he reads everything, from novels to languages, philosophy and the Gospels, and as the end of the term approaches the banker, now ruined, plans to kill him, but finds that the prisoner has come to his own conclusion about the money. The volume adds other stories by Anton Chekhov.
context: Chekhov wrote 'The Bet' in 1889. This translation, by S. S. Koteliansky and John Middleton Murry, the husband of Katherine Mansfield, was published in 1915. Read Chekhov's [The Darling](/book/12036?lang=en) and his last [plays](/book/7966?lang=en).

about: Three young American soldiers in the First World War, Fuselli, a clerk from San Francisco eager for promotion, Chrisfield, a hot-tempered farm boy from Indiana, and John Andrews, a sensitive, Harvard-educated musician, are crushed in different ways by the machine of the army. Andrews, who hates its discipline, finds hope in post-war Paris in music and in love, until his desertion catches up with him.
context: John Dos Passos, who had served as an ambulance driver in France, published the novel in 1921, and it was one of the first American novels to show the war without glory, shocking many readers. Read his [Manhattan Transfer](/book/65650?lang=en), and compare Hemingway's [A Farewell to Arms](/book/68678?lang=en).

about: Rodney Stone, the son of a naval officer in the days of Nelson, tells of his boyhood friendship with Jim Harrison, a blacksmith's nephew, and of his time in London as the guest of his uncle, Sir Charles Tregellis, the most fashionable dandy of the Regency and a friend of the Prince of Wales. At the heart of the novel is the world of prize-fighting, as Jim is put forward as a champion in a great boxing match, and an old murder mystery is solved.
context: Arthur Conan Doyle published the novel in 1896, a lively picture of Regency England with appearances by Nelson and Beau Brummell. Read [The White Company](/book/1171?lang=en) and [The Exploits of Brigadier Gerard](/book/10280?lang=en).

about: This history traces Arabic literature from the poets of the pre-Islamic desert, with their odes of love, war and the deserted encampment, through the Qur'an and the rise of Islam, the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, the golden age of Baghdad with its poets, grammarians, historians and philosophers, the culture of Muslim Spain, and the centuries that followed. Nicholson quotes and translates widely, from Imru' al-Qays and al-Mutanabbi to al-Ghazali and Ibn Khaldun, always connecting literature with religion and politics.
context: Reynold Alleyne Nicholson (1868–1945), a Cambridge scholar of Arabic and Persian, published the book in 1907, and for most of the twentieth century it was the standard introduction in English to Arabic literature, still praised for its learning and its sympathy. Read his [The Mystics of Islam](/book/61477?lang=en) and O'Leary's [Arabic Thought and Its Place in History](/book/56002?lang=en).

about: What is Sufism? In this short, clear book, Reynold Nicholson explains the inner, mystical side of Islam: the path of repentance, poverty and trust in God, the stations and states of the soul, the guidance of the shaikh, illumination and ecstasy, divine love, knowledge of God, and fana, the passing away of the self in God. He illustrates each idea with sayings and stories of the great Sufis, from Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, al-Junayd and Abu Yazid al-Bistami to al-Hallaj, al-Ghazali, Ibn Arabi and Jalal al-Din Rumi.
context: Nicholson, who later translated the whole of Rumi's Masnavi into English, published the book in 1914, and it remains a learned and sympathetic introduction. Read [The Confessions of Al Ghazzali](/book/53565?lang=en), Rumi's [Mesnevi](/book/56129?lang=en) and Nicholson's [A Literary History of the Arabs](/book/34118?lang=en).

about: How did Greek philosophy and science pass to the Arabs, and from them to medieval Europe? De Lacy O'Leary traces the road: from the Hellenistic schools of Alexandria and the Syriac Christian translators of Edessa, Nisibis and Jundishapur to the great translation movement of Abbasid Baghdad; the philosophers al-Kindi, al-Farabi and Ibn Sina; the debates of the theologians and al-Ghazali's critique of philosophy; and the thinkers of al-Andalus, Ibn Bajja, Ibn Tufayl and Ibn Rushd, whose works, translated into Latin, shaped European scholasticism.
context: O'Leary (1872–1957), a British orientalist who taught at Bristol, published the book in 1922. It is a compact account of one of the great chapters in the history of ideas, in which Baghdad and Cordoba carried learning across the centuries. Compare Ibn Tufayl's [Hayy ibn Yaqzan](/book/14976?lang=en) and Aristotle's [Categories](/book/2564?lang=en).

about: The Masnavi of Jalal al-Din Rumi, which Jami called 'the Qur'an in the Persian tongue', is a vast poem of stories, parables and teaching about the soul's journey to God. It begins with the famous lament of the reed flute, torn from its reed bed and longing to return, an image of the soul separated from its source. This volume contains the first of its six books, with the tales of the king and the slave girl, the grocer and the parrot, the lion and the hare, and many more.
context: Rumi (1207–1273), born in Balkh and settled in Konya, inspired the Mevlevi order of 'whirling dervishes', founded by his followers. This translation, published in 1881 by the British orientalist Sir James Redhouse, is accompanied by anecdotes of Rumi's life from Aflaki's 'Acts of the Adepts'. Compare Nicholson's [The Mystics of Islam](/book/61477?lang=en) and [The Persian Mystics: Jami](/book/40774?lang=en).

about: This history tells the story of Jerusalem from the age of Herod and the Roman siege of AD 70 to the end of the Crusades: the city under Romans and Byzantines; its surrender to the Caliph Umar in 638 and the building of the Dome of the Rock; its capture by the Crusaders in 1099 and the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem; and its recovery by Saladin in 1187, together with the history of its holy places and buildings.
context: Walter Besant (1836–1901) wrote the book with the Arabist Edward Henry Palmer (1840–1882), both connected with the Palestine Exploration Fund, and first published it in 1871; Palmer was killed in Sinai in 1882 while on a mission for the British government. Read Scott's [The Talisman](/book/1602?lang=en) and Lessing's [Nathan the Wise](/book/3909?lang=en).

about: In Alexandria in the early fifth century, a city of philosophers, monks, Jews, Goths and Roman officials, the beautiful pagan philosopher Hypatia lectures on Plato to admiring students, while the fierce Christian patriarch Cyril and his monks grow ever more powerful. Philammon, a young monk come down from the desert monasteries, falls under Hypatia's spell and is caught between the two worlds, as the conflict in the city moves towards her murder by a Christian mob in 415.
context: Charles Kingsley published the novel in 1853, and its subtitle, 'New Foes with an Old Face', shows that he meant it as a warning about religious fanaticism in his own time. Hypatia, a real mathematician and philosopher, has become a symbol of reason and of learning destroyed by intolerance. Read Kingsley's [The Water-Babies](/book/1276?lang=en).

about: Jason, sent by his usurping uncle to bring back the Golden Fleece from Colchis at the far end of the Black Sea, gathers the greatest heroes of Greece, Heracles, Orpheus, the twins Castor and Polydeuces and many others, aboard the ship Argo. After adventures among the women of Lemnos, the Harpies and the clashing rocks, they reach Colchis, where the king's daughter Medea, struck by Eros, falls in love with Jason and uses her magic to help him win the fleece, before they flee together.
context: Apollonius of Rhodes, who headed the great Library of Alexandria in the third century BC, wrote the only Greek epic to survive from between Homer and the Roman age, and his portrait of Medea's passion influenced Virgil's Dido. This translation is by R. C. Seaton. Read Euripides's [Medea](/book/31777?lang=en) and Virgil's [Aeneid](/book/541?lang=en).

about: Pindar's odes celebrate the winners of the great athletic games of ancient Greece, at Olympia, Delphi, Nemea and the Isthmus of Corinth: runners, wrestlers, boxers and the owners of chariot teams, many of them kings and nobles of Sicily and the Greek cities. Into each victory song he weaves myths of gods and heroes and reflections on fate, fame and the fleeting glory of human life, which he calls, in one famous line, the dream of a shadow.
context: Pindar (about 518–438 BC), born near Thebes, was considered by the ancients the greatest of the Greek lyric poets, and his complex style inspired the 'Pindaric ode' of later European poetry. This translation is by Ernest Myers. Compare Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en).

about: Gaius Valerius Catullus writes of love with a directness never heard before in Latin: his passion for 'Lesbia', a married woman of Roman high society, from the first kisses ('give me a thousand kisses, then a hundred') to bitterness and betrayal ('I hate and I love'). Alongside the love poems stand tender lines at his brother's grave, savage insults against Julius Caesar and other politicians, wedding songs and a long poem on the marriage of Peleus and Thetis.
context: Catullus (about 84–54 BC) died young, and his poems survived the Middle Ages in a single manuscript found in Verona. This translation, in the metres of the original, is by Robinson Ellis. Compare Ovid's [Art of Love](/book/43040?lang=en).

about: In ten books of furious verse, Lucan tells the story of the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey that destroyed the Roman Republic: Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon, the siege of Massilia, the battle of Pharsalus in 48 BC, Pompey's flight to Egypt and his murder on the shore, and Cato's march through the deserts of Libya, where serpents attack the soldiers. Lucan does away with the gods of epic and makes Caesar a destructive force of nature.
context: Lucan (39–65), the nephew of the philosopher Seneca, wrote the poem under the emperor Nero, who first favoured him and then banned his work; after joining a plot against Nero he was forced to take his own life at twenty-five, leaving the poem unfinished. Compare Caesar's own [De Bello Gallico and Other Commentaries](/book/9772?lang=en).

about: In four books of memories, Xenophon defends his teacher Socrates against the charges of impiety and corrupting the young for which he was executed in 399 BC, by showing him in daily conversation with friends, generals, artists and young men: on piety, friendship, self-control, the duty of sons to their mothers, the art of command, and the choice of Heracles between Virtue and Vice. His Socrates is practical and kindly, a moral adviser rather than the subtle philosopher of Plato.
context: Xenophon (about 430–354 BC), the soldier and writer who led the retreat described in his [Anabasis](/book/1409?lang=en), wrote the book years after Socrates' death. This translation is by Henry Graham Dakyns. Compare Plato's [Apology](/book/75?lang=en).

about: What makes a good ruler? Xenophon answers with a partly fictional life of Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Empire, from his boyhood education in Persia and at the court of his grandfather, the king of the Medes, through his campaigns and the capture of Babylon, the city in today's Iraq, to the organisation of his empire and his death. Cyrus rules by example, justice, generosity and careful planning, and wins the willing obedience of his subjects.
context: Written in the fourth century BC, the Cyropaedia, 'the education of Cyrus', was admired by the Roman general Scipio, by Machiavelli and by Thomas Jefferson, and it became a model for the 'mirrors for princes' of later centuries. This translation is by Henry Graham Dakyns. Read Xenophon's [Memorabilia](/book/1416?lang=en) and [Anabasis](/book/1409?lang=en).

about: What is knowledge? Socrates puts the question to Theaetetus, a brilliant young mathematician who resembles him in his snub nose and bulging eyes, and they examine three answers: that knowledge is perception, that it is true belief, and that it is true belief with an account. Along the way Socrates describes himself as a midwife who helps others give birth to ideas, and examines Protagoras's claim that 'man is the measure of all things'. Each answer fails, and the dialogue ends in an honest puzzle.
context: Written around 369 BC in memory of the real Theaetetus, who had died after a battle, the dialogue is the founding work of the theory of knowledge. The English version is Benjamin Jowett's. Read [Sophist](/book/1939?lang=en), which continues it, and the [Meno](/book/81?lang=en).

about: The day after the Theaetetus, a visitor from Elea, a follower of Parmenides, sets out with the young Theaetetus to define the sophist, the paid teacher of argument, by a method of division, splitting kinds into smaller and smaller kinds. The search leads to a deep problem: how is it possible to say what is false, to speak of what is not? To solve it, the stranger must commit a kind of 'parricide' against Parmenides and show that what is not, in some sense, is.
context: Written in Plato's later years, the dialogue is one of his most difficult and influential works on language and being. This is Benjamin Jowett's Victorian translation. Read [Theaetetus](/book/1931?lang=en), [Statesman](/book/1942?lang=en) and [Parmenides](/book/1894?lang=en).

about: Continuing the conversation of the Sophist, the stranger from Elea and a young man also named Socrates try to define the true statesman. Along the way they tell a great myth of a cosmos that turns first one way and then the other, with a golden age under the gods, and compare the ruler to a shepherd, a doctor and a weaver who weaves the brave and the gentle temperaments of citizens into one cloth. The best ruler, they argue, would be a wise man above the law; failing him, law must rule.
context: Written in Plato's later years, the dialogue stands between the idealism of the [Republic](/book/74?lang=en) and the practical [Laws](/book/1954?lang=en). Benjamin Jowett made the translation used here. Readers who enjoy it often go on to [Sophist](/book/1939?lang=en).

about: On his way to court to answer the charges that will lead to his death, Socrates meets Euthyphro, a confident young priest who is prosecuting his own father over the death of a labourer, because he believes the gods demand it. Socrates asks him to explain what piety is, and in trying they reach the famous question: is something good because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is good? Euthyphro hurries away before they find an answer.
context: Written in the early fourth century BC, this short dialogue opens the series of Plato's works on the trial and death of Socrates, followed by the [Apology](/book/75?lang=en), the [Crito](/book/82?lang=en) and the [Phaedo](/book/77?lang=en). It is given here in Benjamin Jowett's translation.

about: Socrates meets Ion, a famous rhapsode, a professional reciter of Homer, who has just won first prize at a festival and boasts that he understands Homer better than anyone. When Socrates asks what exactly he knows, it turns out that Ion's art is not a skill or a body of knowledge at all: poets and their performers, Socrates suggests, speak not by art but by divine inspiration, like a chain of iron rings hanging from a magnet, each one holding up the next.
context: One of Plato's shortest dialogues, written in the early fourth century BC, the Ion is a founding text in the long debate about poetry and inspiration. The translator is Benjamin Jowett, whose versions shaped how English readers met Plato. Compare Plato's [Republic](/book/74?lang=en), which banishes the poets, and Aristotle's [Poetics](/book/2169?lang=en).
