about: The day after the conversations of the Republic and the Timaeus, Critias begins to tell a story he says came from Egyptian priests by way of the Athenian statesman Solon: nine thousand years before, a primeval Athens of virtuous citizens fought against Atlantis, a great island empire beyond the Pillars of Hercules. He describes Atlantis in detail, its rings of land and water, its temple to Poseidon, its harbours, canals and kings, and its decline into arrogance; then, just as Zeus gathers the gods to punish it, the dialogue breaks off.
context: The unfinished Critias is, with the [Timaeus](/book/79?lang=en), the only ancient source for the legend of Atlantis, which has fascinated readers ever since. Jowett's translation is used here. Read Plato's [Republic](/book/74?lang=en).

about: Are names natural, or merely conventional? Cratylus claims that every thing has a correct name by nature, while Hermogenes thinks names are only agreed labels. Socrates, joking that he has been inspired by a priest named Euthyphro, examines both views, proposing dozens of playful and sometimes absurd derivations of Greek words, from the names of gods and heroes to the elements, and finally argues that to know the truth we should study things themselves rather than their names.
context: Written in the early fourth century BC, the Cratylus is the first work of Western philosophy devoted to language, and its questions are still debated. It is given in Benjamin Jowett's translation, though much of the Greek wordplay inevitably slips away in English. Read Plato's [Theaetetus](/book/1931?lang=en) and [Sophist](/book/1939?lang=en).

about: The young Socrates meets the great philosopher Parmenides of Elea, then about sixty-five, and his pupil Zeno in Athens. Socrates presents his theory of Forms, the perfect, unchanging ideas behind things, and Parmenides raises powerful objections to it, among them the argument later known as the 'third man'. Then the old philosopher gives a demonstration of reasoning: a long series of arguments about whether 'the One' exists or not, which reaches contradictory conclusions.
context: Written in Plato's later years, the Parmenides is the most puzzling of his dialogues, a criticism of his own theory that the later Neoplatonists read as a mystical theology. Benjamin Jowett's translation keeps the long chains of argument as clear as English allows. Read [Sophist](/book/1939?lang=en) and the [Republic](/book/74?lang=en).

about: Which is the good life: pleasure or wisdom? Philebus, who says almost nothing, has argued for pleasure, and his friend Protarchus defends it against Socrates, who argues for knowledge and thought. Dividing all things into the limited, the unlimited, their mixture and its cause, and examining kinds of pleasure, true and false, pure and mixed, Socrates concludes that the best life is a mixture of both, ordered by measure and proportion, with wisdom ranked higher than pleasure.
context: One of Plato's late dialogues, the Philebus is a careful study of pleasure that influenced Aristotle's treatment of it in the [Nicomachean Ethics](/book/8197?lang=en). The translation comes from Benjamin Jowett's collected Dialogues of Plato. Read Plato's [Gorgias](/book/1879?lang=en).

about: At a wrestling school in Athens, Socrates meets a group of boys and young men, among them the handsome Lysis and his friend Menexenus, and an admirer, Hippothales, who writes embarrassing poems in Lysis's praise. Socrates shows him how to talk to the boy instead and begins a conversation about friendship: do we love those who are like us or those who are unlike us? Are we friends of the good because we are bad, or because we are neither? The dialogue ends, characteristically, without an answer.
context: Written in the early fourth century BC, the Lysis is Plato's first exploration of friendship and love, themes he develops in the [Symposium](/book/76?lang=en) and the [Phaedrus](/book/78?lang=en). Benjamin Jowett's translation keeps the talk light and natural.

about: Just back from the siege of Potidaea, Socrates visits a wrestling school and meets the young Charmides, celebrated for his beauty, and his guardian, Critias. Pretending to have a cure for Charmides' headache that must also cure the soul, Socrates asks him what sophrosyne, self-control or temperance, really is. Charmides and then Critias offer definitions, as quietness, as modesty, as doing one's own business and as knowledge of oneself, and each is examined and found wanting.
context: Written in the early fourth century BC, the dialogue carries a dark irony, since Charmides and Critias, Plato's own relatives, later became leaders of the brutal oligarchy of the Thirty Tyrants in Athens. The version here is by the Oxford scholar Benjamin Jowett. Read [Laches](/book/1803?lang=en) and [Lysis](/book/1800?lang=en).

about: Two fathers ask the famous generals Laches and Nicias whether their sons should learn to fight in armour, and the generals call in Socrates. The question soon becomes: what is courage? Laches, a blunt soldier, suggests standing firm in battle and then endurance of the soul; Nicias, more educated, suggests knowledge of what is to be feared and what is not. Each definition fails under Socrates' questions, and the two generals, who have shown courage on the battlefield, find that they cannot say what it is.
context: Written in the early fourth century BC, the Laches is a lively, sometimes comic dialogue, and in it Laches recalls Socrates' bravery beside him at the battle of Delium. This English version is Benjamin Jowett's. Read [Charmides](/book/1801?lang=en) and the [Apology](/book/75?lang=en).

about: Procopius, the official historian of the Byzantine emperor Justinian, wrote glowing accounts of his wars and his buildings, but in this secret book, meant to be read only after their deaths, he tells what he really thought. He describes Justinian as a demon in human form, greedy and cruel; the empress Theodora as a former actress of scandalous life who ruled her husband; and the great general Belisarius as a weak man dominated by his unfaithful wife, Antonina.
context: Written around 550 and unknown until a manuscript was found in the Vatican Library and published in 1623, the Secret History is one of the most scandalous books to survive from the ancient world, and historians still debate how much of it to believe. Compare [Tacitus's Histories](/book/15070?lang=en).

about: In The Conspiracy of Catiline, Sallust tells how, in 63 BC, a ruined, ambitious aristocrat, Lucius Sergius Catilina, plotted to seize power in Rome and was exposed by the consul Cicero; it includes the great debate in the Senate on the conspirators' fate between Julius Caesar, who argued for mercy, and Cato, who demanded death. The Jugurthine War tells of Rome's war in North Africa against Jugurtha, king of Numidia in today's Algeria and Tunisia, who bribed senators until Rome finally defeated him.
context: Sallust (86–about 35 BC), a supporter of Caesar who withdrew from politics to write history, saw in both stories the corruption of the Roman nobility by wealth and ambition. This translation is by J. S. Watson. Read Cicero's [De Officiis](/book/42444?lang=en) and Caesar's [Commentaries](/book/9772?lang=en).

about: In three books addressed to his son Marcus, then a student in Athens, Cicero sets out a practical guide to moral duty: first what is honourable, the virtues of wisdom, justice, courage and self-control; then what is useful, how to win friends, reputation and influence by honest means; and finally what to do when the honourable and the useful seem to conflict, arguing that nothing truly useful can ever be dishonourable.
context: Cicero wrote the book in 44 BC, the year of Caesar's murder and the last full year of his own life, drawing on the Stoic philosopher Panaetius, and for centuries it was one of the most widely read books of moral philosophy in Europe. This translation is by Walter Miller. Read Cicero's [Treatises on Friendship and Old Age](/book/2942?lang=en).

about: How should we give, and how should we receive? In seven books, the Stoic philosopher Seneca examines the gift and the favour, the bonds that hold human society together: give willingly and promptly, without boasting or expecting a return; receive with gratitude and remember the giver; for ingratitude, he argues, is among the worst of vices. He also asks whether a slave can do his master a kindness, whether we can repay the gods, and whether one can benefit oneself.
context: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (about 4 BC–AD 65), tutor and adviser of the emperor Nero, wrote the treatise in the last years of his life, before Nero ordered him to take his own life. This translation is by Aubrey Stewart. Compare Epictetus's [Enchiridion](/book/40729?lang=en) and Marcus Aurelius's [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en).

about: In Medea, the sorceress abandoned by Jason in Corinth takes a terrible revenge, in a version of the story harsher and more rhetorical than Euripides's; in The Daughters of Troy, Hecuba, Andromache and the captive women of fallen Troy await their fate while the Greeks sacrifice the princess Polyxena and Andromache's little son. Seneca's tragedies are full of violent passion, ghosts and long, brilliant speeches.
context: Seneca's plays, probably written to be recited rather than staged, were rediscovered in the Renaissance and strongly influenced Elizabethan tragedy, from Kyd's [The Spanish Tragedy](/book/31670?lang=en) to Shakespeare. This verse translation is by Ella Isabel Harris. Compare Euripides's [Medea](/book/31777?lang=en) and [The Trojan Women](/book/9407?lang=en).

about: The saga of the Volsungs tells the tragic story of a family of heroes descended from the god Odin: Sigmund, who draws the sword Odin thrust into a tree; his son Sigurd, who kills the dragon Fafnir, tastes its blood and understands the speech of birds, wins a cursed treasure and awakens the shield-maiden Brynhild; and the betrayal and vengeance that follow, when Sigurd is tricked into marrying Gudrun and Brynhild seeks his death.
context: Written in Iceland in the thirteenth century from older heroic poems, the saga tells the same legend as the German [Nibelungenlied](/book/1390?lang=en), and it inspired Wagner's Ring and Tolkien. This translation, first published in 1870, is by Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris, with excerpts from the Poetic Edda. Read [The Story of Burnt Njal](/book/894?lang=en).

about: The Poetic Edda gathers the old poems of the Norse gods and heroes preserved in an Icelandic manuscript of the thirteenth century: the Voluspa, a seeress's vision of the creation of the world and its destruction at Ragnarok; the Havamal, the sayings of Odin; the comic tale of Thor's hammer stolen by a giant; and the heroic lays of Sigurd and the Volsungs. This volume also includes the Younger Edda of Snorri Sturluson, his handbook of Norse myth and poetry.
context: The poems were once attributed to the Icelandic scholar Saemund the Learned, though this is now doubted. The translations are by Benjamin Thorpe and J. A. Blackwell. Read [The Story of the Volsungs](/book/1391?lang=en) and [Heimskringla](/book/895?lang=en).

about: Snorri Sturluson's Edda, written in Iceland around 1220, is the richest source of Norse mythology. In its first part, the 'Deluding of Gylfi', a Swedish king visits the hall of the gods in disguise and is told how the world was made from the body of the giant Ymir, about Odin, Thor, Loki, Balder and the world tree Yggdrasil, and how the world will end at Ragnarok and rise again. Other parts explain the poetic language of the skalds.
context: Snorri (1179–1241), an Icelandic chieftain, poet and historian, wrote the book as a handbook for young poets, preserving myths that might otherwise have been lost. This translation, with an introduction and notes, is by Rasmus B. Anderson. Read his [Heimskringla](/book/895?lang=en) and the [Elder Eddas](/book/13147?lang=en).

about: Snorri Sturluson's history of the kings of Norway begins with the legendary Ynglings, descended from the god Odin, and continues through Harald Fairhair, who united Norway; Olaf Tryggvason and Saint Olaf, who brought Christianity; Harald Hardrada, who died invading England in 1066; and the kings of the twelfth century. Full of battles, voyages, feuds and vivid characters, it is both a history and a gallery of sagas.
context: Snorri wrote the work around 1230, and its name comes from its opening words, 'kringla heimsins', 'the circle of the world'. It became a foundation of Norway's national identity. Read Snorri's [Younger Edda](/book/16965?lang=en) and [The Story of Burnt Njal](/book/894?lang=en).

about: In Iceland around the year 1000, Njal Thorgeirsson, a wise and peaceable farmer and the greatest lawyer in the land, and his friend Gunnar of Hlidarend, a heroic warrior, try to keep the peace in a society without kings, where honour demands revenge. A quarrel between their wives begins a chain of killings that runs for decades, through Gunnar's last stand in his house and the conversion of Iceland to Christianity, until Njal's enemies burn him and his family in their home.
context: Njal's Saga, written in the late thirteenth century, is the longest and greatest of the Icelandic family sagas. This translation, of 1861, is by George Webbe Dasent. Compare [Grettir's Saga](/book/650?lang=en) and [Heimskringla](/book/895?lang=en).

about: The young knight Tristan, nephew of King Mark of Cornwall, sails to Ireland to bring back the beautiful princess Iseult as his uncle's bride. On the voyage they drink by mistake a love potion meant for Iseult and Mark, and from then on they are bound together by a love stronger than loyalty, honour or death, through secret meetings, banishment, years in the forest and Tristan's last wait, wounded, for the ship that will bring Iseult to him under white sails or black.
context: The French scholar Joseph Bédier (1864–1938) published this reconstruction of the medieval legend in 1900, piecing together the scattered twelfth-century versions into one moving story; the English translation is by the poet Hilaire Belloc. Compare Tennyson's [Idylls of the King](/book/907?lang=en).

about: Aucassin, the son of the Count of Beaucaire, cares nothing for knighthood or his father's wars, because he loves Nicolete, a beautiful captive of Saracen birth. His father imprisons her, but she escapes from her tower on a rope of knotted sheets, and the lovers' adventures take them through forests, a shipwreck and the absurd kingdom of Torelore, where the king lies in childbed and battles are fought with baked apples and cheeses, until Nicolete, disguised as a minstrel, finds her way back to him.
context: This charming French tale of the late twelfth or early thirteenth century, unique in mixing prose with passages for singing, survives in a single manuscript. This translation is by Andrew Lang. Compare [The Romance of Tristan and Iseult](/book/12722?lang=en).

about: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, the Cid, a Castilian lord, is unjustly banished by King Alfonso VI and leaves Burgos with a small band of loyal knights, his wife and daughters left behind in a monastery. Through courage and loyalty he wins battles and booty, takes Valencia from its Muslim rulers and regains the king's favour. Then his daughters are married to the cowardly Infantes of Carrión, who beat and abandon them, and the Cid seeks justice at the royal court.
context: Composed around 1200, the Poem of the Cid is the great epic of medieval Spain, based on the real Rodrigo Díaz (about 1043–1099), who served both Christian and Muslim rulers and was called al-sayyid, 'the lord', from which his title comes. This translation is by R. Selden Rose and Leonard Bacon. Compare [The Song of Roland](/book/694?lang=en) and Lane-Poole's [The Moors in Spain](/book/33426?lang=en).

about: In eighteen letters, written as if by a puzzled gentleman to a friend in the provinces, Blaise Pascal defends his friend Antoine Arnauld, who was being condemned by the Sorbonne, and turns on the Jesuits, whose casuistry, he claims, found clever excuses for almost any sin, from lying to duelling and even murder. Quoting their own writings with deadpan irony, he makes them look ridiculous, before turning to passionate attack.
context: Pascal published the letters anonymously in 1656 and 1657; they were later burned by royal order, and Voltaire wrote that the best comedies of Molière had no more wit than the first of them. This translation is by Thomas M'Crie. Read Pascal's [Pensées](/book/16334?lang=en).

about: At the glittering court of the French king Henry II in 1558, Mademoiselle de Chartres, a young heiress of perfect beauty and virtue, marries the Prince of Cleves, whom she respects but does not love. Then she falls passionately in love with the charming Duke of Nemours, who loves her in return. Determined to remain faithful, she makes a confession to her husband that no wife in fiction had made before, with tragic consequences.
context: Madame de La Fayette (1634–1693) published the novel anonymously in 1678, and it is often called the first modern novel in French, the first great novel of psychological analysis. Compare [Manon Lescaut](/book/768?lang=en) and Racine's [Phaedra](/book/2172?lang=en).

about: What is the origin of inequality among human beings, and is it authorised by natural law? Jean-Jacques Rousseau imagines natural man before society, solitary, healthy and free, moved by pity rather than pride. Then he traces how property began, when the first man fenced off a piece of land, said 'this is mine' and found people simple enough to believe him, and how society, government and laws arose to protect the rich, turning natural freedom into chains of dependence and inequality.
context: Rousseau (1712–1778) wrote the Discourse in 1754 for a prize competition of the Academy of Dijon, which did not award it the prize, and published it in 1755; it deeply influenced the French Revolution and later critics of society. Read his [The Social Contract](/book/271?lang=en).

about: Kant wrote this short book because readers found his Critique of Pure Reason too difficult. In it he explains, more simply, his central question, how metaphysics is possible as a science, and his answer: our knowledge in mathematics and natural science rests on forms that the mind itself brings to experience, space, time and the categories, so that we can know the world as it appears to us but not things as they are in themselves. He credits David Hume with waking him from his 'dogmatic slumber'.
context: Published in 1783, the Prolegomena remains the best introduction to Kant's philosophy. This edition was edited by Paul Carus. Read Kant's [Critique of Pure Reason](/book/4364?lang=en) and Hume's [Enquiry](/book/277?lang=en).

about: Written in 1850, two years after the French revolution of 1848, this short pamphlet asks what law is for. Frédéric Bastiat answers that law exists only to protect each person's life, liberty and property, and that when it is used instead to take from some and give to others, for the benefit of a class or a party, it becomes 'legal plunder'. It can be recognised, he says, whenever the law takes from some what belongs to them to give it to others to whom it does not belong.
context: Bastiat (1801–1850), a French economist and member of the National Assembly, published the pamphlet shortly before his death, and it remains a classic of classical liberal thought. Compare Proudhon's [What Is Property?](/book/663?lang=en), written from the opposite side.

about: In this unfinished essay, the Russian revolutionary Mikhail Bakunin argues that belief in God and obedience to the state are two forms of the same slavery. Religion, he says, teaches people to accept authority and to look for justice in heaven instead of on earth, and he turns Voltaire's famous saying upside down: 'if God really existed, it would be necessary to abolish him'. He defends science and reason, but warns against government even by scientists.
context: Bakunin (1814–1876), the great rival of Karl Marx in the First International and a founder of anarchism, wrote the text in 1871, and it was published by his friends in 1882, after his death. Compare Kropotkin's [The Conquest of Bread](/book/20838?lang=en) and Proudhon's [What Is Property?](/book/663?lang=en).

about: Peter Kropotkin, born a prince in 1842 and a page at the court of Tsar Alexander II, tells how he became an anarchist: his childhood on a great estate worked by serfs, his years as an army officer exploring Siberia and Manchuria, his work as a geographer, his turn to revolutionary politics, his imprisonment in the Peter and Paul Fortress in St Petersburg and his daring escape in 1876, and his long exile in Switzerland, France and England.
context: Kropotkin first published the memoirs in English in 1899, and they are among the great autobiographies of the nineteenth century. This is the edition of 1906. Read his [Mutual Aid](/book/4423?lang=en) and [The Conquest of Bread](/book/20838?lang=en).

about: In a dark, damp basement lodging house run by a greedy landlord, a group of outcasts live side by side: a thief, a ruined baron, an alcoholic actor, a prostitute, a locksmith whose wife is dying, a card-sharp. Into their bitter lives comes Luka, a gentle old pilgrim who comforts each of them with kind words and hopeful lies, and when he disappears they are left to decide whether truth or illusion is better for human beings.
context: Maxim Gorky wrote the play in 1902, and Stanislavsky's Moscow Art Theatre production made it famous across Europe; this translation, by Jenny Covan, was made for that company's American tour. Read Gorky's [Mother](/book/3872?lang=en) and Chekhov's last [plays](/book/7966?lang=en).

about: Under the pen name Democritus Junior, Robert Burton sets out to analyse every kind of melancholy, its causes, symptoms and cures, from bad diet, idleness, solitude, too much study and love to religious despair. Quoting hundreds of classical, medieval and modern authors, he wanders through medicine, philosophy, theology, astrology and anecdote, with digressions on the air, on spirits and on an ideal commonwealth, in one of the strangest and richest books in English.
context: Burton (1577–1640), a scholar of Christ Church, Oxford, who suffered from melancholy himself, first published the book in 1621 and kept enlarging it for the rest of his life. Samuel Johnson said it was the only book that ever took him out of bed two hours sooner than he wished to rise. Compare Browne's [Religio Medici](/book/883?lang=en).

about: In Religio Medici, 'the religion of a doctor', Thomas Browne, a physician in Norwich, explains with charm and candour how a man of science can also be a Christian: he loves mysteries, tolerates other faiths and finds God in nature as much as in scripture. Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, begins with some ancient burial urns dug up in a field in Norfolk and becomes a magnificent meditation on death, oblivion and human vanity.
context: Browne (1605–1682) wrote Religio Medici around 1635, and it was printed without his permission in 1642; Urn Burial followed in 1658. His rich, musical prose has been admired by writers from Coleridge to Borges. Compare Burton's [The Anatomy of Melancholy](/book/9904?lang=en).

about: Three friends, a fisherman, a hunter and a falconer, walk out of London along the river Lea on a fine May morning, and the fisherman, Piscator, spends five days teaching the hunter, Venator, the art of angling. Between instructions on catching trout, pike, carp and eels, on baits and on recipes for cooking them, they stop at country inns, sing songs, recite poems, meet milkmaids and praise the quiet, contemplative life.
context: Izaak Walton (1593–1683), a London ironmonger, published the book in 1653, during the Civil War, and it became one of the most reprinted books in English; his friend Charles Cotton later added a part on fly-fishing. Compare Thoreau's [A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers](/book/4317?lang=en).

about: John Bunyan tells the story of his spiritual struggles: his youth as a swearing village tinker who loved bell-ringing, dancing and games on the green; his conversion; and then years of terrible doubt and despair, in which he heard voices tempting him to 'sell Christ' and believed himself damned, until at last he found peace in God's grace. He ends with his calling as a preacher and his imprisonment for preaching without a licence.
context: Bunyan published the book in 1666, while in Bedford jail, twelve years before [The Pilgrim's Progress](/book/481?lang=en), and it is one of the great spiritual autobiographies in English. This edition has illustrations by Harold Copping.

about: In the London underworld, Peachum, a receiver of stolen goods who makes his living by selling his own associates to the gallows for the reward, is horrified to learn that his daughter Polly has married the dashing highwayman Macheath. He decides to betray him, while Macheath, also promised to Lucy, the daughter of the jailer of Newgate, is caught between two wives. The play mixes witty dialogue with popular tunes and mocks the politicians of the day as no better than thieves.
context: John Gay (1685–1732) staged the ballad opera in 1728, and it was the greatest theatrical success of its century; two hundred years later Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill turned it into The Threepenny Opera. Compare Fielding's [Jonathan Wild](/book/5307?lang=en).

about: In the autumn of 1773, James Boswell, a young Scottish lawyer, persuaded Samuel Johnson, then sixty-four and famous for his Dictionary, to travel with him through the Highlands and the Western Isles of Scotland. For about three months they rode, sailed and walked through rain and storms to Skye, Raasay, Coll, Mull and Iona, staying with lairds and ministers and meeting Flora MacDonald, who had helped Bonnie Prince Charlie escape. Boswell records everything Johnson said, his opinions, jokes, quarrels and kindnesses.
context: Boswell published the journal in 1785, a year after Johnson's death, as a first trial of the method he perfected in his great Life of Johnson six years later. Johnson wrote his own account, A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland. Read Johnson's [Rasselas](/book/941?lang=en).

about: In this strange, brilliant little book of prose and verse, William Blake turns conventional morality upside down. Heaven, he says, is passive reason and obedience, Hell is active energy and desire, and both are needed: 'Without Contraries is no progression.' It contains the 'Proverbs of Hell', such as 'The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom', visions of a printing house in Hell, and the famous claim that Milton was 'of the Devil's party without knowing it'.
context: Blake engraved and coloured the book himself around 1790 to 1793, partly as a reply to the mystic Emanuel Swedenborg. Its line 'If the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite' gave Aldous Huxley the title of his book The Doors of Perception, and the rock band The Doors their name. Read Blake's [Songs of Innocence and of Experience](/book/2131?lang=en).

about: Samuel Taylor Coleridge calls this book 'biographical sketches of my literary life and opinions'. He tells of his schooldays and early poetry, his journalism and his years in Germany studying philosophy, and sets out his ideas on the imagination, which he distinguishes from mere fancy as the power that creates and unifies. He explains how he and Wordsworth planned the Lyrical Ballads, coining the famous phrase 'that willing suspension of disbelief', and then examines, with great admiration and some disagreement, Wordsworth's poetry and his theory of poetic language.
context: Published in 1817, the Biographia is disorderly and partly borrowed from German philosophers, but it is one of the founding works of English literary criticism. Read [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en) and Coleridge's [The Rime of the Ancient Mariner](/book/494?lang=en).

about: Twenty of Shakespeare's plays are retold here as stories in simple, graceful prose for young readers, from The Tempest, A Midsummer Night's Dream and Twelfth Night to King Lear, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and Othello. The authors keep as much of Shakespeare's own language as they can, so that children can meet his characters and stories before they read the plays themselves.
context: Charles Lamb wrote the tragedies and his sister Mary Lamb the comedies, though only Charles's name appeared on the title page of the first edition in 1807. Mary had killed their mother in a fit of madness in 1796, and Charles cared for her for the rest of his life. The book has never been out of print. Read Shakespeare's [Hamlet](/book/1?lang=en), [King Lear](/book/5?lang=en) and [The Tempest](/book/7?lang=en).

about: Is poetry useless in an age of science and industry? Percy Bysshe Shelley answers his friend Thomas Love Peacock, who had playfully argued that poetry was a relic of barbarous times, with a passionate defence. Poetry, he says, is the expression of the imagination; it awakens and enlarges the mind, teaches us to put ourselves in the place of others, which is the root of morality, and lies behind every great change in society. He ends with his famous claim that 'poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world'.
context: Shelley wrote the Defence in 1821, a year before he drowned in Italy, and it was published only in 1840. This volume also contains some of his other essays. Compare Coleridge's [Biographia Literaria](/book/6116?lang=en) and Wordsworth's preface to [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en).

about: A young Englishman, Guy Mannering, lodging one night at Ellangowan in south-west Scotland, casts the horoscope of the laird's newborn son, Harry Bertram, and finds danger ahead. At five the boy disappears, kidnapped by smugglers, and the family is ruined. Years later a young officer, Captain Brown, returns from India, unaware of his origins, and with the help of the old gypsy Meg Merrilies, the learned and simple Dominie Sampson and the farmer Dandie Dinmont, the lost heir is restored.
context: Walter Scott published the novel in 1815, the year after [Waverley](/book/2224?lang=en), and it was an immediate success; the Dandie Dinmont terrier is named after its farmer. Read Scott's [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en).

about: Darsie Latimer, a young man of mysterious birth, and his friend Alan Fairford, an Edinburgh law student, write letters to each other until Darsie disappears near the Solway Firth on the border of Scotland and England. Alan follows him and finds that he has been kidnapped by his uncle, Hugh Redgauntlet, a fanatical Jacobite who is plotting, around 1765, one last rising for Prince Charles Edward Stuart, long after the cause was lost.
context: Walter Scott published the novel in 1824, his last great novel about the Jacobites. It contains 'Wandering Willie's Tale', a story told by a blind fiddler about a journey to Hell to recover a receipt from a dead laird, which is often called one of the finest short stories in English. Read Scott's [Waverley](/book/2224?lang=en) and [Guy Mannering](/book/2736?lang=en).

about: Macaulay imagined what the lost ballads of early Rome might have sounded like and wrote four of them: 'Horatius', in which three Romans hold the bridge over the Tiber against the Etruscan army while it is cut down behind them; 'The Battle of the Lake Regillus', where the twin gods Castor and Pollux fight for Rome; 'Virginia', the story of a father who kills his daughter to save her from a tyrant; and 'The Prophecy of Capys', on the future greatness of Rome.
context: Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800–1859), the historian and politician, published the poems in 1842, and generations of British schoolchildren learned 'Horatius' by heart, with its lines 'And how can man die better / Than facing fearful odds'. Compare Livy's stories of early Rome and Virgil's [Aeneid](/book/541?lang=en).

about: Two sisters, Laura and Lizzie, hear the goblin men crying their fruits in the glen each evening: 'Come buy, come buy.' Laura pays with a lock of her golden hair, eats the fruit, and begins to waste away with longing for more, until Lizzie goes to the goblins herself, endures their attack without tasting, and saves her. This volume collects 'Goblin Market' with 'The Prince's Progress' and many other poems of love, loss, faith and death.
context: Christina Rossetti (1830–1894), the sister of the painter and poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti, published Goblin Market in 1862, and readers still debate its meaning, whether as fairy tale, religious allegory or poem about temptation and desire. Compare Tennyson's [Idylls of the King](/book/907?lang=en) and Blake's [Songs of Innocence and of Experience](/book/2131?lang=en).

about: Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote poems unlike any others of his time, praising God in the beauty of the world in packed, musical language and a new 'sprung rhythm' based on stresses rather than syllables: 'The Windhover', 'Pied Beauty' ('Glory be to God for dappled things'), 'God's Grandeur', 'Spring and Fall', the long ode 'The Wreck of the Deutschland', and the dark 'terrible sonnets' of his last years in Dublin.
context: Hopkins (1844–1889), a Jesuit priest, published almost nothing in his lifetime. His friend Robert Bridges, the Poet Laureate, edited this first collection in 1918, almost thirty years after his death, and it made Hopkins one of the most influential poets of the twentieth century. Compare [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en).

about: There was an Old Man with a beard, who said, 'It is just as I feared!' So begins one of the verses in one of the most famous books of comic verse in English: limerick after limerick about absurd old men and young ladies from places all over the world, who are swallowed by fish, carried off by birds, dance with cats or grow birds' nests in their beards, each with a funny drawing by the author.
context: Edward Lear (1812–1888), a painter of birds and landscapes, wrote the verses for the grandchildren of the Earl of Derby and published them in 1846, popularising the limerick form. He later wrote 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat'. Compare Lewis Carroll's nonsense in [Alice's Adventures in Wonderland](/book/189?lang=en).

about: In the city of Pompeii in AD 79, the young Athenian Glaucus loves the beautiful Ione, a Greek woman of Naples, but the sinister Arbaces, an Egyptian priest of Isis, wants her for himself and plots to destroy Glaucus. Nydia, a blind flower girl who secretly loves Glaucus, is caught up in the intrigue. Then, as Glaucus is about to be thrown to a lion in the amphitheatre, Mount Vesuvius erupts, and in the darkness only the blind girl can find the way to the sea.
context: Edward Bulwer-Lytton (1803–1873) wrote the novel in 1834 after visiting the excavations and seeing Karl Bryullov's painting The Last Day of Pompeii in Milan, and it became one of the most popular historical novels of the century. Compare Kingsley's [Hypatia](/book/6341?lang=en).

about: In the Netherlands of the fifteenth century, Gerard, a young scribe and illuminator meant by his family for the Church, falls in love with Margaret, the daughter of a poor scholar. Separated from her by his family's plots, he travels on foot through Germany, Burgundy and Italy, meeting thieves, soldiers, inns, plague and the Renaissance in Rome, while Margaret, pregnant, waits for him. Deceived into believing that she is dead, he becomes a friar, and when he returns, their love must live between the cloister and the hearth.
context: Charles Reade (1814–1884) published the novel in 1861, imagining the parents of the great humanist Erasmus, who is their child in the story, and it was long ranked among the finest historical novels in English. Compare George Eliot's [Romola](/book/21341?lang=en).

about: Mark Robarts, the young vicar of Framley, owes his good living to the formidable Lady Lufton, but he is flattered into the company of a fashionable set and signs bills for a charming, penniless member of Parliament, Mr Sowerby, which soon threaten him with ruin. Meanwhile his sister Lucy and Lady Lufton's son, Lord Lufton, fall in love, though Lady Lufton has chosen a grander bride for him, and Lucy proudly refuses to marry without his mother's consent.
context: The fourth of Anthony Trollope's six Barsetshire novels, Framley Parsonage was serialised in the new Cornhill Magazine in 1860 and 1861 and made him a famous novelist. Read [The Warden](/book/916?lang=en), [Barchester Towers](/book/2583?lang=en) and [Doctor Thorne](/book/3292?lang=en).

about: Frank Gresham, heir to the old estate of Greshamsbury, which his father has burdened with debts, is told by his family that he must marry money. But he loves Mary Thorne, the penniless niece of the village doctor, whose birth is a family secret. Doctor Thorne alone knows that Mary is also related to Sir Roger Scatcherd, a former stonemason turned rich railway contractor, who is drinking himself to death and whose fortune may decide everyone's future.
context: Published in 1858, the third of Anthony Trollope's Barsetshire novels, Doctor Thorne was the most popular of his books in his lifetime, and it still pleases readers with its gentle comedy about money, class and love. Read [Barchester Towers](/book/2583?lang=en) and [Framley Parsonage](/book/2991?lang=en).

about: The Reverend Josiah Crawley, the proud, learned and desperately poor curate of Hogglestock, is accused of stealing a cheque for twenty pounds and cannot explain how he came by it. While the scandal divides the county and the bishop's domineering wife, Mrs Proudie, pursues him, his daughter Grace refuses to marry the man she loves, Major Grantly, until her father's name is cleared. Around them, Trollope brings the stories of Barsetshire's clergy and families to a close.
context: Published in 1867, the last of the six Barsetshire novels, The Last Chronicle of Barset was the one Trollope himself thought his best, and it includes the death of Mrs Proudie and of the gentle Mr Harding, the hero of [The Warden](/book/916?lang=en). Read [Doctor Thorne](/book/3292?lang=en).

about: Phineas Finn, the handsome, likeable son of an Irish country doctor, is elected to Parliament at twenty-five and goes to London, where he must make his way in politics and society without money. Helped by influential women, the clever Lady Laura Standish, the spirited heiress Violet Effingham and the mysterious widow Madame Max Goesler, he rises in office, until his conscience forces him to choose between his career and his principles on the question of Irish tenant rights.
context: Published in 1869, the second of Anthony Trollope's six Palliser novels, it offers a lively, realistic picture of Victorian politics, which Trollope knew well, having stood for Parliament himself and lost. Read his [The Last Chronicle of Barset](/book/3171?lang=en).

about: In the London literary world of the 1880s, Edwin Reardon, a sensitive novelist of real talent, can no longer write, and poverty slowly destroys his marriage to the ambitious Amy. His friend Jasper Milvain, a cheerful, cynical journalist, writes whatever sells and rises steadily. Around them struggle the bitter scholar Alfred Yule, his daughter Marian, who loves Jasper, and Harold Biffen, who starves while writing a realistic novel called 'Mr Bailey, Grocer'.
context: George Gissing (1857–1903), who knew poverty himself, published the novel in 1891, and it remains one of the most honest books ever written about the business of writing. The title comes from Grub Street, the old London street of hack writers. Compare Dickens's [David Copperfield](/book/32?lang=en).

about: Esther Waters, a plain, honest girl from a strict religious family, goes into service at Woodview, a country house whose owners live for horse-racing. Seduced by William, a footman, and abandoned when she becomes pregnant, she is dismissed and goes to London, where she fights through workhouses, hard jobs as a wet nurse and servant, and the scorn of employers to raise her son. When William returns, now a publican and bookmaker, she must choose her life again.
context: George Moore (1852–1933), an Irish novelist influenced by Zola, published the novel in 1894, and its sympathetic, realistic portrait of a servant and unmarried mother was banned by some libraries but praised by Gladstone. Compare Hardy's [Tess of the d'Urbervilles](/book/306?lang=en).

about: Adam Weir, Lord Hermiston, the harsh, coarse and powerful 'hanging judge' of Edinburgh, despises his gentle son Archie. When Archie publicly protests against the hanging of a man his father condemned, he is sent away to the family's lonely estate at Hermiston in the hills, where he falls in love with Christina Elliott, the niece of his housekeeper. But the arrival of the treacherous Frank Innes threatens them, and the story moves towards a confrontation between father and son.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson was writing the novel in Samoa when he died suddenly in 1894, and it breaks off in mid-sentence; many critics think it would have been his masterpiece. The judge was modelled on the real Lord Braxfield. Read Stevenson's [The Master of Ballantrae](/book/1135?lang=en) and [Kidnapped](/book/187?lang=en).

about: On the beach at Papeete, in Tahiti, three ruined men are starving: Herrick, an Oxford graduate who has failed at everything; Davis, an American captain who lost his ship while drunk; and Huish, a vicious London clerk. Given command of a schooner whose captain has died of smallpox, they plan to steal it with its cargo of champagne, but the cargo is not what it seems, and they come to an unknown island ruled by Attwater, a pearl fisher, a religious fanatic and a deadly shot.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the novella with his stepson Lloyd Osbourne in Samoa, and it was published in 1894, the year of his death. It is one of his darkest stories, about the moral collapse of men far from home. Read Stevenson's [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en) and Conrad's [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en).

about: At a boys' boarding school on the coast of Devon, which trains boys for the army, three friends, the cunning Stalky, the Irish M'Turk and the bookish, bespectacled Beetle, fight a long war of wits against the masters, the prefects and the bullies. They trap a rival house with a dead cat, avenge themselves on a hated master, punish two bullies by bullying them, and learn the lessons of loyalty and leadership that will later serve them on the frontiers of the Empire.
context: Rudyard Kipling published the stories in 1899, based on his own years at the United Services College at Westward Ho!; Beetle is Kipling himself, and Stalky was modelled on his friend Lionel Dunsterville, later a general. Read Kipling's [Kim](/book/356?lang=en) and [The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en).

about: Old Mrs Rabbit warns her four children not to go into Mr McGregor's garden. Flopsy, Mopsy and Cottontail obey and pick blackberries, but naughty Peter squeezes under the gate, eats lettuces, beans and radishes, and is chased by Mr McGregor himself. He loses his shoes and his new blue jacket with brass buttons, hides in a watering can and finally escapes home, where he is put to bed with camomile tea while his sisters have bread, milk and blackberries for supper.
context: Beatrix Potter (1866–1943) first told the story in a picture letter to a sick child in 1893 and published it in 1902; it became one of the best-selling children's books of all time. This early American edition has illustrations by Virginia Albert instead of Potter's own pictures. Read [The Wind in the Willows](/book/595?lang=en).

about: In a village near Antwerp, Nello, a poor orphan boy, lives with his old grandfather and Patrasche, a big Flemish working dog that they rescued when it was beaten and left to die by a cruel master. Every day the boy and the dog pull a cart of milk cans to the city. Nello dreams of becoming a painter and of seeing the great paintings by Rubens in Antwerp Cathedral, but poverty, injustice and a hard winter bring the story to a heartbreaking end on Christmas Eve.
context: Ouida, the pen name of the English novelist Maria Louise Ramé (1839–1908), published the story in 1872. It has been filmed many times and is especially loved in Japan, where an animated series made it famous. Compare Anna Sewell's [Black Beauty](/book/577?lang=en).

about: Writing as 'Farmer James', a settler in Pennsylvania, Crèvecœur describes life in the American colonies in twelve letters to an English friend: the farmer's work and his family, the whalers of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard, the wildlife of the woods and the bees in his garden. He asks the famous question, 'What then is the American, this new man?', and answers that here people of all nations are melted into a new race. But he also describes the horror of slavery in Charleston, and in the last letter the farmer is torn apart by the Revolution.
context: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur (1735–1813), a French-born soldier and farmer who settled in New York, published the book in London in 1782, and it is one of the first works to define the American identity. Compare Franklin's [Autobiography](/book/18052?lang=en).

about: In 1809, newspapers in New York printed notices about an elderly gentleman, Diedrich Knickerbocker, who had disappeared from his hotel, leaving behind a strange manuscript. Soon the manuscript appeared: a comic history of New York from the creation of the world to the end of Dutch rule, with its pompous Dutch governors, the sleepy Wouter Van Twiller, William the Testy and the fiery, one-legged Peter Stuyvesant, who finally surrendered New Amsterdam to the English in 1664.
context: The whole affair was a hoax by the young Washington Irving, and the book was the first great work of American comic literature; 'Knickerbocker' became a nickname for New Yorkers, and the New York Knicks basketball team takes its name from it. Read Irving's [Rip Van Winkle](/book/55419?lang=en) and [The Alhambra](/book/45043?lang=en).

about: In 1834, Richard Henry Dana, a Harvard student whose eyesight had been weakened by measles, left his studies and signed on as a common sailor on the brig Pilgrim, bound around Cape Horn for California, then a remote province of Mexico. He describes the hard, dangerous life of the forecastle, storms and icebergs off the Horn, a cruel captain who flogs two of the crew, and months spent collecting and curing cattle hides along the Californian coast, before he returns home on the ship Alert.
context: Published in 1840, the book was a great success and gave a true picture of the sailor's life; Dana became a lawyer who defended sailors and escaped slaves, and Melville admired the book. Read Melville's [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en) and [Typee](/book/143?lang=en).

about: In 1839, Henry David Thoreau and his brother John spent two weeks travelling by boat on the Concord and Merrimack rivers in Massachusetts and New Hampshire. Thoreau shapes the journey into a book of seven days, one for each day of the week, mixing scenes of the rivers, the fish and the farms along the banks with long reflections on friendship, religion, poetry, history and the Hindu scriptures.
context: John died of tetanus in 1842, and the book, published in 1849, is partly a memorial to him. It sold so badly that the publisher returned the unsold copies, and Thoreau joked that he owned a library of nearly nine hundred volumes, over seven hundred of which he had written himself. Read [Walden](/book/287?lang=en) and Walton's [The Compleat Angler](/book/972?lang=en).

about: What is a great man, and what use is he to the rest of us? In seven lectures, Ralph Waldo Emerson answers through six figures, each the representative of a kind of mind: Plato the philosopher, Swedenborg the mystic, Montaigne the sceptic, Shakespeare the poet, Napoleon the man of the world and Goethe the writer. Great men, he argues, do not rule us; they show us what we ourselves are capable of.
context: Emerson gave the lectures in the 1840s in England and America and published them in 1850, as a democratic answer to his friend Thomas Carlyle's [On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History](/book/1340?lang=en). Read Emerson's [Essays: First Series](/book/286?lang=en).

about: Mark Twain sets out on a walking tour of Europe with his friend 'Harris' and mostly avoids walking, taking trains, carriages and rafts instead. In Germany he watches students duel in Heidelberg and floats down the Neckar on a raft; in Switzerland he climbs the Riffelberg with a huge expedition of guides and mules; and along the way he tells tall tales, such as the story of the blue jay who tries to fill a house with acorns, and adds the famous essay 'The Awful German Language'.
context: Twain published the book in 1880, after a trip of 1878 with his friend Joseph Twichell. This edition reproduces the engravings of the first edition. Read Twain's [The Innocents Abroad](/book/52?lang=en) and [Roughing It](/book/3302?lang=en).

about: Tom Sawyer, Huckleberry Finn and Jim climb into the basket of a strange balloon at a fair in St Louis, and when its inventor, a mad professor, takes off, they are carried across the Atlantic. After he falls overboard, they fly on alone over the Sahara, where they see a caravan, a lion hunt and a mirage, and land on the Sphinx and the pyramids of Egypt, while Tom and Huck argue about geography, the Crusades and the size of the world.
context: Mark Twain published the short novel in 1894, narrated, like [Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](/book/49?lang=en), by Huck himself. Compare Jules Verne's [Five Weeks in a Balloon](/book/126?lang=en) and read [The Adventures of Tom Sawyer](/book/48?lang=en).

about: Ambrose Bierce fought for the North in the American Civil War, and his stories of soldiers are among the most terrible and powerful war stories ever written: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge', in which a man about to be hanged imagines his escape; 'Chickamauga', in which a deaf child plays among the dying; and 'One of the Missing'. His stories of civilians are tales of horror and the supernatural, often with a cruel twist at the end.
context: The stories were first collected in 1891 as Tales of Soldiers and Civilians, and this is the second volume of Bierce's Collected Works, published in 1909. Bierce disappeared in Mexico during the revolution, around 1914. Read his [The Devil's Dictionary](/book/1233?lang=en) and Crane's [The Red Badge of Courage](/book/442?lang=en).

about: A woman writer comes to spend a summer in Dunnet Landing, a small fishing town on the coast of Maine, lodging with Mrs Almira Todd, a widow who gathers herbs and makes remedies. As the summer passes, she meets the people of the town and the islands: Mrs Todd's old mother and her shy brother William on Green Island; old Captain Littlepage, with his tale of a ghostly town near the North Pole; and the memory of Joanna, who lived alone on an island after a broken heart.
context: Sarah Orne Jewett (1849–1909) published the book in 1896. Its quiet, tender portrait of a fading community moved Willa Cather to rank it, with The Scarlet Letter and Huckleberry Finn, among the American books most likely to last. Read [The Scarlet Letter](/book/411?lang=en).

about: These stories show the hard lives of farmers in the American Midwest, on the prairies of Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota, at the end of the nineteenth century: endless work, mortgages, failing harvests, land speculators who raise the rent on improvements a tenant has made himself, and wives worn out before their time. In 'The Return of a Private' a soldier comes home from the Civil War; in 'Up the Coulé' a successful actor visits the brother he left behind on the farm.
context: Hamlin Garland (1860–1940), who grew up on Midwestern farms himself, published the book in 1891, and its honest realism helped end the sentimental picture of country life. Compare Willa Cather's [O Pioneers!](/book/404?lang=en).

about: Jack London calls this his 'alcoholic memoirs'. He tells how John Barleycorn, the personification of alcohol, first got hold of him when he was five and drank beer he was carrying to his father, and how drink became part of his life as an oyster pirate on San Francisco Bay, a sailor, a tramp and finally a famous writer. He describes the 'White Logic', the cold, despairing truth that alcohol shows him, and argues for prohibition so that young men will not be tempted.
context: London published the book in 1913, three years before his death at forty, and it was used by the campaigners who brought Prohibition to the United States in 1920. Read London's [Martin Eden](/book/312?lang=en) and [The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en).

about: A modern man has dreamed since childhood of another life, and he comes to understand that he is remembering, through 'racial memory', the life of his remote ancestor, Big-Tooth, a creature of the Stone Age half way between ape and man. In his dreams he lives among the Cave People in the forest, with his friend Lop-Ear and the girl Swift One, fleeing from the terrible Red-Eye and from the more advanced Fire People, who have bows and arrows.
context: Jack London published the novel in 1907, inspired by the new science of evolution, and it influenced later stories of prehistoric life. Read London's [The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en) and Wells's [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en).

about: J. Arnold Ross, a self-made oil man, drills for oil across Southern California, buying land, officials and politicians, while his son Bunny, who grows up beside him in the oil fields, falls under the influence of the poor, rebellious Paul Watkins and begins to sympathise with the striking workers and the socialists. Between them stand Paul's brother Eli, a greedy evangelist, film stars, college radicals and the oil scandals that reached the White House in the 1920s.
context: Upton Sinclair based the novel on the real Teapot Dome scandal and published it in 1927; it was banned in Boston, and Sinclair protested by selling a 'fig leaf edition'. The film There Will Be Blood (2007) was loosely based on it. Read Sinclair's [The Jungle](/book/486?lang=en).

about: George Darrow, an American diplomat in London, is on his way to France to join Anna Leath, the widow he loved in his youth and now hopes to marry, when a telegram tells him to wait. Hurt, he spends a few days in Paris with Sophy Viner, a poor and lively young woman he meets on the journey. Months later, at Anna's château at Givré, he finds Sophy there as the governess, engaged to Anna's stepson, and the past rises between them all.
context: Edith Wharton published the novel in 1912, and Henry James praised its intense, almost classical concentration, comparing it to the tragedy of Racine. Read Wharton's [The House of Mirth](/book/590?lang=en) and [The Age of Innocence](/book/840?lang=en).

about: This collection contains Claude McKay's poems of the Harlem streets and of his lost Jamaican home: 'The Harlem Dancer', 'The Tropics in New York', with its memories of fruits that bring tears to his eyes, poems of love and loneliness, and fierce sonnets against racism and lynching, such as 'America' and 'If We Must Die', written in 1919 after the anti-Black riots of the 'Red Summer': 'If we must die, O let us nobly die'.
context: McKay (1889–1948), born in Jamaica, published the book in 1922 with an introduction by Max Eastman, and it is often seen as one of the works that began the Harlem Renaissance. Read Langston Hughes's [The Weary Blues](/book/68231?lang=en) and Jean Toomer's [Cane](/book/54587?lang=en).

about: Countee Cullen was a student at New York University when he published this first book of poems, which made him famous at twenty-two. It includes 'Heritage', which begins 'What is Africa to me?'; 'Yet Do I Marvel', which ends with the lines 'Yet do I marvel at this curious thing: / To make a poet black, and bid him sing!'; and 'Incident', a short, painful memory of a racial insult in Baltimore, alongside poems of love, faith and death in traditional forms.
context: Cullen (1903–1946) was one of the leading poets of the Harlem Renaissance, and Color, published in 1925, was among its most praised books. Read Claude McKay's [Harlem Shadows](/book/59236?lang=en) and Langston Hughes's [The Weary Blues](/book/68231?lang=en).

about: In 1685, Peter Blood, an Irish doctor living quietly in Somerset, is arrested for treating a wounded rebel after the failed rising of the Duke of Monmouth, condemned by the brutal Judge Jeffreys and sold as a slave in Barbados. Bought by a cruel planter, Colonel Bishop, he wins the sympathy of the colonel's niece Arabella. When Spanish raiders attack the island, Blood and his fellow convicts seize their ship and sail away to become the most feared and honourable pirates of the Caribbean.
context: Rafael Sabatini (1875–1950) published the novel in 1922, and the 1935 film made a star of Errol Flynn. Read Sabatini's [Scaramouche](/book/2143?lang=en) and Stevenson's [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en).

about: 'He was born with a gift of laughter and a sense that the world was mad.' André-Louis Moreau, a young lawyer in Brittany with no faith in anything, swears revenge when his idealistic friend is killed in a duel by the arrogant Marquis de La Tour d'Azyr, just before the French Revolution. Hunted for his fiery speeches, he hides with a troupe of travelling actors and becomes famous as Scaramouche, the clown, then a fencing master and a deputy in the revolutionary Assembly.
context: Rafael Sabatini published the novel in 1921, and its first sentence is one of the best known in popular fiction. Read his [Captain Blood](/book/2160?lang=en) and Dickens's [A Tale of Two Cities](/book/30?lang=en).

about: One night at the Château du Glandier near Paris, cries and shots are heard from the locked room where Mathilde Stangerson, the daughter of a famous scientist, is sleeping. When the door is broken down, she is found badly injured, but the attacker has vanished from a room with no way out. The great detective Frédéric Larsan takes on the case, and so does Joseph Rouletabille, an eighteen-year-old newspaper reporter who trusts in 'the right end of reason'.
context: Gaston Leroux (1868–1927), later the author of [The Phantom of the Opera](/book/512?lang=en), published the novel in 1907–1908, and it is one of the most famous 'locked-room' mysteries; Agatha Christie and John Dickson Carr admired it. Compare Conan Doyle's [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en).

about: One September at the start of the twentieth century, Carruthers, a bored young official of the Foreign Office, accepts an invitation from Davies, an old acquaintance, to join him for some duck shooting on his small yacht in the Baltic. He finds a tiny, uncomfortable boat, and Davies takes him to the sands and channels among the Frisian Islands off the German coast, where they slowly uncover a secret German plan to invade England.
context: Erskine Childers (1870–1922) published the novel in 1903 as a warning that Britain was unprepared, and it is often called the first modern spy novel. Childers later fought for Irish independence and was executed in 1922 during the Irish Civil War. Compare Buchan's [The Thirty-Nine Steps](/book/857?lang=en).

about: Sigsbee Manderson, an American millionaire of enormous power, is found shot dead in the grounds of his English country house. Philip Trent, a painter and amateur detective, is sent by a newspaper to investigate, and he builds a brilliant chain of deductions. But he also falls in love with the dead man's young widow, Mabel, and finds that his clever solution may not be the whole truth.
context: E. C. Bentley (1875–1956), a journalist and friend of G. K. Chesterton, to whom the book is dedicated, published it in 1913 as a gentle mockery of the infallible detective, and it is often called the first modern detective novel. Compare Conan Doyle's [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en) and Christie's [The Murder of Roger Ackroyd](/book/63067?lang=en).

about: Antony Gillingham, a young man of private means, arrives at the Red House to visit his friend Bill Beverley just after a shot is heard. Robert Ablett, the black sheep brother of the owner, back from Australia after fifteen years, lies dead in a locked office, and the owner, Mark Ablett, has disappeared. With the cheerful Bill as his Watson, Antony begins to investigate the house, its secret passage and its guests.
context: A. A. Milne (1882–1956), the author of Winnie-the-Pooh, published his only detective novel in 1922, and it was very popular in the golden age of detective fiction, though Raymond Chandler later mocked its plot. Compare Bentley's [Trent's Last Case](/book/2714?lang=en).

about: Henry Fielding tells the life of Jonathan Wild, a real London criminal hanged in 1725, who controlled a gang of thieves while posing as a 'thief-taker' who caught them for rewards. With savage irony, Fielding treats him as a 'great man' in the manner of conquerors and statesmen, and sets his career of robbery, betrayal and murder against the sufferings of Heartfree, a good, simple jeweller whom Wild ruins.
context: Fielding published the book in 1743, and its real target was the 'great man' of British politics, the prime minister Robert Walpole. Compare Gay's [The Beggar's Opera](/book/2572?lang=en), which also used Wild, and Fielding's [Tom Jones](/book/6598?lang=en).

about: Abandoned with five children by her foolish husband, a beautiful young Frenchwoman in London decides to live by her beauty. She becomes the mistress of a rich jeweller, then of a prince in Paris, and amasses a great fortune; at a masked ball in London, dancing in Turkish dress, she is given the name Roxana. Years later, married and respectable, she is pursued by Susan, one of the daughters she abandoned, and her faithful maid Amy takes a terrible step to protect her secret.
context: Roxana, published in 1724, was Daniel Defoe's last novel and his darkest, a study of guilt and of a woman who chooses independence over marriage. This edition has both parts. Read Defoe's [Moll Flanders](/book/301?lang=en) and [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en).

about: Fleeing his creditors and the law with his wife, Pierre de La Motte is given charge of a beautiful, frightened girl, Adeline, by a stranger who threatens to kill her. They take refuge in a ruined abbey deep in a forest in the south of France, where Adeline finds a hidden room, a rusty dagger and the manuscript of a prisoner who was murdered there. Then the powerful Marquis de Montalt appears, and his interest in Adeline places her in great danger.
context: Ann Radcliffe (1764–1823) published the novel in 1791, and it was her first great success, followed by [The Mysteries of Udolpho](/book/3390?lang=en). It helped to establish the Gothic novel of mystery and suspense. Compare Walpole's [The Castle of Otranto](/book/983?lang=en).

about: Pierre Glendinning, a rich, idealistic young man in the country of upstate New York, lives happily with his proud mother and is engaged to the gentle Lucy Tartan. Then he meets Isabel, a dark, mysterious young woman who claims to be his father's illegitimate daughter. To protect her and his father's memory, Pierre pretends to marry her, loses his inheritance and goes to New York City to live by his writing, with tragic results.
context: Herman Melville published the novel in 1852, after Moby-Dick, and it was a disaster: one newspaper headline read 'Herman Melville Crazy'. Modern readers find in it a strange, daring study of idealism, family secrets and the life of a writer. Read Melville's [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en) and [Typee](/book/143?lang=en).

about: This single volume gathers everything Shakespeare is known to have written: all the comedies, histories and tragedies, from The Comedy of Errors to The Tempest, including Pericles and The Two Noble Kinsmen, which were left out of the First Folio, together with the 154 Sonnets and the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece. In one place the reader can follow a phrase, a character type or an idea across the whole of his career, from the farces and chronicle plays of his twenties to the great tragedies and the late romances.
context: William Shakespeare (1564–1616), an actor and shareholder in the Globe Theatre, wrote for a popular stage, and his works have been translated into every major language, including Arabic, where Khalil Mutran's versions of Othello and Hamlet were landmarks. This collection is in modern spelling. The library also has each play on its own, such as [Hamlet](/book/1?lang=en), and the [Sonnets](/book/11?lang=en).

about: The King James Version, also called the Authorized Version, is the English translation of the Bible made by some fifty scholars at the command of King James I and published in 1611. It contains the books of the Old Testament, from the creation in Genesis, the stories of Abraham, Joseph, Moses, David and Solomon, the Psalms and the prophets, and the New Testament, with the four Gospels of the life of Jesus, the Acts of the Apostles, the letters of Paul and the Book of Revelation. Many of its figures, Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses and Mary among them, are also honoured in the Qur'an.
context: Its translators built on the earlier work of William Tyndale, and its rhythmic prose shaped the English language for centuries; phrases such as 'the salt of the earth', 'a labour of love' and 'the powers that be' come from it. Writers from Bunyan and Milton to Lincoln drew on it; see [The Pilgrim's Progress](/book/481?lang=en) and [Paradise Lost](/book/297?lang=en).

about: Michel de Montaigne retired to the tower library of his château near Bordeaux in 1571 and began to write short pieces he called essais, 'attempts', and in doing so invented the essay. In 107 chapters he writes on everything: friendship, inspired by his dead friend Étienne de La Boétie; the education of children; solitude, idleness, cruelty and repentance; the native peoples of Brazil, who, he suggests, are less barbarous than the Europeans who call them savages; and, above all, himself, his habits, illnesses and changing moods, asking always 'What do I know?'
context: The Essays appeared between 1580 and 1588, and they influenced Shakespeare, whose Tempest borrows from the essay on cannibals, as well as Bacon, Pascal and Emerson. This complete edition gives Charles Cotton's lively translation of 1685–86, revised by William Carew Hazlitt. It belongs beside Bacon's [Essays](/book/874?lang=en) and Pascal's [Pensées](/book/16334?lang=en).

about: Plutarch of Chaeronea, a Greek scholar and priest at Delphi in the time of the Roman Empire, wrote biographies of the great men of Greece and Rome in pairs, each Greek matched with a Roman whose life seemed to echo his: Theseus with Romulus, Lycurgus with Numa, Pericles with Fabius Maximus, Alexander the Great with Julius Caesar, Demosthenes with Cicero. He tells their battles and their politics, but he is most interested in character, which, he writes, is often revealed better by a small act, a phrase or a jest than by the greatest battles.
context: The Lives were among the most influential books of the Renaissance and after: Shakespeare took the plots of his Roman plays from them, and Montaigne, Rousseau and the founders of the United States read them as lessons in public virtue. This is the translation made under John Dryden in 1683, revised by the poet Arthur Hugh Clough. Compare Shakespeare's [Julius Caesar](/book/9?lang=en) and [Antony and Cleopatra](/book/1370?lang=en).

about: In 1348, as the Black Death sweeps through Florence, seven young women and three young men leave the dying city for a villa in the hills. To pass the time, each of them tells a story every day for ten days, on a theme chosen by the day's king or queen, making a hundred tales in all. They range from bawdy comedy and clever tricks to tragic love and noble generosity: the swindler Ser Ciappelletto who is taken for a saint; the parable of the three rings told by a Jewish moneylender to Saladin; Federigo, who serves his beloved falcon to the woman he loves; and patient Griselda.
context: Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375) finished the book around 1353, and its lively Italian prose made it a model for later storytellers, from Chaucer to Shakespeare and Lessing, whose [Nathan the Wise](/book/3909?lang=en) takes up the ring parable. This complete translation is by John Payne. Chaucer's English frame of tales is [The Canterbury Tales](/book/298?lang=en).

about: Jean-Jacques Rousseau sets out to show himself to his fellow men exactly as he was, good and bad. He tells of his childhood in Geneva, where his mother died at his birth; a stolen ribbon he blamed on an innocent servant girl, a lie that haunted him for life; years of wandering and his deep attachment to Madame de Warens, who took him in at Annecy and Chambéry; his struggles in Paris as a music copyist and writer; his sudden fame; his companion Thérèse and the five children he gave to a foundling hospital; and the quarrels and persecutions of his later years.
context: Rousseau wrote the twelve books between 1765 and 1770, and they were published only after his death, in 1782 and 1789. Their frank self-examination and their attention to feeling and childhood made them a founding work of modern autobiography and of Romanticism. Compare the earlier [Confessions of St. Augustine](/book/3417?lang=en), and read Rousseau's ideas on education in [Emile](/book/273?lang=en).

about: In Rome under Nero, around AD 64, a young patrician officer, Marcus Vinicius, falls passionately in love with Lygia, a barbarian king's daughter brought up as a hostage, who is secretly a Christian and is protected by her giant servant Ursus. Vinicius's uncle, the elegant and witty Petronius, Nero's 'arbiter of taste', helps him pursue her, and through her Vinicius meets the apostles Peter and Paul. Then Rome burns, Nero blames the Christians, and the persecution begins, with its horrors in the arena.
context: Henryk Sienkiewicz (1846–1916), who won the Nobel Prize in 1905, published the novel in 1895 and 1896, and it became one of the best-selling books in the world; its title, 'Where are you going?', comes from the legend of Peter meeting Christ on the road out of Rome. This translation is by Jeremiah Curtin. The emperors of its world are portrayed in Suetonius's [Lives of the Twelve Caesars](/book/6432?lang=en), and its spirit is close to [Ben-Hur](/book/2330?lang=en).

about: A thousand years in the future, the citizens of the One State live in houses of glass, wear identical uniforms, have numbers instead of names, and do everything at the same moment according to the Table of Hours, under the rule of the Benefactor. D-503, a mathematician building the spaceship Integral, keeps a journal in praise of this perfect, rational happiness, until he meets I-330, a mysterious woman who smokes, drinks and laughs, and who leads him to the wild world beyond the Green Wall and to a secret rebellion. To his horror, he discovers that he has developed a soul.
context: Yevgeny Zamyatin wrote the novel in Soviet Russia in 1920 and 1921; it was banned there, and its first publication was this English translation by Gregory Zilboorg, in New York in 1924. It is the first great modern dystopia, and George Orwell reviewed it before writing Nineteen Eighty-Four. Its ancestor is the optimistic [Looking Backward](/book/920?lang=en), and Ayn Rand's [Anthem](/book/1484?lang=en) follows its path.

about: On a remote island, the factory of Rossum's Universal Robots produces artificial workers by the million. They look like people, are made from a synthetic living substance and feel nothing, and they do the world's work and fight its wars. Helena Glory, an idealistic young woman from a society for the rights of robots, comes to set them free and stays to marry the factory's director. As human beings stop working and even stop having children, the robots begin to rise against their makers, until only one man is left alive.
context: Karel Čapek's play opened in Prague in 1921 and gave the world the word 'robot', from the Czech robota, forced labour, an idea of his brother Josef. Its questions about machines, work and what makes us human are more pressing than ever. This English version, of 1923, is by Paul Selver and Nigel Playfair. Its ancestors include [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en) and the 'Book of the Machines' in Butler's [Erewhon](/book/2104?lang=en).

about: In a dark future, after a disaster called the Unmentionable Times, people live in a collective society where the word 'I' has been forgotten; everyone speaks of himself as 'we', and the state chooses each person's work, home and companions. Equality 7-2521, assigned to be a street sweeper, secretly loves learning, and in an old tunnel he discovers, alone, how to make electric light. When the Council of Scholars condemns his discovery as a sin, he flees into the Uncharted Forest with a young woman he calls the Golden One, and there he finds the forbidden word.
context: Ayn Rand (1905–1982), who left the Soviet Union in 1926, wrote the short novel in 1937, and it was first published in England in 1938. It is a fable of individualism against collectivism, and it reads quickly. It shares much with Yevgeny Zamyatin's earlier [We](/book/56360?lang=en).

about: What is war, and how should it be understood? The Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz begins by defining it as an act of force to compel the enemy to do our will, and then famously as 'a continuation of policy by other means'. He explains why real war never matches its theory: chance, danger, uncertainty and what he calls 'friction', the thousand small difficulties that make the simplest thing hard. He discusses genius in command, the moral forces of courage and morale, the relationship between attack and defence, and why defence is the stronger form of war.
context: Clausewitz (1780–1831) fought against Napoleon, including at Borodino in the Russian army, and left the book unfinished at his death; his widow Marie published it in 1832. It is still studied in military academies around the world. This translation is by J. J. Graham. Compare the much older [The Art of War](/book/256?lang=en) of Sun Tzu, and see Borodino in [War and Peace](/book/21?lang=en).

about: In seven books, Arrian follows Alexander the Great from his accession in 336 BC to his death in Babylon in 323: the destruction of Thebes, the crossing into Asia, the cutting of the Gordian knot, the victory over the Persian king Darius at Issus, the long siege of Tyre, the founding of Alexandria in Egypt and the visit to the oracle of Ammon in the Siwa desert, the decisive battle of Gaugamela near Erbil in today's Iraq, and the march through Persia, Central Asia and into India, until his soldiers refuse to go further.
context: Arrian of Nicomedia, a Greek who served as a Roman governor under Hadrian, wrote in the second century AD from the memoirs of Alexander's own officers, and his book is the most reliable ancient account of the conquests. He was also the pupil of Epictetus whose [Discourses](/book/9776?lang=en) he recorded. This translation is by E. J. Chinnock. His model was Xenophon's [Anabasis](/book/1409?lang=en).

about: Suetonius tells the lives of the first twelve rulers of imperial Rome, from Julius Caesar and Augustus through Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero to the brief reigns of the year of four emperors and the Flavians, Vespasian, Titus and Domitian. He arranges each life by topic rather than by date: ancestry, career, public deeds, private habits, appearance and death. He loves telling details: Caesar's baldness, the superstitions of Augustus, Caligula's plan to make his horse a consul, Nero singing while Rome burned, and Vespasian's dying joke that he must be turning into a god.
context: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus was for a time a secretary to the emperor Hadrian, with access to the imperial archives, and wrote the book around AD 121. Its gossip has shaped the popular image of the Caesars ever since. This translation is by Alexander Thomson, revised by T. Forester. A darker and more serious view of the same age is [Tacitus's Histories](/book/15070?lang=en).

about: In ten books, Diogenes Laertius collects the lives, sayings and doctrines of the Greek philosophers, from the Seven Sages and Thales to Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the Cynics, the Stoics and the Sceptics. Much of it is anecdote: Thales falling into a well while looking at the stars, Diogenes the Cynic living in a tub and asking Alexander the Great to stand out of his sunlight, Zeno founding the Stoic school in a painted colonnade. The whole of the last book is given to Epicurus, and it preserves three of his letters and his Principal Doctrines, our main source for his teaching.
context: Almost nothing is known about Diogenes Laertius, who probably wrote in the third century AD, and he can be credulous, but without him much of Greek philosophy would be lost. This translation is by C. D. Yonge. The Epicurean view of the world is set out in verse in Lucretius's [On the Nature of Things](/book/1067?lang=en).

about: Herodotus of Halicarnassus opens by saying that he writes so that the great deeds of men may not be forgotten. This first volume contains Books I to IV of the Histories. They tell of Croesus, the rich king of Lydia, warned by Solon to call no man happy until he is dead; the rise of Cyrus and the Persian Empire; a long description of Babylon, its walls, its temples and its customs; a whole book on Egypt, the Nile, the pyramids, embalming and the priests of Memphis; and the campaigns of Cambyses and Darius, including his expedition against the Scythians north of the Black Sea.
context: Herodotus (about 484–425 BC) travelled widely to gather his stories, and Cicero called him the father of history; his later books tell of the Persian invasions of Greece. He is curious about every people he meets and often lets them speak for themselves. This translation is by G. C. Macaulay. His successor was Thucydides, author of [The History of the Peloponnesian War](/book/7136?lang=en).

about: Ovid's great poem tells, in one flowing story from the creation of the world, hundreds of myths in which people and gods change shape. This volume contains the first seven of its fifteen books: the four ages of mankind and the great flood; Apollo's pursuit of Daphne, who becomes a laurel tree; Phaethon, who drives the chariot of the sun and sets the earth on fire; Narcissus and Echo; the lovers Pyramus and Thisbe of Babylon; Perseus and the Gorgon Medusa; Arachne, turned into a spider for weaving better than a goddess; and Medea's magic.
context: Ovid (43 BC–AD 17 or 18) finished the poem shortly before Augustus exiled him to the Black Sea, and it became the great storehouse of classical myth for European poets and painters, from Chaucer and Shakespeare to Titian and Bernini. This prose translation is by Henry T. Riley. Shakespeare's mechanicals perform Pyramus and Thisbe in [A Midsummer Night's Dream](/book/6?lang=en), and Ovid's lighter side is in the [Art of Love](/book/43040?lang=en).
