about: In four books of Odes, Horace turns Greek lyric forms into Latin poetry of perfect polish: invitations to friends to drink wine by the fire as snow covers Mount Soracte, love poems that laugh at love, praise of the quiet life on his Sabine farm, reflections on death and the passing seasons, and public poems celebrating Augustus and the victory over Cleopatra. Here are the famous phrases 'carpe diem', seize the day, and 'dulce et decorum est pro patria mori', and the proud last ode of Book III, in which he declares that he has built a monument more lasting than bronze.
context: Horace (65–8 BC), the son of a freed slave, fought on the losing side at Philippi before Virgil introduced him to the patron Maecenas. The volume also includes the hymn he wrote for Augustus's Secular Games of 17 BC. This verse translation is by John Conington. His friend's epic is the [Aeneid](/book/541?lang=en).

about: This volume collects the oldest Greek poetry after Homer. Hesiod's Works and Days gives a farmer's calendar and stern advice to his idle brother, and tells the myths of Pandora and the five ages of man; his Theogony tells how the gods were born from Chaos and how Zeus overthrew his father Kronos. The Homeric Hymns, once credited to Homer, praise the gods with lively stories: Demeter searching for her daughter Persephone, the baby Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle and inventing the lyre. The Homerica adds fragments of the lost epics and the comic Battle of the Frogs and Mice.
context: Hesiod lived in Boeotia around 700 BC and is the first Greek poet to speak in his own voice. This translation, of 1914, is by Hugh G. Evelyn-White, without the Greek text of the original Loeb edition. Read Homer's [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en) and [Odyssey](/book/173?lang=en) alongside it.

about: Tacitus's Annals open with the death of Augustus in AD 14, and these first six books follow the reign of his stepson Tiberius: the mutinies of the legions, the campaigns of the popular Germanicus across the Rhine and his mysterious death in Antioch, the treason trials in which senators destroyed each other, the rise of the ambitious prefect Sejanus and his fall, and the old emperor's retreat to the island of Capri. This volume adds Tacitus's description of the Germanic tribes and his life of his father-in-law Agricola, the governor of Britain, with its famous charge that the Romans make a desert and call it peace.
context: Tacitus wrote in the early second century AD, and his compressed, ironic style makes him the greatest historian of imperial Rome. This is the translation by Thomas Gordon, an eighteenth-century political writer, edited by Arthur Galton. His account of the following civil wars is [The Histories](/book/15070?lang=en).

about: These eleven essays by the Stoic philosopher Seneca, written as letters or dialogues to friends and family, offer practical guidance for living. Why do good men suffer, if there is a providence? How can we control anger, which he calls a brief madness? What makes a happy life, and how can we find peace of mind? In On the Shortness of Life he argues that life is long enough if we know how to use it, but that we waste it on busy nothings. There are consolations to a mother who has lost her son and to his own mother on his exile, and a treatise on clemency addressed to the young Nero.
context: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (about 4 BC–AD 65) wrote in exile on Corsica and as Nero's adviser, and his clear, quotable Latin made him one of the most widely read moralists in Europe. This translation is by Aubrey Stewart, who also translated Seneca's [On Benefits](/book/3883?lang=en). For the Stoic emperor's private notes, read the [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en).

about: Epictetus, born a slave in Phrygia, became one of the most influential teachers of Stoic philosophy, and his student Arrian wrote down his lessons in the Discourses. Their central idea is simple and demanding: some things are within our power, our judgements, desires and actions, and everything else, our bodies, property, reputation and even our lives, is not. Happiness, he argues, comes from caring only about what is ours to control. This volume gives a selection of the Discourses, lively, ironic and full of examples, followed by the Encheiridion, the short handbook that summarises them.
context: Epictetus (about 50–135) taught in Rome until the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers, and then at Nicopolis in Greece; he wrote nothing himself. His teaching deeply influenced Marcus Aurelius, whose [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en) quote him. This translation is by George Long. The library also has another edition of [The Enchiridion](/book/40729?lang=en).

about: Besides his famous Lives, Plutarch wrote dozens of essays on moral questions, and this volume gathers some of the most humane of them. He writes on the education of children and the love of parents for their offspring, on virtue and vice, on how to tell a flatterer from a true friend, on restraining anger, on envy and hatred, on how a man may praise himself without giving offence, on the dangers of borrowing money, on exile and on fortune. Among them is a moving letter of consolation to his wife on the death of their little daughter.
context: Plutarch (about 46–120) was a priest at Delphi, and his essays, known as the Moralia, were loved by Montaigne and many later writers for their good sense and kindness. This translation is by A. R. Shilleto. His biographies are in [Plutarch's Lives](/book/963?lang=en), and Seneca's [Minor Dialogues](/book/58849?lang=en) treat many of the same subjects.

about: When the Goths sacked Rome in 410, many pagans blamed the disaster on the Christians, who had abandoned the old gods. Augustine, Bishop of Hippo in North Africa, answered them in this vast work. This first volume contains Books I to XIII: he argues that the Roman gods never protected Rome, examines Roman history and the philosophers, especially the Platonists, and then begins his great contrast between two cities, the earthly city founded on love of self and the city of God founded on love of God, telling the story of creation, the angels and the fall of mankind.
context: Augustine worked on the book from 413 to 426, and it shaped Christian thought about history, politics and the state for a thousand years. This translation was edited by Marcus Dods. Augustine's own story is told in [The Confessions of St. Augustine](/book/3417?lang=en), and the fall of Rome is retold in Gibbon's [Decline and Fall](/book/1017?lang=en).

about: Where do our ideas come from? John Locke argues that there are no innate ideas, no truths stamped on the mind at birth, and that the mind begins as 'white paper', on which experience writes. All our knowledge, he says, comes from sensation, our experience of the outside world, and reflection, our awareness of our own minds, and from these simple ideas the mind builds complex ones. This first volume contains Books I and II, including his discussions of primary and secondary qualities, power and freedom, and personal identity, which he locates in consciousness and memory.
context: Locke (1632–1704) published the Essay in 1689, the same year as his political [Second Treatise of Government](/book/7358?lang=en), and it founded British empiricism. This edition follows the second edition, with its original seventeenth-century spelling, hence 'Humane'. The empiricist line continues in Hume's [Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding](/book/277?lang=en).

about: 'The world is my idea.' So begins Arthur Schopenhauer's main work, and this first volume contains its four books. The world we know, he argues, following Kant, is only representation, the way things appear to our minds; but behind it lies the will, a blind, endless striving that drives everything in nature, from gravity to human desire, and makes life a cycle of want and suffering. Escape comes for a moment in art, especially in music, which he sees as a direct copy of the will, and more lastingly in compassion and in the denial of the will to live, which he compares with the teachings of the Upanishads and the Buddha.
context: Schopenhauer published the book in 1818, and it was neglected for decades before it influenced Wagner, Nietzsche, Tolstoy, Freud and Thomas Mann. This translation is by R. B. Haldane and John Kemp. His lighter, more popular writings are in his [Essays](/book/284?lang=en).

about: Rama, the noble prince of Ayodhya, is about to be crowned when his father, bound by a promise to one of his queens, sends him into exile in the forest for fourteen years. His wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana go with him. In the forest, Ravana, the ten-headed demon king of Lanka, carries Sita away, and Rama, with the help of the monkey king Sugriva and the mighty Hanuman, who leaps across the sea to find her, builds a bridge to Lanka and wins her back in a great battle.
context: Attributed to the sage Valmiki, who is called the first poet, the Ramayana is one of the two great epics of India, and its story is still performed and celebrated across South and South-East Asia; the festival of Diwali marks Rama's return home. This verse translation, published in the 1870s, is by Ralph T. H. Griffith, principal of the college at Benares. India's other great epic is the [Mahabharata](/book/13790?lang=en).

about: The Mahabharata, the longest epic poem in the world, tells of the war between two branches of a royal family, the five Pandava brothers and their cousins the Kauravas. This first volume contains its first three books: the origins of the dynasty and the birth and youth of the heroes; the Pandavas' marriage to Draupadi; the fatal game of dice in which the eldest brother, Yudhishthira, gambles away his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi, who is dragged before the court; and the beginning of their twelve years of exile in the forest, full of tales such as the love story of Nala and Damayanti.
context: Composed over many centuries and traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa, the epic is a storehouse of Indian myth, law and philosophy; the Bhagavad Gita is part of a later book. Kisari Mohan Ganguli's prose version, published between 1883 and 1896, was the first complete English translation. Its sister epic is the [Rámáyan of Válmíki](/book/22137?lang=en).

about: This volume brings together three masterpieces of Persian poetry in English. The longest is the Shah Nameh, the Book of Kings, in which Firdausi tells the history of Iran from its first kings, through the tyrant Zahhak with serpents growing from his shoulders and the blacksmith Kaveh who rose against him, to the deeds of the hero Rustam, and his tragic fight with his own son, Sohrab, whom he does not recognise until it is too late. It is followed by the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam and by poems from the Divan of Hafiz.
context: Firdausi (940–1020) of Tus spent some thirty years on the Shah Nameh, writing in a Persian almost free of Arabic words, and the poem preserved Iran's language and memory. The versions here are by James Atkinson (an abridged Shah Nameh), Edward FitzGerald and Herman Bicknell, edited by Richard Gottheil; the Gulistan of Saadi is in the second volume. Read also the [Rubaiyat](/book/120?lang=en) and the [Poems from the Divan of Hafiz](/book/68368?lang=en).

about: Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, became ruler of the small kingdom of Fergana in Central Asia at the age of eleven. In his memoirs he tells how he won and lost Samarkand, wandered as a fugitive, took Kabul in 1504, and finally invaded India, where his victory at Panipat in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire. But the book is as much about the man as his wars: he writes with honesty about his failures, his friends and enemies, his love of poetry, gardens and melons, his struggle with wine, and the plants, animals and people of the lands he saw.
context: Babur (1483–1530) wrote in his native Chagatai Turkish, and the Baburnama is one of the first true autobiographies in Islamic literature. This translation, of 1922, by Annette Beveridge, was made directly from the Turkish text. Babur admired the Persian poets of his day; for their great predecessor, read the [Poems from the Divan of Hafiz](/book/68368?lang=en).

about: This is the first volume of Edward William Lane's famous English translation of the Thousand and One Nights. It begins with the frame story: King Shahriyar, betrayed by his wife, marries a new bride each night and has her killed at dawn, until Shahrazad, the vizier's clever daughter, tells him stories that she breaks off unfinished each morning. Among the tales here are the Merchant and the Jinni, the Fisherman and the Jinni with its sealed brass bottle, and the Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad, with the stories of the three wandering dervishes.
context: Lane (1801–1876) lived for years in Cairo and translated from the Arabic edition printed at Bulaq, adding long notes on Arab customs and beliefs; he left out tales he thought unsuitable for family reading. This edition, prepared by his nephew Edward Stanley Poole, has hundreds of engravings by William Harvey. Lane's notes were later published as [Arabian Society in the Middle Ages](/book/36996?lang=en), and Burton's fuller version begins in [The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night](/book/46359?lang=en).

about: William Ukers spent years gathering material for this huge history of coffee. He begins with the legends of its discovery, the Ethiopian goatherd Kaldi and his dancing goats, and with its first certain use among the Sufis of Yemen, who drank qahwa to stay awake during their night prayers. He follows coffee from Yemen and the port of Mocha to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul, where the first coffee houses opened and were sometimes banned, and then to Venice, London, Paris and the Americas. Later chapters cover cultivation, trade, chemistry, roasting, brewing and coffee in art and literature.
context: Ukers (1873–1945), the editor of an American trade journal for tea and coffee, published the book in 1922, and it is still a standard reference, full of old illustrations. It shows how a drink from the Arab world changed social life everywhere. The coffee shops of nineteenth-century Cairo are described in Lane's [Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians](/book/64633?lang=en).

about: Sir Thomas Malory gathered the French and English legends of King Arthur into a single great prose story. This first volume begins with the birth of Arthur, the son of King Uther Pendragon, taken away by Merlin at birth and raised in secret; the sword in the stone that only he can draw; Excalibur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake; his marriage to Guinevere and the founding of the Round Table; his war against the emperor of Rome; and the adventures of his knights, Sir Gareth, who serves in the kitchen before proving himself, Sir Lancelot, the greatest knight of all, and the young Sir Tristram.
context: Malory finished the book around 1470, apparently in prison, and William Caxton printed it in 1485; it is the source of most later retellings of the Arthurian legend. The story of the Grail and the death of Arthur is in the second volume. Tennyson retold it in [Idylls of the King](/book/907?lang=en), and Mark Twain mocked it in [A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court](/book/51?lang=en).

about: Chrétien de Troyes, a poet at the court of Champagne in the twelfth century, wrote the first great Arthurian romances, and this volume translates four of them. In Erec and Enide a knight neglects his duties for love of his wife, then tests her on a perilous journey; Cligès is a story of love and deception in Constantinople; in Yvain, the Knight of the Lion, a knight who breaks his promise to his wife goes mad, recovers and is followed everywhere by a grateful lion; and in Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, Lancelot accepts the shame of riding in a criminal's cart to rescue Queen Guinevere.
context: Chrétien's poems, written between about 1170 and 1190, introduced Lancelot as Guinevere's lover and Camelot as Arthur's court, and they made courtly love the heart of the legend. This prose translation, of 1914, is by W. W. Comfort. Welsh tales of some of the same heroes are in [The Mabinogion](/book/5222?lang=en).

about: At King Arthur's New Year feast, a giant knight, green from head to foot, rides into the hall and offers a game: anyone may strike him with his axe, if he will receive the same blow a year later. Sir Gawain beheads him, and the Green Knight picks up his head and rides away, reminding Gawain of his promise. The next winter Gawain sets out to find the Green Chapel and stays at a castle where, for three days, the lord goes hunting while his lady tempts Gawain, and the two men exchange whatever they have won each day.
context: The poem was written in the late fourteenth century by an unknown poet from the north-west Midlands and survives in a single manuscript. This edition, by the scholar Richard Morris, gives the original Middle English text with notes, not a modern translation, so it suits readers who want to meet the poem's alliterative music directly. For Malory's prose Arthur, read [Le Morte d'Arthur](/book/1485?lang=en).

about: The Redcrosse Knight, who stands for Holiness, rides out with the lady Una, who stands for Truth, to free her parents from a dragon that has besieged their kingdom for years. On the way he kills the monster Error, but the enchanter Archimago separates him from Una, and he falls under the spell of the false and beautiful Duessa, visits the House of Pride, is imprisoned by the giant Orgoglio and nearly yields to the voice of Despair, before he is rescued, learns true faith in the House of Holiness and finally fights the dragon for three days.
context: Edmund Spenser (about 1552–1599) published the first books of The Faerie Queene in 1590, dedicated to Queen Elizabeth, and invented for it the nine-line Spenserian stanza later used by Byron and Keats. This school edition of Book I, by G. A. Wauchope, has an introduction and notes to help with the allegory. Its spiritual journey anticipates [The Pilgrim's Progress](/book/481?lang=en).

about: One night Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband Ailill argue in bed about which of them is richer, and find that they are equal in everything except one thing: Ailill owns a magnificent white-horned bull. To match him, Medb sets out with a huge army to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley from the kingdom of Ulster. The warriors of Ulster lie helpless under an ancient curse, and only the seventeen-year-old hero Cú Chulainn stands against the invaders, holding the fords in single combat day after day, until he must fight his own foster brother and dearest friend, Ferdiad.
context: The Táin Bó Cúalnge, the 'Cattle Raid of Cooley', is the central epic of early Ireland, preserved in manuscripts of the twelfth century but much older in origin. This translation, of 1914, is by Joseph Dunn. Its Old English cousin among heroic poems is [Beowulf](/book/14518?lang=en).

about: Young Robin, eighteen years old, kills one of the king's foresters in a quarrel and becomes an outlaw in Sherwood Forest, where he gathers a merry band of yeomen. Pyle tells their adventures in a series of lively episodes: Robin's fight with Little John on a narrow bridge, his meeting with the jolly Friar Tuck, the wedding of Allan a Dale, the Sheriff of Nottingham's archery contest with its golden arrow, Robin's many disguises, and his meeting with King Richard, before the sad story of his death.
context: Howard Pyle (1853–1911), an American illustrator, wrote the book in 1883 in an old-fashioned English style and illustrated it himself, and it has shaped the image of Robin Hood ever since. It is a delightful book to read aloud. Robin also appears in Walter Scott's [Ivanhoe](/book/449?lang=en).

about: Matthew Bramble, a Welsh squire who suffers from gout and a sour temper but has a generous heart, travels through England and Scotland with his sister Tabitha, a husband-hunting spinster; his nephew Jery, an Oxford student; his romantic young niece Lydia; and Tabitha's maid, Win Jenkins, who mangles every long word she uses. They describe the same places, Bath, London, Harrogate, Edinburgh and the Highlands, in very different letters home. On the way they pick up a ragged, pious young servant, Humphry Clinker, who turns out to be more closely related to the family than anyone expected.
context: Tobias Smollett (1721–1771) published his last and gentlest novel in the year of his death. Its many voices make it one of the funniest comic novels in English, and it offers a lively picture of Britain in the eighteenth century. His first novel is [Roderick Random](/book/4172?lang=en).

about: Roderick Random, the grandson of a rich Scottish judge, is disowned after his father marries against the family's wishes, and he sets out penniless to seek his fortune, accompanied by his loyal friend Strap, a barber. He is cheated in London, pressed into the navy as a surgeon's mate, survives the horrors of a disastrous attack on Cartagena in South America, serves as a soldier in the French army, and tries to marry an heiress, before chance and his long-lost father change everything.
context: Tobias Smollett published the novel in 1748, drawing on his own service as a naval surgeon at Cartagena in 1741, and its brutal picture of life at sea shocked readers. Its rough energy delighted the young Charles Dickens, who has David read it in [David Copperfield](/book/32?lang=en). Smollett's last and mellowest novel is [Humphry Clinker](/book/2345?lang=en).

about: This handbook retells the myths of ancient Greece and Rome in clear, simple prose. The first part describes the gods, from Chaos, Uranus and Cronus to Zeus and the Olympians, the lesser gods of the sea, the earth and the underworld, and the Roman names and forms of each, together with their worship, temples, oracles and festivals. The second part tells the legends of the heroes: Heracles and his twelve labours, Perseus, Theseus and the Minotaur, Jason and the Golden Fleece, Oedipus and the heroes of the Trojan War.
context: E. M. Berens published the book in 1880 for students, illustrated with pictures of ancient statues, and it remains a handy reference for anyone who meets these names in literature and art. For the myths told as stories for children, read Hawthorne's [Tanglewood Tales](/book/1237?lang=en); for the poem that told many of them first, read the [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en).

about: In the seventeenth century, the wild valley of the Doones, a family of outlaw nobles, terrorises the countryside of Exmoor in south-west England. John Ridd, a farmer's son whose father the Doones have murdered, climbs as a boy up a waterfall into their hidden valley and meets Lorna, a little girl who lives among them. He grows into the strongest man in the county and falls in love with her, but she is promised to the violent Carver Doone, and the story moves through the terrible frost of 1683 and the rebellion of the Duke of Monmouth to the secret of Lorna's birth.
context: R. D. Blackmore (1825–1900) published the novel in 1869, and it became one of the most popular historical romances of the Victorian age; its narrator, John, tells it with homely humour in the voice of an old man. The same rebellion sends the hero of Sabatini's [Captain Blood](/book/2160?lang=en) into slavery.

about: George Talboys returns to England after three years in the Australian gold fields, rich and eager to see his young wife, only to read her death notice in a newspaper. His friend Robert Audley, an idle young barrister, takes him to stay with his uncle, Sir Michael Audley, who has just married a beautiful, golden-haired governess, Lucy. Lady Audley avoids meeting George, and then George vanishes. Robert, determined to find out what happened to his friend, begins to suspect that his charming new aunt has a terrible secret.
context: Mary Elizabeth Braddon (1835–1915) published the novel in 1862, and it was one of the great best sellers of the century, the classic 'sensation novel' of crime and secrets behind respectable doors, with a heroine who is far from a passive victim. Wilkie Collins's [The Woman in White](/book/880?lang=en) began the fashion.

about: Lady Isabel Vane, the beautiful daughter of a ruined earl, marries the honourable lawyer Archibald Carlyle, who has bought her father's estate, East Lynne. Misled by jealousy about her husband's secret meetings with a young neighbour, Barbara Hare, which concern Barbara's brother, falsely accused of murder, she runs away with the seductive Captain Levison, who soon abandons her. Believed dead after a railway accident and disfigured, she returns in disguise as a governess to her own children in her husband's house, where Barbara is now his wife.
context: Ellen Wood (Mrs Henry Wood, 1814–1887) published the novel in 1861, and it was one of the great best sellers of its time, adapted for the stage again and again. Note that this edition is an abridged version of the long original. It belongs with Braddon's [Lady Audley's Secret](/book/8629?lang=en).

about: Old Thady Quirk, a faithful servant, tells the history of the Rackrent family, the Irish landlords he has served for generations: Sir Patrick, who drank himself to death; Sir Murtagh, a miser who loved lawsuits; Sir Kit, a gambler who kept his wife locked in her room for seven years; and good-natured, spendthrift Sir Condy, who loses everything. Thady admires them all, but his simple account reveals their folly and cruelty, and the estate ends up in the hands of his own son, Jason, a clever attorney.
context: Maria Edgeworth (1768–1849) published the short novel in 1800, with a glossary explaining Irish customs to English readers. It is often called the first regional novel in English, and Walter Scott said that Edgeworth's Irish portraits inspired him to write about Scotland in [Waverley](/book/2224?lang=en).

about: These are the writings of Jane Austen as a teenager, full of the mischief she later refined. In Love and Freindship, written at fourteen in letters, the heroine Laura tells of her adventures with her equally sensitive friend Sophia: they faint, weep and run mad at every opportunity, steal money with a clear conscience and despise anyone with common sense ('Run mad as often as you chuse, but do not faint'). The volume also contains Lesley Castle, the comic History of England 'by a partial, prejudiced, and ignorant Historian', and other short pieces.
context: Austen wrote these pieces around 1790 to amuse her family; they were published only in 1922. They mock the sentimental novels of her day, a theme she returned to in [Northanger Abbey](/book/42?lang=en). Her short novel in letters, written a little later, is [Lady Susan](/book/1209?lang=en).

about: In the Highlands of Scotland in the sixteenth century, a hunter who calls himself James Fitz-James loses his way while chasing a stag near Loch Katrine and is rowed across the lake by the beautiful Ellen Douglas, daughter of an outlawed lord. Three men love her: the young Malcolm Graeme, the fierce Highland chief Roderick Dhu, who sends the fiery cross through the glens to raise his clan, and the mysterious stranger, whose true identity is revealed only at the end. Scott tells the story in six cantos of fast-moving verse, with songs and ballads.
context: Walter Scott published the poem in 1810, and it was so popular that tourists began to visit Loch Katrine. Its 'Hail to the Chief' became the official music of the President of the United States, and Schubert set Ellen's song as his famous 'Ave Maria'. Scott later turned to prose, beginning with [Waverley](/book/2224?lang=en).

about: Aurora Leigh, born in Florence to an English father and an Italian mother, is orphaned young and raised by a stern aunt in England, where she secretly reads her father's books and decides to be a poet. On her twentieth birthday she refuses her cousin Romney, a serious social reformer, who tells her that women can write no great poetry. She goes to London to live by her pen, while Romney tries to marry Marian Erle, a poor seamstress, as an act of social reform, and the lives of the three are tested by betrayal, violence and disaster before they meet again in Italy.
context: Elizabeth Barrett Browning published this 'novel in verse', in nine books of blank verse, in 1856, and called it the most mature of her works; it is one of the great Victorian statements on women and art. Her love sequence is [Sonnets from the Portuguese](/book/2193?lang=en), and her husband's collection of the same years is [Men and Women](/book/15507?lang=en).

about: In fifty-one poems, Robert Browning lets men and women from many ages speak for themselves in dramatic monologues. Fra Lippo Lippi, a Renaissance monk and painter caught by the night watch, defends his love of the flesh; the painter Andrea del Sarto, technically perfect but uninspired, says 'a man's reach should exceed his grasp, or what's a heaven for?'; a knight rides through a nightmare landscape in 'Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came'; and in 'An Epistle', Karshish, an Arab physician, writes to his teacher about a strange case he met in Bethany, a man named Lazarus.
context: Browning published the collection in 1855, nine years after his secret marriage to Elizabeth Barrett, and closed it with 'One Word More', addressed to her. These poems, difficult and brilliant, taught later poets how to speak through other voices. His best-loved poem for children is [The Pied Piper of Hamelin](/book/16401?lang=en).

about: In the year 878, the Danes have conquered most of England, and King Alfred of Wessex is a fugitive in the marshes. After a vision of the Virgin Mary, who promises him nothing but that 'the sky grows darker yet and the sea rises higher', he goes out to gather his allies, a Saxon farmer, a Roman nobleman and a wild Celtic chief, and enters the camp of the Danish king Guthrum disguised as a minstrel. The poem builds to the great battle of Ethandune, near the ancient white horse cut into the chalk hills.
context: G. K. Chesterton published the ballad in 1911, and its message of courage without hope of reward was quoted often in Britain during the dark days of the Second World War. It mixes legend, such as the story of Alfred burning the cakes, with Chesterton's own ideas about faith and civilisation, set out in prose in [Orthodoxy](/book/480?lang=en).

about: Arsène Lupin, the gentleman-burglar, is elegant, witty and a master of disguise; he steals only from the rich, never kills, and enjoys making fools of the police. These nine stories begin with his arrest on board a transatlantic liner and go on to show him robbing a castle while sitting in a Paris prison, escaping from his own trial, stealing a queen's necklace as a boy, and finally meeting the great English detective Sherlock Holmes, who arrives too late.
context: Maurice Leblanc (1864–1941) created Lupin in 1905 for the magazine Je sais tout, as a French answer to Conan Doyle; after Doyle objected, later editions renamed the detective 'Herlock Sholmes'. Lupin is still popular, most recently through a successful television series. Compare the English gentleman-thief of [The Amateur Cracksman](/book/993?lang=en) and the original of [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en).

about: Bunny Manders, a young man ruined by gambling debts, goes one night to his old school friend A. J. Raffles, the most admired amateur cricketer in England, intending to shoot himself if no help comes. Raffles helps him, and reveals his secret: he pays for his elegant life in London society by stealing jewels from the people who invite him to dinner. Bunny becomes his loyal, nervous partner, and in eight stories he describes their burglaries of country houses and city flats, their narrow escapes from the police, and the strange code of honour of a gentleman who is also a thief.
context: E. W. Hornung (1866–1921) was the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle and dedicated the book to him, and Raffles and Bunny are a deliberate reversal of Holmes and Watson. Published in 1899, it created the English 'gentleman thief'. Compare [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en) and the French gentleman-burglar of [The Extraordinary Adventures of Arsène Lupin](/book/6166?lang=en).

about: Mr and Mrs Bunting, former servants, are close to ruin in their dreary London lodging house when a polite, nervous gentleman calling himself Mr Sleuth takes their rooms and pays well in advance. He reads the Bible, hates drink, conducts strange experiments with a gas ring and goes out alone late at night. At the same time, a murderer who signs himself 'The Avenger' is killing women in the fog, and Mrs Bunting, reading every newspaper report, begins to fear the truth about her lodger, while her stepdaughter is courted by a young detective working on the case.
context: Marie Belloc Lowndes (1868–1947), the sister of the writer Hilaire Belloc, based the novel on the Jack the Ripper murders and published it in 1913. Its power lies in suspense and psychology rather than detection, and Alfred Hitchcock made it into his first great thriller in 1927. Compare Stevenson's [The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde](/book/419?lang=en).

about: On the eve of his regiment's departure for the war in the Sudan, Harry Feversham, the son of a famous general, resigns his commission. Three of his fellow officers send him white feathers, the symbol of cowardice, and his fiancée, Ethne, adds a fourth. Disgraced, Harry decides to win back his honour by returning each feather, and travels in disguise into the Sudan, where he saves his former friends one by one, among them Jack Durrance, who loses his sight, and Captain Trench, imprisoned in the terrible prison of Omdurman.
context: A. E. W. Mason (1865–1948) published the novel in 1902, and it has been filmed several times. It is a study of fear and courage, although its picture of the Sudanese reflects the imperial attitudes of its age. Kipling's [The Light That Failed](/book/3007?lang=en) is also shaped by the Sudan campaigns.

about: On a stormy night, Sergeant-Major Morris, back from years in India, shows his friends the Whites a dried monkey's paw: an old fakir put a spell on it, he says, so that three men could each have three wishes, to show that fate rules people's lives and that those who interfere with it do so to their sorrow. Against his warning, Mr White wishes for two hundred pounds. The money comes the next day, in a way that destroys the family, and the old couple's next wish leads to a knocking at the door in the dead of night that has frightened readers for over a century.
context: W. W. Jacobs (1863–1943) was best known for comic stories of sailors and dockside life, and this volume of his collection The Lady of the Barge (1902), illustrated by Maurice Greiffenhagen, mixes 'The Monkey's Paw' with several of them. The tale has been adapted endlessly for stage and screen. For more classic horror, read the tales in [The Works of Edgar Allan Poe — Volume 2](/book/2333?lang=en).

about: This first volume of the 'Raven Edition' of Poe's works opens with James Russell Lowell's account of his life and N. P. Willis's notice of his death, and then gathers some of his most inventive tales. 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue', in which the detective Auguste Dupin solves a double murder in a locked room in Paris, is often called the first modern detective story, and Dupin returns in 'The Mystery of Marie Rogêt'. 'The Gold-Bug' turns on a secret code and Captain Kidd's buried treasure, and 'The Balloon-Hoax' was printed in a New York newspaper in 1844 as a true report of a crossing of the Atlantic by balloon.
context: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) invented the detective story and shaped science fiction and horror, and Conan Doyle acknowledged his debt to Dupin when he created Sherlock Holmes in [A Study in Scarlet](/book/56?lang=en). His great horror tales are collected in [Volume 2](/book/2333?lang=en).

about: When a society figure claimed that only four hundred people in New York really mattered, O. Henry answered with this collection about the other four million: shop girls, clerks, waiters, tramps and lonely people in rented rooms. It contains twenty-five stories, among them 'The Gift of the Magi', in which a poor young couple each sell their dearest possession to buy the other a Christmas present; 'The Cop and the Anthem', about a tramp who tries to get himself arrested so as to spend the winter in prison; and 'The Furnished Room', 'The Green Door' and 'Mammon and the Archer'.
context: O. Henry was the pen name of William Sydney Porter (1862–1910), who began writing stories while serving a prison sentence for embezzlement. Published in 1906, this was his first great success, and his warm humour and famous twist endings made him the most popular short story writer in America. A separate edition of [The Gift of the Magi](/book/7245?lang=en) is also in the library.

about: From 1842 to 1845 Nathaniel Hawthorne and his wife lived in the Old Manse in Concord, Massachusetts, and this collection opens with a loving description of the old house and its garden. Then come some of his finest tales: 'Young Goodman Brown', in which a young Puritan goes into the forest at night and finds his neighbours at a witches' meeting; 'The Birthmark', about a scientist determined to remove the only flaw from his wife's face; 'Rappaccini's Daughter', set in a poisonous garden in Padua; 'Feathertop', about a scarecrow brought to life; and 'The Celestial Railroad', a satire on easy modern religion.
context: Hawthorne published the collection in 1846, and Herman Melville's enthusiastic essay 'Hawthorne and His Mosses' helped make its author famous. These are tales of guilt, pride and the dangers of science and fanaticism. His earlier stories are in [Twice-Told Tales](/book/808?lang=en), and 'The Celestial Railroad' parodies [The Pilgrim's Progress](/book/481?lang=en).

about: This collection gathers Mark Twain's early comic pieces, including the story that first made him famous, 'The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County', in which a gambler's champion frog is beaten by a stranger who fills it with quail shot. Twain adds a French translation of the story and his own word-for-word translation back into English, to show how absurd it sounds. Other pieces include 'Journalism in Tennessee', where a newspaper office is a battlefield, the stories of the good little boy and the bad little boy, and a family's panic over a child's sore throat.
context: Twain published the book in 1875, bringing together sketches written over a decade of journalism in the American West and East. They show the deadpan exaggeration that runs through all his work. His travel humour is at its best in [The Innocents Abroad](/book/52?lang=en) and [Roughing It](/book/3302?lang=en).

about: The Hawkins family of Tennessee owns seventy-five thousand acres of wild land that the father believes will one day make them rich, and they move to Missouri full of hope. Years later the land is still unsold, and the family's dreams are kept alive by the irrepressible Colonel Sellers, who sees a fortune in every scheme. The beautiful Laura Hawkins goes to Washington as a lobbyist and charms congressmen into supporting a corrupt land bill, while a crooked senator, railway promoters and speculators show how money and politics have become one.
context: Mark Twain wrote the novel in 1873 with his neighbour Charles Dudley Warner, and its title gave a name to the whole era of American history that followed, an age of glittering wealth over corruption. It was Twain's first novel. His later, darker satire is [The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson](/book/464?lang=en).

about: Ten years after he was carried back to Earth, John Carter returns to Mars, longing for his wife, the princess Dejah Thoris, but finds himself in the beautiful valley of Dor, the paradise to which Martians make their last pilgrimage. It is a trap: the pilgrims are devoured by monstrous plant men and white apes, and the survivors are enslaved by the Holy Therns, the priests of a false religion. Fighting his way out with his old friend Tars Tarkas, Carter uncovers one secret after another, meets the black pirates who rule above the therns and their goddess Issus, and finds a young warrior who turns out to be his son.
context: Edgar Rice Burroughs serialised the novel in 1913, as the sequel to [A Princess of Mars](/book/432?lang=en), and its sword-and-planet adventure inspired later science fiction and films. It ends with a cliffhanger, resolved in the next book of the series.

about: Eleven-year-old Pollyanna Whittier, the orphaned daughter of a poor minister, comes to live with her rich, stern aunt Polly in a small Vermont town. Her father taught her the 'glad game': whatever happens, look for something to be glad about, as when she hoped for a doll from the missionary barrel and received crutches instead, and was glad that she did not need them. Pollyanna plays the game with everyone, the sour invalid Mrs Snow, the lonely recluse John Pendleton, the discouraged minister, and slowly changes the whole town, until an accident puts her own gladness to the test.
context: Eleanor H. Porter (1868–1920) published the novel in 1913, and it was so popular that 'Pollyanna' became an English word for a person who is always optimistic. It is a gentle book about the power of kindness. It belongs on the same shelf as [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en) and [Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm](/book/798?lang=en).

about: Rebecca Randall, ten years old, the second of seven children on a poor farm, is sent to live with her two aunts in the village of Riverboro in Maine so that she can get an education. She arrives on the stagecoach talking non-stop and making up poems, to the delight of the driver and the dismay of her stern aunt Miranda, while gentle aunt Jane softens the strict household. As Rebecca grows up, her imagination, warmth and courage win over the village, a kindly young businessman she calls 'Mr Aladdin', her teachers at the academy and, at last, Miranda herself.
context: Kate Douglas Wiggin (1856–1923), who founded the first free kindergarten in San Francisco, published the novel in 1903, and it was an immediate best seller. Rebecca is a forerunner of Anne Shirley in [Anne of Green Gables](/book/421?lang=en), and Pollyanna follows her in [Pollyanna](/book/1673?lang=en).

about: Jerusha Abbott, the oldest orphan in the John Grier Home, is sent to college by a rich trustee whom she has seen only as a long shadow thrown by car headlights. The only condition is that she write him a letter every month, which he will never answer. She calls him Daddy-Long-Legs, and the whole novel consists of her lively letters, with her own funny drawings, about lessons, friends, books she has never read before, clothes, socialism, votes for women and her slow discovery of who she is. Meanwhile she falls in love with her roommate's charming uncle, Jervis Pendleton.
context: Jean Webster (1876–1916), a grandniece of Mark Twain, published the book in 1912, and its wit and warmth have kept it popular around the world; it has been adapted into a musical and Japanese animation. Its heroine's appetite for books and independence recalls Jo in [Little Women](/book/313?lang=en).

about: In the Netherlands, Hans Brinker and his sister Gretel are the poorest children in their village. Ten years earlier their father fell from a dyke during a storm, and the injury left him unable to recognise his family or remember where he hid their savings. While the children dream of winning the silver skates in the great race on the frozen canal, Hans seeks help from the famous surgeon Dr Boekman, and a group of village boys skate to Haarlem, Leiden and The Hague, learning the history and customs of Holland along the way.
context: Mary Mapes Dodge (1831–1905) published the novel in 1865, before she had ever visited the Netherlands, and it made the country's skating, canals and dykes famous among young readers. It also popularised the legend, told in one chapter, of the boy who saved Haarlem by holding his finger in a leaking dyke. Another classic set in the mountains of Europe is [Heidi](/book/1671?lang=en).

about: These are rhymed cautionary tales about children who misbehave, each with its own brightly coloured pictures. Shock-headed Peter will not cut his nails or comb his hair; cruel Frederick torments animals until a dog bites him; Harriet plays with matches and burns to ashes, leaving her cats to weep; three boys who mock a Black child are dipped in ink by Saint Nicholas; Conrad sucks his thumbs until the tailor cuts them off; Augustus refuses his soup and wastes away; and Fidgety Philip, Johnny Head-in-Air and Flying Robert meet their own ridiculous fates.
context: Heinrich Hoffmann (1809–1894), a doctor in Frankfurt, wrote and drew the book in 1844 as a Christmas present for his three-year-old son, because he found the picture books in the shops too dull, and it was published the next year. Its exaggerated punishments are meant to make children laugh as much as to frighten them. For gentler classic tales, read [Grimms' Fairy Tales](/book/317?lang=en).

about: Peter Schlemihl, a poor young man at a garden party, meets a strange, thin man in a grey coat who pulls from his pocket a telescope, a carpet, a tent and even saddled horses. The grey man offers Peter a purse that is never empty in exchange for his shadow, and Peter agrees. He becomes rich, but everyone who notices that he casts no shadow shuns him, and he loses the girl he loves. When the grey man offers to return the shadow in exchange for his soul, Peter refuses, and with a pair of seven-league boots he finds a new life as a wandering naturalist.
context: Adelbert von Chamisso (1781–1838), a French-born German poet and botanist who later sailed around the world, published the tale in 1814, and through it the old Yiddish word 'schlemihl', an unlucky fool, became known everywhere. This edition, edited by Henry Morley, adds Carové's 'The Story Without an End' and Novalis's 'Hymns to the Night'. Its bargain with the devil echoes Goethe's [Faust](/book/165?lang=en).

about: Undine is a water spirit raised by an old fisherman and his wife in a cottage by a haunted forest, a lively, mischievous girl with no soul. When the knight Huldbrand takes shelter there in a storm, they fall in love and marry, and through her marriage Undine gains a human soul, becoming gentle and loving. But her stormy uncle Kühleborn, a spirit of the waters, haunts them, and when Huldbrand turns to the proud Bertalda and breaks the rules of Undine's world, the waters claim her and fate follows him to his wedding day.
context: Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué (1777–1843) published the fairy tale in 1811, and it became one of the best-loved works of German Romanticism, inspiring operas, ballets, Dvořák's Rusalka and Andersen's 'The Little Mermaid'. It is short and beautifully sad. Read Andersen's [Fairy Tales](/book/192?lang=en) beside it.

about: In the port of Le Havre, a retired jeweller and his wife have two grown sons: Pierre, a doctor, dark, clever and restless, and Jean, a lawyer, fair, calm and gentle. When an old family friend dies and leaves his whole fortune to Jean alone, Pierre is tormented by jealousy and then by a terrible suspicion: that his brother is the dead man's son, and that their quiet mother once had a secret love. Tracing every memory and every look, he cannot let the question rest, and the family's peace is destroyed.
context: Guy de Maupassant published the short novel in 1888 with a famous essay on the art of the novel. It is one of his finest works, a tense psychological drama in a few chapters. This translation is by Clara Bell. Maupassant's novel of an ambitious seducer is [Bel-Ami](/book/319?lang=en), and his most famous story is [Boule de Suif](/book/320?lang=en).

about: Russia, 1598: the son of Ivan the Terrible has died, and the powerful boyar Boris Godunov is begged to accept the crown. But it is whispered that he arranged the murder of the young prince Dmitri years before. In a monastery cell, the old monk Pimen writes his chronicle while a young novice, Grigory, listens; Grigory escapes, claims to be the murdered Dmitri, wins the support of Poland and the love of the proud Marina, and marches on Moscow, while Boris, haunted by guilt, faces the end of his reign. The play closes with a famous stage direction: the people stand silent.
context: Alexander Pushkin wrote the drama in 1825, modelling it on Shakespeare's history plays, and Mussorgsky turned it into one of the greatest Russian operas. This verse translation is by Alfred Hayes. Shakespeare's own drama of a guilty usurper is [King Richard III](/book/1352?lang=en), and Pushkin's novel in verse is [Eugene Onegin](/book/21318?lang=en).

about: On a country estate beside a lake, a famous actress, Irina Arkadina, spends the summer with her lover, the successful writer Trigorin. Her son Konstantin dreams of creating new forms of theatre, and stages his strange symbolic play with Nina, the young girl from the next estate who longs to be an actress, but his mother laughs at it. Konstantin shoots a seagull and lays it at Nina's feet; Trigorin sees in it the subject for a short story, a girl destroyed by a man who has nothing better to do, and the summer's loves and ambitions lead to a quiet tragedy two years later.
context: Anton Chekhov's play failed at its first performance in St Petersburg in 1896, then triumphed in 1898 at the new Moscow Art Theatre, which took the seagull as its emblem. It is a play about art, love and wasted lives, full of humour and sadness. Chekhov's next great play is [Uncle Vanya](/book/175?lang=en).

about: In 1634, during the Thirty Years' War, the soldiers of the imperial army are camped outside the city of Pilsen in Bohemia. In this one-act play there is no plot and no hero, only the camp itself: sergeants and recruits, Croatian and Irish troops, a trumpeter, a cheating peasant, a woman selling provisions and a Capuchin friar who preaches a comic sermon against the soldiers' sins. Through their talk the audience feels the power of their absent general, Wallenstein, whom they follow with blind loyalty, and hears the rumours that the emperor plans to break up his army.
context: Friedrich Schiller wrote the play in 1798 as the prelude to his great Wallenstein trilogy, which continues in The Piccolomini and The Death of Wallenstein, and it was first performed at Weimar under Goethe's direction. It ends with a rousing cavalry song. Schiller's first play, written in his youth, is [The Robbers](/book/6785?lang=en).

about: Isak, a strong, slow, silent man, walks into the wild Norwegian uplands with a sack on his back and begins to clear a farm with his bare hands. Inger, a woman with a hare lip whom no one else would marry, comes to live with him, and year by year they build a home, raise children and turn the wilderness into fields. Their life is shaken by tragedy and crime, and by the arrival of the modern world: traders, speculators, a copper mine and the restless hopes of their sons, while Isak goes on ploughing.
context: Knut Hamsun (1859–1952) published the novel in 1917 and won the Nobel Prize in 1920, largely because of it; his later support for the Nazi occupation of Norway left a shadow over his name. This translation is by W. W. Worster. The novel that made Hamsun famous, very different in mood, is [Hunger](/book/8149?lang=en).

about: After seven years of study in Europe, Crisóstomo Ibarra returns to Manila to marry his childhood sweetheart, María Clara, and to open a school in his home town. He learns that his father died in prison after a quarrel with a powerful Spanish friar, Padre Dámaso, and as Ibarra tries to bring progress to the town, the friars and their allies turn against him. Around him Rizal paints a whole society: the mysterious boatman Elías, the poor mother Sisa driven mad by the loss of her sons, corrupt officials and pretentious social climbers.
context: José Rizal (1861–1896), a Filipino doctor and writer, published the novel in Berlin in 1887 under the Latin title Noli Me Tangere, 'touch me not'; it was banned by the Spanish authorities, and Rizal was executed in 1896. He is the national hero of the Philippines. This translation is by Charles Derbyshire. The story continues in [The Reign of Greed](/book/9789?lang=en).

about: Thirteen years after the events of Noli Me Tangere, a rich jeweller named Simoun, with long white hair and dark blue spectacles, has become the trusted adviser of the Spanish Governor-General in the Philippines. In secret he is Crisóstomo Ibarra, the hero of the first novel, and he encourages greed and abuse in the government so that the people will be driven to revolution. Meanwhile a group of students campaigns for an academy to teach Spanish, and Simoun prepares a terrible plan for a wedding feast.
context: José Rizal published this darker sequel, El Filibusterismo, in Ghent in 1891, dedicating it to three Filipino priests executed by the Spanish in 1872. It debates whether a colonised people should seek freedom by reform or by violence. This translation is by Charles Derbyshire. The first novel is [The Social Cancer](/book/6741?lang=en).

about: This long poem in two parts describes a fox hunt in the English countryside. In the first part, the riders gather at an inn on a bright morning, and Masefield paints a portrait of each, the squire, the parson, the doctor, the farmers, the young lovers and the hunt servants, much as Chaucer described his pilgrims. In the second part the poem changes sides: the reader runs with the fox, feeling his fear, his cunning and his exhaustion as he flees across miles of fields, woods and streams with the hounds close behind him.
context: John Masefield (1878–1967), who later became Poet Laureate, published the poem in 1919, just after the First World War, and its vivid, galloping verse made it one of his most popular works. This edition is illustrated by Carton Moore-Park. Its gallery of riders recalls the prologue to [The Canterbury Tales](/book/298?lang=en).

about: This volume contains four plays by Susan Glaspell. The most famous, Trifles, is set in a cold farmhouse kitchen, where a farmer has been found strangled in his bed and his wife is in jail. While the sheriff and the county attorney search the house for clues and laugh at the women's concern with 'trifles', the two women who came with them notice a half-finished quilt, a broken birdcage and a dead canary, understand what happened, and decide what to do with what they know. The volume also includes The Outside, The Verge and Inheritors.
context: Glaspell co-founded the Provincetown Players, the theatre that discovered Eugene O'Neill, and later won the Pulitzer Prize for drama. Trifles, first performed in 1916, is now one of the most widely taught American plays, an early classic of feminist theatre. Its theme of a woman's hidden life recalls Kate Chopin's [The Awakening](/book/500?lang=en).

about: In February 1676, during the bloody war between the English colonists of New England and the Native American peoples led by the Wampanoag chief Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, warriors attacked the frontier town of Lancaster in Massachusetts. Mary Rowlandson, the minister's wife, was carried off with three of her children; her wounded six-year-old daughter died in her arms. In this narrative she tells of the eleven weeks of her captivity, the 'removes' from camp to camp through the winter forest, her hunger, her bargaining with her sewing and knitting, her meeting with Metacom himself, and her ransom.
context: Published in 1682, it was one of the first American best sellers and the model for a whole genre of captivity narratives. Rowlandson reads every event as a test sent by God, and quotes the Bible constantly, but she also records, sometimes despite herself, the humanity of her captors. The frontier wars live on in fiction in [The Last of the Mohicans](/book/1204?lang=en).

about: Ten years after his famous Narrative, Frederick Douglass told his life again at much greater length. He describes his childhood on a Maryland plantation, where he was separated from his mother and raised by his grandmother; the cruelty he witnessed and suffered; how he learned to read in Baltimore; his fight with the 'slave-breaker' Edward Covey, which he calls the turning point of his life; his escape to the North in 1838; and his new life as a speaker against slavery, his travels in Britain and the founding of his own newspaper.
context: Douglass published the book in 1855, with an introduction by the Black physician James McCune Smith. It is a deeper and more reflective account than the first, written by a man who had become one of the great orators of his age. His first autobiography is the [Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass](/book/403?lang=en).

about: In March 1892, three Black businessmen, friends of the journalist Ida B. Wells, were lynched by a white mob in Memphis, Tennessee. Wells began to investigate lynchings across the American South and in this pamphlet showed that the usual excuse for them, the claim that Black men had attacked white women, was false in most cases; many of the victims were killed for economic competition or for consensual relationships. When she published her findings, a mob destroyed her newspaper office, and she continued her campaign from the North, calling on Black Americans to defend themselves, to boycott and, if necessary, to leave.
context: Ida B. Wells (1862–1931) published the pamphlet in 1892 with a letter of support from Frederick Douglass, and it began her lifelong campaign against lynching; she is now recognised as a pioneer of investigative journalism. Read it with W. E. B. Du Bois's [The Souls of Black Folk](/book/710?lang=en).

about: In 1890, Jacob Riis, a police reporter for New York newspapers, took his readers into the crowded tenement buildings of the Lower East Side, where hundreds of thousands of immigrants lived in dark, airless rooms. He describes the families crowded into single rooms, the sweatshops, the cheap lodging houses and the street children who slept in alleys, and he examines each immigrant community in turn, sometimes with the prejudices of his day. His photographs, taken by the new flash powder in rooms that had never seen light, made the misery impossible to ignore.
context: Riis, himself a Danish immigrant who had known poverty, helped bring about housing reforms, and the young Theodore Roosevelt, then police commissioner, became his ally. The book is a founding work of documentary photography and reporting. Compare Jack London's study of London's East End, [The People of the Abyss](/book/1895?lang=en), and Upton Sinclair's [The Jungle](/book/486?lang=en).

about: Ulysses S. Grant, the general who won the American Civil War and later served two terms as president, tells his life from his boyhood in Ohio and his reluctant years at West Point to the Mexican War, which he called one of the most unjust wars ever waged by a stronger nation against a weaker one, and then through the Civil War: the capture of Fort Donelson, the battle of Shiloh, the long siege of Vicksburg, the campaigns against Robert E. Lee in Virginia, and Lee's surrender at Appomattox in 1865.
context: Ruined by a fraudulent business partner and dying of throat cancer, Grant wrote the memoirs in 1884 and 1885 to provide for his family, and finished them only days before his death; Mark Twain published them, and they earned his widow a fortune. Their clear, modest prose has made them one of the most admired military memoirs ever written. For the war seen from the ranks, read [The Red Badge of Courage](/book/442?lang=en).

about: William Bradford, for many years governor of the Plymouth Colony, tells the history of the Pilgrims: their persecution in England, their flight to Leiden in Holland, their voyage to America on the Mayflower in 1620, and the agreement known as the Mayflower Compact. He describes the first terrible winter, when half of them died, the help they received from the Native Americans Squanto and Massasoit, their quarrels with investors in London and with rival settlers, and the slow growth of the colony until 1647.
context: Bradford's manuscript disappeared from Boston during the American Revolution and was found decades later in the library of the Bishop of London, who returned it to Massachusetts in 1897; this edition includes the report of that ceremony. It is one of the founding documents of American history. A later New England narrative is that of [Mary Rowlandson](/book/1122?lang=en).

about: Adopted by the Continental Congress in Philadelphia on 4 July 1776, the Declaration announced that the thirteen American colonies were breaking away from British rule. Drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it begins with the principles that would shape modern democracy: that all men are created equal, that they have unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. It then lists the grievances against King George III and ends with the signers pledging their lives, fortunes and honour.
context: This text has a special place in the history of books: on 4 July 1971, Michael Hart typed it into a university computer in Illinois and shared it, creating the first electronic book and founding Project Gutenberg, the source of many of the books in this library. Its ideas came from works such as Paine's [Common Sense](/book/491?lang=en), and they echo in his [Rights of Man](/book/3831?lang=en).

about: In 1914, Sir Ernest Shackleton set out to cross the whole Antarctic continent on foot. His ship, the Endurance, was trapped in the pack ice of the Weddell Sea before reaching land, drifted for months and was finally crushed and sank. Shackleton tells how his twenty-eight men camped on the drifting ice, escaped in three small boats to the bleak rock of Elephant Island, and how he and five companions then sailed eight hundred miles in an open boat across the stormiest ocean in the world to South Georgia, crossed its unmapped mountains and came back to rescue every one of his men.
context: Shackleton (1874–1922) published the book in 1919; it also tells the hard story of the expedition's other party on the Ross Sea side. It is one of the greatest true stories of survival and leadership, and Frank Hurley's photographs from the voyage are famous. The race to the Pole a few years earlier is told by Roald Amundsen in [The South Pole](/book/3534?lang=en).

about: In 1910 the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen sailed from Norway in the ship Fram, apparently heading for the North Pole; only at Madeira did he tell his crew that their real goal was the South Pole, which the British expedition under Robert Falcon Scott was also seeking. This first volume tells the history of earlier Antarctic voyages, Amundsen's careful planning, built on skis, sledge dogs and experience learned from Arctic peoples, the voyage south, the building of the base Framheim on the Great Ice Barrier, the laying of supply depots and the long polar winter.
context: Amundsen's team reached the Pole on 14 December 1911, five weeks before Scott, whose party died on the return; the march to the Pole is told in the second volume. This translation is by A. G. Chater. Compare Shackleton's [South](/book/5258?lang=en), the story of the next great Antarctic expedition.

about: 'What one fool can do, another can.' With this motto, the physicist Silvanus P. Thompson sets out to free readers from their fear of calculus. He explains that the frightening symbol d simply means 'a little bit of', so that dx is a little bit of x, and that integration is just adding up all the little bits. Step by step, with friendly humour and many worked examples, he shows how to differentiate and integrate common functions, find maxima and minima, and solve practical problems, with exercises and answers at the end of each chapter.
context: Thompson (1851–1916), a professor of physics in London, first published the book anonymously in 1910, and it has never gone out of print; it is still recommended to students who find the usual textbooks hard. Calculus is the language of modern physics, as Einstein's own popular book, [Relativity](/book/5064?lang=en), shows.

about: William Strunk, a professor of English at Cornell University, wrote this little book of rules for his students. In a few dozen pages he sets out elementary rules of usage, such as how to form the possessive and where to place commas, and principles of composition: make the paragraph the unit of composition, use the active voice, put statements in positive form, use definite, specific, concrete language, and, most famously, 'Omit needless words'. He ends with lists of common errors of form and of words and expressions often misused.
context: Strunk privately printed the book in 1918. One of his students, E. B. White, later revised and expanded it, and in that form it became one of the most influential guides to writing in English; this is Strunk's original text. Its advice in favour of short, vigorous sentences fits Francis Bacon's [Essays](/book/874?lang=en).

about: 'Men, it has been well said, think in herds; it will be seen that they go mad in herds, while they only recover their senses slowly, and one by one.' The Scottish journalist Charles Mackay collects the great follies of history: the Mississippi scheme of John Law in France and the South Sea Bubble in England, when whole nations bought worthless shares; the tulip mania of seventeenth-century Holland, when a single bulb could cost as much as a house; and the alchemists, false prophets, fortune-tellers, witch hunts, poisoners, haunted houses and crusades that carried crowds away.
context: Mackay published the book in 1841, and it is still read by investors and anyone who wants to understand financial bubbles, panics and mass enthusiasm. It is lively and full of anecdotes, although modern historians think some of its stories, such as the tulip mania, exaggerated. Its lessons for the stock market are retold in [Reminiscences of a Stock Operator](/book/55422?lang=en).

about: Larry Livingston starts work at fourteen chalking up stock prices in a Boston brokerage office and discovers that he can read patterns in the numbers. He makes his first fortune in the 'bucket shops', gambling dens where people bet on price movements, until they ban him, and then moves to Wall Street, where he makes and loses several fortunes, learning painful lessons about patience, the crowd, his own hopes and fears, and the danger of taking tips. 'There is nothing new in Wall Street,' he concludes, because human nature never changes.
context: Edwin Lefèvre (1871–1943), a financial journalist, published the book in 1923 as a thinly disguised biography of the famous speculator Jesse Livermore, and it is still one of the most recommended books among traders. It reads like a novel. For the history of earlier manias, read Mackay's [Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds](/book/21798?lang=en).

about: Why, asks Henry George, does poverty grow alongside progress? In the booming cities of nineteenth-century America, new railways, machines and industries had created vast wealth, yet wages stayed low and the poor grew poorer. His answer is land: as a community grows, the value of its land rises, and that unearned increase goes to landowners as rent, taking the gains of progress from labour and capital. His remedy was a single tax on the value of land, replacing all other taxes, so that the wealth created by the community would return to it.
context: George (1839–1897), a self-taught journalist in San Francisco, published the book in 1879, and it sold millions of copies, inspiring reformers around the world, from Tolstoy to Sun Yat-sen; a game invented to illustrate his ideas became the ancestor of Monopoly. Compare Adam Smith's [The Wealth of Nations](/book/3421?lang=en) and Marx and Engels's [The Communist Manifesto](/book/151?lang=en).

about: What is religion, at its root? To find out, Émile Durkheim studies what he considers its simplest known form, the totemism of the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, where each clan is linked to a sacred animal or plant. He defines religion as beliefs and practices concerning sacred things, set apart from the ordinary, which unite people into a moral community, and he argues that in worshipping the totem the clan is really worshipping the power of society itself, which it feels most strongly in the excitement of collective ceremonies.
context: Durkheim (1858–1917), a founder of sociology, published the book in 1912, and its ideas about the sacred, ritual and social solidarity still shape anthropology and the study of religion. This translation, of 1915, is by Joseph Ward Swain. Compare Frazer's [The Golden Bough](/book/3717?lang=en) and William James's [The Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en).

about: In the Trobriand Islands, off the eastern tip of New Guinea, men sail dangerous ocean voyages in carved canoes to exchange two kinds of ornaments, long necklaces of red shell, which travel around a vast ring of islands in one direction, and white shell armbands, which travel in the other. These objects have no practical use, yet the Kula, as this exchange is called, governs friendships, status, magic and trade across the islands. Bronislaw Malinowski describes it in detail, together with canoe building, gardening, myths and spells.
context: Malinowski (1884–1942), born in Poland, spent years living among the Trobrianders during the First World War, and this book, published in 1922 with a preface by James Frazer, founded modern anthropology's method of fieldwork, trying to see a society from its own people's point of view. Read it with Durkheim's [The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life](/book/37234?lang=en).

about: John Forster was Charles Dickens's closest friend, adviser and literary agent for more than thirty years, and after Dickens's death he wrote the first great biography of him. In it he revealed a secret that Dickens had told almost no one: that at twelve, when his father was imprisoned for debt, the boy was sent to work in a blacking factory, an experience that haunted him all his life. Forster quotes Dickens's own account of those months and follows his career from journalist to the most famous novelist in the world, with his travels, public readings and endless energy.
context: Forster published the three volumes between 1872 and 1874, and they remain the starting point for every life of Dickens, rich in letters and first-hand memories. The blacking factory reappears in fiction in [David Copperfield](/book/32?lang=en), and the debtors' prison in [Little Dorrit](/book/36?lang=en).

about: Edward Gibbon begins his history in the second century AD, in what he calls the happiest period in the history of the human race, under the emperors from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius, and then traces how the empire began to decline. This first volume, chapters I to XV, covers the cruelty of Commodus, the soldier emperors and civil wars of the third century, the rise of the new Persian empire of the Sasanians, the first invasions of the Goths, the reforms of Diocletian and the rise of Constantine, and ends with Gibbon's famous and controversial account of the growth of Christianity.
context: Gibbon (1737–1794) had the idea in Rome in 1764 while sitting among the ruins of the Capitol, and published this first volume in 1776, the year of American independence; the whole work, completed in 1788, carries the story to the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its ironic, majestic prose and witty footnotes make it a classic of English literature. Read Augustine's answer to the fall of Rome in [The City of God](/book/40907?lang=en).

about: Livy's history of Rome 'from the founding of the city' begins with legend: Aeneas reaching Italy after the fall of Troy, the twins Romulus and Remus nursed by a she-wolf, and the founding of Rome. These first eight books tell of the seven kings and the expulsion of the last, the proud Tarquin, after the rape of Lucretia; the heroes of the young republic, Horatius holding the bridge, Mucius Scaevola thrusting his hand into the fire and Cincinnatus called from his plough to save the state; the struggles between patricians and plebeians; the capture of Rome by the Gauls; and the wars with the Samnites.
context: Livy (59 BC–AD 17) wrote 142 books in the age of Augustus, of which only 35 survive, and his stories became the models of Roman virtue for Europe. This translation is by D. Spillan. Macaulay turned some of these legends into ballads in [Lays of Ancient Rome](/book/1118?lang=en), and Plutarch retold the lives of early Romans in [Plutarch's Lives](/book/963?lang=en).

about: Why did Britain, a small island, come to dominate the world? Alfred Thayer Mahan, an American naval officer, answers that the key was sea power: the ability to control the oceans through a strong navy, a large merchant fleet and bases around the world. He sets out the elements that make a nation a sea power, such as its geography, coastline, population, national character and government, and then examines the naval wars of Europe from 1660 to 1783, from the struggles with the Dutch to the American Revolution, to show how control of the sea decided the fate of empires.
context: Mahan (1840–1914) published the book in 1890 from his lectures at the Naval War College, and it was read by presidents, kaisers and admirals; it helped inspire the naval arms race before the First World War. It belongs beside Clausewitz's [On War](/book/2142?lang=en) among the classics of strategy.

about: How do we think well, and how can schools teach it? John Dewey argues that real thinking begins when we meet a problem, a doubt or a puzzle, and he describes the stages of reflective thought: feeling the difficulty, defining it, suggesting possible solutions, reasoning out their consequences and testing them by observation and experiment. He then asks how teachers can train this habit by building on children's natural curiosity, connecting lessons with real activity and experience, and avoiding mere memorising.
context: Dewey (1859–1952), a philosopher who founded an experimental school in Chicago, published the book in 1910, and it became one of the most influential works on education in the twentieth century. It applies the American pragmatism of William James, set out in [Pragmatism](/book/5179?lang=en).

about: Joseph Jacobs set out to do for English folk tales what the Brothers Grimm had done for German ones, and this collection gathers forty-three of them, told in plain, lively language for children: Jack and the Beanstalk, The Story of the Three Little Pigs, The Three Bears, Henny-Penny, Dick Whittington and his cat, and Jack the Giant-Killer, together with less familiar tales such as Tom Tit Tot, an English cousin of Rumpelstiltskin, Molly Whuppie, who outwits a giant, and the eerie Mr Fox.
context: Jacobs (1854–1916), a folklorist and historian born in Australia, published the book in 1890 with pictures by John D. Batten and notes on the sources of each tale for adult readers. Many of these stories are still the first that English-speaking children hear. Compare [Grimms' Fairy Tales](/book/317?lang=en).

about: This collection introduced English readers to the folk tales of Russia, in a world of forests, frozen rivers and village huts. Here are the witch Baba Yaga, who lives in a hut that turns on chicken legs; Koshchei the Deathless, whose death is hidden in an egg inside a duck inside a hare; the warrior princess Marya Morevna; the Water King and his clever daughter Vasilissa the Wise; and a host of devils, ghosts, vampires and wise fools. Ralston arranges the tales by theme and comments on their beliefs and their connections with the folklore of other lands.
context: William Ralston Shedden-Ralston (1828–1889), a librarian at the British Museum, published the book in 1873, translating mostly from the great collection of Alexander Afanasyev. It remains a fine introduction to Slavic folklore. Compare [English Fairy Tales](/book/7427?lang=en) and [Grimms' Fairy Tales](/book/317?lang=en).

about: In March 1796, two days after his marriage to the elegant widow Josephine de Beauharnais, the young general Napoleon Bonaparte left Paris to command the French army in Italy, and from the battlefield he wrote her passionate letters, full of longing and jealousy, begging her to join him and reproaching her for not writing. This collection follows their relationship through his rise to emperor, his campaigns across Europe and the divorce of 1809, when he left her because she had not given him an heir, and the kinder letters he sent her afterwards.
context: The letters were collected and translated in 1901 by Henry Foljambe Hall, with notes on the events behind each one. They show a side of Napoleon that his battles hide. His invasion of Russia, as seen by the Russians, is told in Tolstoy's [War and Peace](/book/21?lang=en).

about: The Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest great poem in the world, tells of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk in southern Iraq, and his friend Enkidu. This book is a scholarly edition of one clay tablet from the Old Babylonian period, about four thousand years old, acquired by the University of Pennsylvania Museum. It tells how Gilgamesh dreams of a coming companion, how the wild man Enkidu, who lived among the animals, is brought to the shepherds' camp, learns to eat bread and drink beer and becomes human, and how he comes to Uruk, blocks the king's way and wrestles with him, until the two become friends.
context: Stephen Langdon (1876–1937), an Oxford Assyriologist, published the tablet in 1917 with an introduction, a transliteration of the cuneiform and a translation; some of his early readings were later corrected by other scholars. The better-known later version of the epic, found at Nineveh, includes the story of the flood that Genesis also tells in the [King James Version of the Bible](/book/70524?lang=en). For the literature of Mesopotamia's neighbour, read [Egyptian Literature](/book/25221?lang=en).

about: The Kalevala is the national epic of Finland, fifty songs, or runos, about the heroes of the land of Kalevala and their struggles with the dark northern land of Pohjola. Its hero is the old, wise singer Väinämöinen, whose music enchants all nature; beside him are the smith Ilmarinen, who forges the Sampo, a magic mill that grinds out grain, salt and gold, for the witch-queen Louhi in exchange for her daughter; the reckless adventurer Lemminkäinen; and the tragic Kullervo, a slave who takes terrible revenge. The poem ends with the theft of the Sampo and the coming of a new age.
context: Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884), a country doctor, collected the songs from village singers in Karelia and published the epic in 1835 and in its full form in 1849; it became a symbol of Finnish identity and inspired Sibelius and Tolkien. This translation, of 1888, by John Martin Crawford, keeps the original's trochaic metre, which Longfellow had already borrowed for [The Song of Hiawatha](/book/400?lang=en).
