about: This anthology gathers the writings of ancient Egypt in English translation: ancient tales, hymns to the gods and to the sun, litanies and invocations, and long sections of the Book of the Dead, the spells placed in tombs to guide the dead through the dangers of the underworld, to keep their hearts and to let them 'come forth by day'. It ends with a selection of the Amarna letters, cuneiform tablets in which the kings of Babylon, Assyria and other lands wrote to the pharaohs about gifts of gold, royal marriages and alliances.
context: The volume was edited by Epiphanius Wilson in 1901 for a series of the world's great classics, using the translations of leading Egyptologists of the time. The Amarna letters, found in Egypt in 1887 and written in the Akkadian language of Mesopotamia, show the diplomacy of the ancient Near East more than three thousand years ago. For the full guide to the afterlife, read [The Book of the Dead](/book/7139?lang=en).

about: The Book of Enoch is an ancient Jewish work attributed to Enoch, the great-grandfather of Noah, who 'walked with God'. It tells how two hundred angels, the Watchers, came down to earth, took human wives and taught people metalwork, weapons, cosmetics and magic, and how their children, the giants, filled the world with violence before the flood. It follows Enoch on journeys through heaven, the earth and the places of punishment, and contains visions of a coming judge called the Son of Man, a book on the movements of the sun and moon, a history of Israel told as a dream about animals, and warnings to the wicked.
context: Written in parts between about the third and the first century BC, the book survives complete only in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia, where it is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Church; fragments in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. In Islamic tradition Enoch is often identified with the prophet Idris. This translation is by R. H. Charles, with an introduction by W. O. E. Oesterley. Compare the war of the angels in [Paradise Lost](/book/297?lang=en).

about: Year by year, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the history of England in the language of its people, from the Roman invasion to the twelfth century. Short entries note kings crowned and killed, bishops appointed, comets and famines; longer ones tell of the arrival of the Saxons, the first Viking raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793, King Alfred's long war against the Danes, the battle of Brunanburh, celebrated in a poem, the Norman Conquest of 1066, and, in the troubled reign of Stephen, a time when, the chronicler says, men said openly that Christ and his saints slept.
context: The chronicle was begun in Alfred's reign around 890 and continued in several monasteries, the last entries at Peterborough reaching 1154; it is the first continuous history in English and a priceless source. This translation was made by James Ingram and revised by J. A. Giles. Alfred's struggle with the Danes is the subject of Chesterton's [The Ballad of the White Horse](/book/1924?lang=en), and the older heroic world of the Anglo-Saxons is in [Beowulf](/book/14518?lang=en).

about: In 533 the Byzantine emperor Justinian issued this short textbook of Roman law for first-year law students in Constantinople and Beirut. In four books it sets out the whole system: the law of persons, free and slave, citizens and foreigners, marriage, adoption and guardianship; the law of things, property, possession, gifts, wills and inheritance; obligations, contracts and wrongs such as theft and injury; and legal actions. It opens with famous definitions: justice is the constant will to give every man his due, and the precepts of law are to live honestly, to harm no one and to give each his own.
context: The Institutes formed part of the great code later called the Corpus Juris Civilis, prepared by a commission under the jurist Tribonian, and when it was rediscovered in medieval Bologna it became the foundation of the civil law of Europe and of many legal systems beyond. This translation is by J. B. Moyle of Oxford. A very different view of Justinian is in Procopius's [Secret History](/book/11605?lang=en).

about: 'The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience.' With this famous sentence, Oliver Wendell Holmes sets out to show that the common law of England and America grew from history, custom and the practical needs of each age rather than from abstract principles. He traces the roots of liability in ancient ideas of vengeance, examines criminal law, torts, possession, contracts and inheritance, and argues that the law judges people by external standards, by what a reasonable man would have done, rather than by their inner intentions.
context: Holmes (1841–1935), who had been wounded three times in the Civil War, gave the lectures in Boston and published them in 1881; he later served for thirty years on the United States Supreme Court, where his dissents made him a legend. The book remains a classic of legal thought. Its oldest ancestor in Western law is [The Institutes of Justinian](/book/6019?lang=en).

about: 'We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union...' The Constitution, drafted at the convention in Philadelphia in 1787 and ratified in 1788, sets out the framework of the American federal government in seven articles: a Congress of two houses that makes the laws, a President who carries them out and commands the armed forces, and a Supreme Court, with the powers of each limited by the others, together with the relations between the federal government and the states and the process for amending the document itself.
context: It is the oldest written national constitution still in force, and its system of separated powers and checks and balances has influenced constitutions around the world. Note that this text gives the original Constitution without the later amendments, beginning with the Bill of Rights of 1791. Its arguments were defended in [The Federalist Papers](/book/1627?lang=en), and its principles go back to the [Declaration of Independence](/book/388?lang=en).

about: This collection gathers the speeches, letters and state papers of Abraham Lincoln, from his early years in Illinois politics to his death in 1865: the 'House Divided' speech of 1858 and the debates with Stephen Douglas, the Cooper Union address that made him a national figure, his inaugural addresses, the Emancipation Proclamation, the brief Gettysburg Address, the Second Inaugural with its promise of 'malice toward none' and 'charity for all', and hundreds of letters to generals, politicians and grieving families.
context: Lincoln, largely self-taught, became one of the greatest writers of English prose among statesmen, and these texts show his thought developing on slavery, union and democracy. The edition, by Arthur Brooks Lapsley, includes an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt and essays by Carl Schurz and Joseph Choate. The war he led is told by his general in the [Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant](/book/4448?lang=en), and the novel he is said to have credited with starting it is [Uncle Tom's Cabin](/book/522?lang=en).

about: In 1919, John Maynard Keynes, a young economist at the British Treasury, attended the Paris peace conference after the First World War and resigned in protest at the treaty it produced. In this book he describes the conference and its leaders, the vengeful Clemenceau, the idealistic but outmanoeuvred President Wilson and the agile Lloyd George, and argues that the huge reparations demanded from Germany could never be paid and would ruin the economy of Europe, breeding poverty, resentment and new disorder instead of peace.
context: The book was an international best seller and made Keynes famous; many historians believe its warnings were borne out by the crisis and dictatorship that followed in Germany. Keynes (1883–1946) went on to transform economics in the 1930s. For the classical economics he later challenged, read Ricardo's [Principles of Political Economy and Taxation](/book/29773?lang=en).

about: David Ricardo, a stockbroker who made a fortune and then turned to economics, sets out a rigorous theory of how wealth is divided between landowners, capitalists and workers. He explains value by the labour needed to produce goods; rent as the extra yield of better land over the worst land in use, which rises as population grows; and wages, profits and the effects of every kind of tax. His chapter on foreign trade introduces the theory of comparative advantage, with the example of English cloth and Portuguese wine: both countries gain by trading even if one produces both goods more cheaply.
context: Ricardo (1772–1823) published the book in 1817, and with Adam Smith's [The Wealth of Nations](/book/3421?lang=en) it founded classical economics; comparative advantage is still the basis of the argument for free trade. His ideas were developed by John Stuart Mill in his [Principles of Political Economy](/book/267?lang=en).

about: How do we know anything, and how can we reason correctly about the world? In this great treatise John Stuart Mill examines words and propositions, the syllogism and deduction, and then induction, the reasoning from particular facts to general laws on which all science depends. He sets out five methods for discovering causes, the methods of agreement, of difference, of residues, of concomitant variations and their joint use, which are still taught today, and in the last book he asks how the same methods can be applied to the study of human character and society.
context: Mill (1806–1873) published the book in 1843, and it was the standard work on logic and scientific method in the English-speaking world for half a century. It is demanding but clear. Mill describes its long preparation in his [Autobiography](/book/9548?lang=en), and his best-known work is [On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en).

about: Walter Lippmann opens with Plato's allegory of the cave and a story about islanders who, in 1914, went on living for weeks as friends of their German and French neighbours because the news of the war had not yet reached them. We all act, he argues, not on the world itself but on 'the pictures in our heads', simplified images shaped by habit, censorship, limited time and what he calls stereotypes. He examines how news is made and why it differs from truth, how leaders shape what the public believes, and whether ordinary citizens can know enough to govern a complex modern society.
context: Lippmann (1889–1974), one of the most influential American journalists of the century, published the book in 1922; it gave the word 'stereotype' its modern meaning and popularised the phrase 'the manufacture of consent'. It is a founding work in the study of media. The allegory he begins with is in Plato's [Republic](/book/74?lang=en).

about: Why do we laugh? Henri Bergson argues that we laugh when a living person behaves like a machine: when someone keeps walking into the same trap, repeats the same gesture, sticks rigidly to a fixed idea or is suddenly reduced to a puppet by circumstances. The comic, he says, is 'something mechanical encrusted on the living'. Laughter requires a momentary absence of feeling, and it is a social act, a way in which society corrects stiffness and eccentricity. He studies comedy of situation, of words and of character, with many examples from Molière and from Don Quixote.
context: Bergson (1859–1941), one of the most famous philosophers of his time and a Nobel laureate in literature, published the essay in 1900. It remains one of the most often quoted theories of humour. This translation is by Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell. Test his theory on Cervantes's [Don Quixote](/book/168?lang=en) and Wilde's [The Importance of Being Earnest](/book/63?lang=en).

about: This volume gathers three books by the French mathematician Henri Poincaré about the nature of science. In Science and Hypothesis he argues that the axioms of geometry are neither self-evident truths nor facts of experience but convenient conventions, and examines the role of hypothesis in physics; in The Value of Science he defends science as a search for objective truth; and in Science and Method he discusses chance, the foundations of mathematics and how mathematical discoveries are made, describing how the solution to a problem came to him suddenly as he stepped onto a bus.
context: Poincaré (1854–1912), one of the greatest mathematicians of his age and a pioneer of the theory of relativity and of chaos, wrote with unusual clarity for general readers. This translation, of 1913, is by George Bruce Halsted. Read it with Einstein's own popular account, [Relativity](/book/5064?lang=en).

about: In twelve books, Georgius Agricola describes everything known about mining and metallurgy in the sixteenth century: how to find veins of ore, how to survey a mine and dig its shafts and tunnels, how to drain the water with pumps driven by water wheels and horses, how to ventilate the galleries, how to assay, crush, wash and smelt ores of gold, silver, copper, lead and tin, and how to make salt, glass and acids. He begins by defending mining against those who called it a wicked trade, and his hundreds of woodcuts show the machines and the miners at work.
context: Agricola (1494–1555), a German doctor who lived among the mining towns of Bohemia and Saxony, died a year before the book was published in 1556, and it remained the standard work for two centuries. This translation, of 1912, with extensive notes, is by the mining engineer Herbert Hoover, later President of the United States, and his wife Lou Henry Hoover. Compare Babbage's [On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures](/book/378?lang=en).

about: Goethe believed his work on colour was more important than his poetry. In this book he challenges Newton's theory that white light is made of coloured rays and studies colour as we actually experience it: physiological colours created by the eye itself, such as after-images and coloured shadows; physical colours seen through prisms, which he argues appear at the edges where light meets darkness; and chemical colours in substances. The last part, on the 'sensory and moral effect' of colour, explores how yellow, blue, red and green affect our feelings.
context: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe published Zur Farbenlehre in 1810. Physicists rejected his attack on Newton, but painters such as Turner and philosophers such as Schopenhauer and Wittgenstein drew on his observations. This translation, of 1840, is by the painter Charles Lock Eastlake. Newton's own account is in his [Opticks](/book/150?lang=en), and Goethe's masterpiece is [Faust](/book/165?lang=en).

about: Francis Bacon dedicated this book to King James I as a survey of human knowledge and a plan for its improvement. In the first part he defends learning against those who say it makes men unfit for business or leads them away from religion, while admitting the faults of scholars: fantastical learning, quarrelsome learning and learning that cares only for words. In the second part he maps the whole field of knowledge, divided by the faculties of the mind into history (memory), poetry (imagination) and philosophy (reason), and points out where knowledge is lacking and new work is needed.
context: Bacon (1561–1626) published the book in 1605, and it prepared the way for his [Novum Organum](/book/41517?lang=en), with its new method of science, and for his scientific utopia, the [New Atlantis](/book/2585?lang=en). This edition was edited by Henry Morley.

about: In 1907, in a poor district of Rome, Maria Montessori opened a 'Children's House' for the small children of working families, and in this book she describes the method she developed there. Children, she argues, learn best when they are free to choose their own work in a prepared environment, with materials designed to train the senses: wooden cylinders of different sizes, textured surfaces, colour tablets and sandpaper letters. Teachers observe more than they instruct, and the children, she reports, taught themselves to write and read with surprising joy and discipline.
context: Montessori (1870–1952), one of the first women in Italy to qualify as a doctor, built her method on her earlier work with disabled children, and this book, translated by Anne E. George in 1912, spread it around the world. Montessori schools still follow its principles. Compare Rousseau's [Emile](/book/273?lang=en) and Dewey's [How We Think](/book/33615?lang=en).

about: William James gave these lectures to schoolteachers in Cambridge, Massachusetts, to show what the new science of psychology could offer them. He talks plainly about the stream of consciousness, the formation of habits, attention, interest, memory and the association of ideas, and gives practical advice: make useful actions automatic as early as possible, connect new knowledge with what pupils already care about, and never let an exception occur while a new habit is being formed. The volume adds three talks to students, including 'On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings', about our failure to see the inner lives of others.
context: James published the book in 1899; it is the friendliest introduction to the ideas of his great [Principles of Psychology](/book/383?lang=en). Its practical spirit was carried on by John Dewey in [How We Think](/book/33615?lang=en).

about: In 1893, the young historian Frederick Jackson Turner read a paper that changed the writing of American history. The census of 1890 had announced that there was no longer a frontier line of unsettled land, and Turner argued that the frontier, the moving edge of settlement westward over three centuries, had shaped American character: its individualism, practical energy, restlessness and democracy were born from the constant rebuilding of society in the wilderness. This book collects that essay with his later studies of the West, the Ohio Valley, the Middle West and the place of the pioneer in American life.
context: Turner (1861–1932) published the collection in 1920. His 'frontier thesis' has been criticised for ignoring the Native Americans, women and the violence of conquest, but it remains one of the most debated ideas about the United States. The great journey westward is recorded in [The Journals of Lewis and Clark](/book/8179?lang=en).

about: In 1849 the journalist Henry Mayhew began to walk the streets of London interviewing the people who made a living there, and this first volume is devoted to the street sellers: costermongers with their barrows of fruit, fish and vegetables, sellers of flowers, watercress, books, toys and old clothes. Mayhew records their trades, earnings, food, homes, slang, amusements and beliefs, and above all their own words, as in the interview with an eight-year-old watercress girl who had almost forgotten how to play and talked like a careworn woman.
context: Mayhew (1812–1887) first published the interviews in the Morning Chronicle and collected them in 1851; the work is a founding document of social investigation and oral history, and Dickens's London lives in it. Compare [Oliver Twist](/book/31?lang=en) and Jacob Riis's study of New York, [How the Other Half Lives](/book/41078?lang=en).

about: Mary Antin was born in 1881 in Polotsk, in the Russian Empire, where Jews were confined by law to the Pale of Settlement and lived under constant restrictions and fear. She describes her childhood there with warmth and sharp detail: the family's religion, the market, the school she could barely attend, and the dream of America. At thirteen she emigrated with her family to Boston, where the free public school opened a new world to her: she learned English with passion, published a poem in a newspaper, and became, as she says, a new person.
context: Antin published the book in 1912, and it became one of the most widely read accounts of the immigrant experience in the United States, used in schools to teach the meaning of citizenship. Its hopeful view of America is balanced by the harder stories of Anzia Yezierska's [Hungry Hearts](/book/37110?lang=en).

about: These ten stories tell of Jewish immigrant women from Eastern Europe in the crowded tenements of New York's Lower East Side, hungry for more than bread: for education, love, beauty and a place in America. A young woman who scrubs the stairs of a tenement falls in love with a sociologist who sees her only as a subject of study; an old mother whose children have become rich is lost in their luxurious apartment; a washerwoman scrubs her kitchen to make it beautiful for a visit; a girl learns that America is not given but must be built.
context: Anzia Yezierska (about 1880–1970), herself an immigrant, published the collection in 1920; the film producer Samuel Goldwyn bought it and briefly made her famous as the 'sweatshop Cinderella'. Her English carries the rhythms of Yiddish. Compare Mary Antin's [The Promised Land](/book/18639?lang=en) and Jacob Riis's [How the Other Half Lives](/book/41078?lang=en).

about: Zitkala-Sa, a Yankton Dakota (Sioux) woman, tells of her happy early childhood with her mother on the reservation, and then of the day missionaries persuaded her, at eight, to go east to a boarding school in Indiana, where her long hair was cut off against her will and she was forced to give up her language and customs. She describes her years as a student and as a teacher at another Indian school, torn between two worlds, and adds stories drawn from Dakota life and an essay on why she chose the old religion of her people.
context: Zitkala-Sa (1876–1938), also known as Gertrude Simmons Bonnin, was a writer, musician and campaigner for Native American rights, and she co-wrote the first American opera based on Native American music. The book, published in 1921, collects pieces that first appeared in leading magazines. For the frontier as white novelists imagined it, compare [The Last of the Mohicans](/book/1204?lang=en).

about: Mary Prince was born into slavery in Bermuda around 1788. In this short narrative she tells how she was sold away from her mother and sisters as a child, beaten by cruel owners, and sent to work for years in the salt ponds of the Turks Islands, standing in salt water until her legs were covered with boils. Later she was taken to Antigua and then to London by her owners, where she left them and sought help from the Anti-Slavery Society. 'I have been a slave myself,' she says, 'I know what slaves feel.'
context: Published in London in 1831, two years before slavery was abolished in the British colonies, it was the first account of the life of a Black woman published in Britain, and it caused a sensation and two libel trials. She dictated it to the writer Susanna Strickland. Compare the [Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass](/book/403?lang=en).

about: Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then returned again and again to lead others to freedom along the secret routes of the Underground Railroad, guiding some seventy people north without losing a single one; she was called the Moses of her people. This short biography, written while she was still alive, tells her story from her own words and from the letters of those who knew her: her childhood injuries, her escapes and rescues, and her service in the Civil War as a nurse, scout and spy, including a raid on the Combahee River that freed hundreds of slaves.
context: Sarah Bradford wrote the book in 1869 to raise money for Tubman, who was living in poverty; it includes letters of praise from Frederick Douglass and others. Tubman (about 1822–1913) is now one of the best-known heroes of American history. Compare the [Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass](/book/403?lang=en).

about: Emmeline Pankhurst, the leader of the militant campaign for women's right to vote in Britain, tells how she founded the Women's Social and Political Union in Manchester in 1903 with the motto 'Deeds, not words'. After years of peaceful petitions had been ignored, the suffragettes interrupted politicians, marched, broke windows and set fire to empty buildings; hundreds were imprisoned, went on hunger strike and were force-fed. She describes her own arrests and her defence of militancy as the only language the government would hear.
context: Pankhurst (1858–1928) published the book in 1914, just as the First World War led her to suspend the campaign; British women won the vote in stages in 1918 and 1928. Read it with John Stuart Mill's [The Subjection of Women](/book/266?lang=en) and the memoirs of the American suffragist Elizabeth Cady Stanton, [Eighty Years and More](/book/10811?lang=en).

about: Elizabeth Cady Stanton tells the story of her life from her childhood in upstate New York, where she learned from her lawyer father how the law treated married women as property, to old age. In 1848, with Lucretia Mott, she organised the first women's rights convention at Seneca Falls and wrote its Declaration of Sentiments, which demanded, among other rights, the vote. She describes her long friendship and partnership with Susan B. Anthony, her work against slavery, her travels, her seven children and her campaigns for women's equality in law, education and religion.
context: Stanton (1815–1902) published the memoir in 1898; she did not live to see American women win the vote in 1920. It is lively, humorous and full of portraits of the reformers of her century. Compare Emmeline Pankhurst's [My Own Story](/book/31224?lang=en) and Mill's [The Subjection of Women](/book/266?lang=en).

about: In these essays the anarchist Emma Goldman explains what anarchism really stands for: a society based on free cooperation without the coercion of state, church or private property. She writes on minorities and majorities, the psychology of political violence, prisons as a social crime and failure, patriotism as a menace to liberty, the Spanish educator Francisco Ferrer, the hypocrisy of Puritanism, the trafficking of women, marriage and love, and the modern drama as a weapon of social criticism.
context: Goldman (1869–1940), born in Lithuania, was a famous speaker in the United States until she was deported to Russia in 1919, where she soon broke with the Bolsheviks. The book, published in 1910, includes a biographical sketch by Hippolyte Havel. Her teachers included Peter Kropotkin, author of [The Conquest of Bread](/book/20838?lang=en), and Mikhail Bakunin, author of [God and the State](/book/32814?lang=en).

about: Frederick Winslow Taylor argues that the great waste of industry is the inefficiency of human work, and that it can be cured by science. Instead of leaving each worker to his own rule of thumb, managers should study every task with a stopwatch, find the one best way to do it, choose and train the right workers, and pay them for higher output. His famous examples include a labourer at a steel works whom he trained to load forty-seven tons of pig iron a day instead of twelve and a half, and the redesign of shovels for different materials.
context: Taylor (1856–1915) published the book in 1911, and his 'scientific management' transformed factories and offices around the world, from Henry Ford's to Lenin's Russia, while critics accused it of turning workers into machines. It is a founding text of modern management. Read it with Henry Ford's [My Life and Work](/book/7203?lang=en).

about: Henry Ford tells how a farm boy who loved machines built his first car, founded the Ford Motor Company and created the Model T, a simple, strong car cheap enough for ordinary families. He explains the ideas behind mass production: standard parts, the moving assembly line introduced in 1913, constant cutting of costs and prices, and the famous decision of 1914 to pay workers five dollars a day, double the usual wage, so that they could buy what they made. He also gives his opinions on money, business, wages, charity and education.
context: Ford (1863–1947) wrote the book in 1922 with the journalist Samuel Crowther, and it was a best seller; 'Fordism' became a name for the age of mass production. It is also a document of his strong and sometimes notorious opinions. Its methods built on Frederick Taylor's [The Principles of Scientific Management](/book/6467?lang=en).

about: For more than thirty years, the Earl of Chesterfield, one of the most polished statesmen and wits of eighteenth-century England, wrote letters to his illegitimate son Philip to make him a perfect gentleman and diplomat. He gives advice on history, languages and reading, but above all on manners: how to please, how to listen, how to dress, how to control one's temper and conceal one's feelings, how to avoid loud laughter and how to speak well in company, insisting that knowledge without grace is of little use in the world.
context: The letters were published in 1774, after both father and son had died, by the son's widow, and they became a famous manual of worldly wisdom. Samuel Johnson, who had his own quarrel with Chesterfield, said that they taught 'the morals of a whore, and the manners of a dancing master'. Johnson's remark is preserved in [Boswell's Life of Johnson](/book/1786?lang=en).

about: The Duke of Saint-Simon spent his life at the court of Louis XIV at Versailles and wrote down everything he saw: the endless ceremony that governed the king's day from his rising to his going to bed, the rivalries of princes and dukes over the smallest points of rank, the influence of Madame de Maintenon, the wars and the misery of the country in the king's last years, the deaths of the king's heirs, the death of Louis XIV himself in 1715 and the Regency of the Duke of Orléans that followed.
context: Saint-Simon (1675–1755) wrote the memoirs in his later years from his notes, and they were published in full only in the nineteenth century; with their sharp portraits and passionate prejudices, they are one of the great works of French prose. For fiction set at an earlier French court, read [The Princess of Cleves](/book/767?lang=en).

about: Madame Campan entered the service of the French royal family as a young reader to the daughters of Louis XV and became the first lady of the bedchamber to Queen Marie Antoinette. In these memoirs she describes life inside Versailles: the queen's arrival from Austria as a girl of fourteen, the rigid etiquette she struggled against, her friendships, her children, the scandal of the diamond necklace, and then the Revolution, the attack on the Tuileries in 1792 and the end of the monarchy.
context: Jeanne-Louise-Henriette Campan (1752–1822) survived the Revolution, opened a school for girls, and was later appointed by Napoleon to direct a school for the daughters of members of the Legion of Honour. Her memoirs, published in 1823, are a sympathetic first-hand portrait of the queen. Compare the court of the previous century in [Saint-Simon's memoirs](/book/3964?lang=en), and the Revolution in [A Tale of Two Cities](/book/30?lang=en).

about: Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne was Napoleon's schoolfellow at the military academy of Brienne and later, from 1797 to 1802, his private secretary, at his side day and night. He describes the young Bonaparte at school, the Italian campaign, the expedition to Egypt and Syria, including Napoleon's time in Cairo and the siege of Acre, the coup that made him First Consul, and the daily working of his mind and his government, before Bourrienne's dismissal over money scandals and his later career under the restored Bourbons.
context: Bourrienne's memoirs, published in 1829, were popular but often hostile and inaccurate, and this edition, by R. W. Phipps, adds notes correcting and completing them. They remain a vivid close-up portrait. Napoleon's own voice is in [Napoleon's Letters to Josephine](/book/33685?lang=en).

about: James Boswell first met Samuel Johnson in a London bookshop in 1763, and for more than twenty years he recorded Johnson's conversation and character, his poverty and struggles as a young writer, the making of his great Dictionary, his melancholy, his kindness, his prejudices and his brilliant talk. Here are many of the sayings that made Johnson the most quoted Englishman after Shakespeare: 'when a man is tired of London, he is tired of life', 'patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel', and many more.
context: Boswell published the Life in 1791, and it is often called the greatest biography in English. This edition, by Charles Grosvenor Osgood, is an abridgement, which makes the long original easier to read while keeping its best scenes. Boswell's earlier account of their travels together is [The Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides](/book/6053?lang=en), and Johnson's own fable is [Rasselas](/book/941?lang=en).

about: Cicero wrote and received hundreds of letters, to his closest friend Atticus, to his brother Quintus and to the leading men of Rome, and this first volume of a complete chronological collection begins with letters of 68 BC. They follow his rise to the consulship, his suppression of Catiline's conspiracy, his bitter exile and triumphant return, and the politics of the age of Pompey and Caesar, but they also show the private man: worrying about money and his villas, asking for books, joking, complaining and loving his family.
context: The letters were rediscovered by the poet Petrarch in Verona in 1345, and they give the most intimate picture we have of any person of the ancient world. This translation is by Evelyn S. Shuckburgh. Cicero's public voice is in his [De Officiis](/book/42444?lang=en), and the conspiracy of Catiline is told by Sallust in [The Conspiracy of Catiline](/book/7970?lang=en).

about: In 1519 five Spanish ships under the Portuguese captain Ferdinand Magellan sailed west to reach the Spice Islands. The young Italian Antonio Pigafetta sailed with them and kept a journal: the giants of Patagonia, a mutiny, the passage through the stormy strait that now bears Magellan's name, the crossing of the vast Pacific, on which the starving crew ate leather and rats, the arrival in the Philippines, where Magellan was killed in battle on Mactan in 1521, the Muslim kingdoms of Brunei and the Moluccas, and the return of a single ship, the Victoria, with eighteen survivors in 1522.
context: It was the first voyage around the world, and Pigafetta noticed that the survivors had lost a day on the way. This translation, published by the Hakluyt Society in 1874 and edited by Lord Stanley of Alderley, adds other accounts by contemporaries. Compare the conquest of Mexico in [The Memoirs of Bernal Díaz del Castillo](/book/29015?lang=en).

about: In May 1804, soon after the United States bought the vast Louisiana territory from France, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out from near St Louis with the Corps of Discovery to find a route to the Pacific. Their journals record two and a half years of travel: up the Missouri River, the winter among the Mandan people, the Shoshone woman Sacagawea who guided and interpreted with her baby on her back, the grizzly bears and buffalo herds, the crossing of the Rocky Mountains on the edge of starvation, and Clark's cry on reaching the Columbia estuary: 'Ocian in view! O! the joy.'
context: This edition gives the journal entries from the day the expedition left to its return to St Louis in September 1806, keeping the captains' famously inventive spelling and punctuation. It is one of the founding stories of the American West. The meaning of that West is debated in Turner's [The Frontier in American History](/book/20453?lang=en).

about: Bernal Díaz del Castillo was a common soldier in the small Spanish army that Hernán Cortés led into Mexico in 1519, and in old age he wrote his own account, angry that historians gave all the credit to Cortés. This first volume tells of the earlier expeditions to the coasts of Yucatán, the landing in Mexico, the indigenous woman Malinche, who became Cortés's interpreter, the alliance with the Tlaxcalans, and the march to Tenochtitlan, the great city on the lake, where the emperor Moctezuma received the strangers.
context: Díaz (about 1496–1584) wrote the True History in Guatemala, and it is the most vivid eyewitness account of the conquest, full of wonder at the cities, markets and temples of the Aztecs as well as the violence of the conquerors. This translation, of 1844, is by John Ingram Lockhart. Another eyewitness of the age of discovery is Pigafetta in [The First Voyage Round the World](/book/68209?lang=en).

about: This book, published in 1724, tells the lives of the most notorious pirates of the early eighteenth century: Henry Avery, who captured a treasure ship of the Mughal emperor; Edward Teach, called Blackbeard, who went into battle with lighted fuses in his beard; the gentleman pirate Stede Bonnet; Calico Jack Rackham; and the women pirates Mary Read and Anne Bonny, who fought beside the men. It also records the articles, the written rules, by which pirate crews governed themselves, shared their plunder and compensated the wounded.
context: The author, 'Captain Charles Johnson', has never been identified; some scholars once believed he was Daniel Defoe. The book is the main source for much of what we know, and imagine, about pirates, and Stevenson drew on it for [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en). For a pirate hero of fiction, read Sabatini's [Captain Blood](/book/2160?lang=en).

about: This first volume of Mozart's letters begins in 1769, when the thirteen-year-old prodigy toured Italy with his father, Leopold, and wrote home in high spirits about operas, concerts and the people he met. It follows him through his journeys to Munich, Mannheim and Paris, where his mother died in 1778, his hopeless love for the singer Aloysia Weber, his frustrations in the service of the Archbishop of Salzburg and his decisive break with him in 1781, when he settled in Vienna as an independent musician.
context: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791) wrote with humour, affection and sometimes startling frankness, and the letters show a real person behind the legend. This translation is by Lady Wallace. For the autobiography of another great composer of opera, read Wagner's [My Life](/book/5256?lang=en).

about: Richard Wagner dictated his memoirs to his wife Cosima, and this first volume covers his life from his birth in Leipzig in 1813 to 1850. He tells of his family and his stepfather, an actor; his early passion for Beethoven and the theatre; his years as a conductor in small German theatres and his marriage to the actress Minna Planer; their flight from creditors in Riga by sea, through storms that inspired The Flying Dutchman; poverty in Paris; his success in Dresden with Rienzi and Tannhäuser, and the composition of Lohengrin; and his part in the revolution of 1849, which forced him into exile in Switzerland.
context: Wagner (1813–1883) began the memoirs in 1865 at the request of his patron, King Ludwig II of Bavaria; they were printed privately and published only in 1911. They are self-serving but full of vivid scenes. In Dresden in 1849 he fought beside the anarchist Bakunin, author of [God and the State](/book/32814?lang=en).

about: In 1876, Charles Darwin wrote a short account of his life for his children and grandchildren. He describes his childhood, his boredom at school and in medical studies at Edinburgh, which he abandoned after watching operations without anaesthetic, his passion for collecting beetles at Cambridge, the invitation to sail on the Beagle that changed his life, and the long years of work at home in Kent that led to his theory. He also reflects honestly on his loss of religious faith and on how his mind had become 'a kind of machine for grinding general laws out of large collections of facts', at the cost of his love of poetry and music.
context: This edition, by his son Francis Darwin, was published in 1887 in the Life and Letters, with some passages on religion left out that were later restored. It is a modest and moving self-portrait. The voyage is told in [The Voyage of the Beagle](/book/147?lang=en), and the theory in [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en).

about: In these lectures the novelist E. M. Forster looks at the novel not by period or influence but by its parts. He begins with the story, the most basic element, which makes us ask 'and then?'; then people, where he distinguishes 'flat' characters, built around a single idea, from 'round' ones that can surprise us; then plot, which adds causality ('The king died, and then the queen died of grief'); and then fantasy, prophecy, pattern and rhythm, with examples from Tolstoy, Dickens, Austen, Dostoevsky, Proust and many others, all imagined as writing side by side in one room.
context: Forster gave the Clark Lectures at Cambridge in 1927, and the book has been a favourite of readers and writers ever since for its wit and common sense. His own masterpiece is [A Passage to India](/book/55646?lang=en), and [Howards End](/book/3074?lang=en) is close behind.

about: In four essays, two of them written as witty dialogues, Oscar Wilde sets out his ideas about art. In 'The Decay of Lying' he argues that art should not imitate nature and that, on the contrary, 'Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life'. 'Pen, Pencil and Poison' is a sketch of Thomas Griffiths Wainewright, an artist and critic who was also a poisoner. 'The Critic as Artist' claims that criticism is itself a creative art, and 'The Truth of Masks' discusses costume and archaeology in Shakespeare's plays.
context: Wilde published the book in 1891, the same year as the book version of [The Picture of Dorian Gray](/book/62?lang=en), and it is the clearest statement of his aestheticism. Its paradoxes are still quoted wherever art and criticism are discussed. His later, sorrowful testament is [De Profundis](/book/68?lang=en).

about: John Calvin's Institutes is the most important work of the Protestant Reformation's theology. Calvin sets out the Christian faith systematically: the knowledge of God and of ourselves, which he says are bound together; God as creator and ruler of the world through his providence; the fall of humankind and the depth of human sin; and God as redeemer through Christ. Writing with clarity and force, he bases every argument on scripture and on the early Church Fathers, especially Augustine. This is the first of two volumes.
context: Calvin (1509–1564), a French theologian who led the Reformation in Geneva, first published the book in 1536 and expanded it until the final edition of 1559; it shaped Reformed churches in Switzerland, France, the Netherlands, Scotland and America. This translation, of 1813, is by John Allen. Calvin's great teacher was Augustine, whose [City of God](/book/40907?lang=en) is also in the library.

about: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was the most popular poet of nineteenth-century America, and this volume gathers all his poetry: the long narrative poems Evangeline, The Song of Hiawatha and The Courtship of Miles Standish; the Tales of a Wayside Inn, including 'Paul Revere's Ride'; short lyrics that generations learned by heart, such as 'A Psalm of Life', 'The Village Blacksmith', 'The Wreck of the Hesperus' and 'The Children's Hour'; his sonnets; and translations from many European languages.
context: Longfellow (1807–1882), a professor at Harvard who also translated Dante, wrote in clear, musical verse that made American history and legend part of popular memory. His reputation fell in the twentieth century, but many of his lines remain part of the language. Two of his long poems are also in the library separately: [Evangeline](/book/2229?lang=en) and [The Song of Hiawatha](/book/400?lang=en).

about: This volume gathers all of Edgar Allan Poe's poems, from the youthful Tamerlane to his last works: 'The Raven', with its haunting refrain 'Nevermore'; 'Annabel Lee', about a love so great that the angels envied it; 'The Bells', which rings with the sounds it describes; 'Ulalume', 'Lenore', 'To Helen' and 'Eldorado'. It also contains his essays on poetry: 'The Poetic Principle', and 'The Philosophy of Composition', in which he claims to explain, step by step, how he wrote 'The Raven'.
context: Poe (1809–1849) thought poetry should aim at beauty and a single intense effect, and his musical, melancholy verse deeply influenced Baudelaire and the French Symbolists. This edition was edited by John Henry Ingram, one of his early biographers. 'The Raven' also has its own page in the library, [The Raven](/book/1321?lang=en), and his tales are in [Volume 2 of his Works](/book/2333?lang=en).

about: Ralph Waldo Emerson is best known for his essays, but he was also a poet, and this volume gathers his verse. It includes the 'Concord Hymn', written for the monument to the first battle of the American Revolution, with its 'shot heard round the world'; 'The Rhodora', about a wild flower blooming unseen in the woods; 'Days', 'Brahma' and 'Each and All'; the long, grieving 'Threnody' for his young son Waldo; and poems inspired by the Persian poets he admired, among them 'Saadi' and versions from Hafiz.
context: Emerson (1803–1882) wrote compressed, thoughtful verse in which nature reveals spiritual laws, and he was one of the first Americans to read and praise the poetry of Persia. This is the 'Household Edition' of his poems. His ideas are set out in prose in [Nature](/book/26193?lang=en) and his [Essays: First Series](/book/286?lang=en), and the Persian master he loved is in the [Poems from the Divan of Hafiz](/book/68368?lang=en).

about: This selection, published in 1923, gathers poems from Robert Frost's first three books, A Boy's Will, North of Boston and Mountain Interval. Here are some of the best-known poems in American literature: 'The Road Not Taken', about two roads diverging in a yellow wood; 'Mending Wall', with its neighbour who insists that 'good fences make good neighbors'; 'Birches', 'After Apple-Picking', the dramatic dialogues 'The Death of the Hired Man' and 'Home Burial', and the terrible farm accident of 'Out, Out—'.
context: Frost (1874–1963) used the plain speech and rhythms of New England country people to write poems that look simple and turn out to be deep and often dark; he won the Pulitzer Prize four times. Two of the books from which these poems come are also in the library: [A Boy's Will](/book/3147?lang=en) and [North of Boston](/book/3152?lang=en).

about: These fourteen stories, published in 1927, show Ernest Hemingway at the height of his powers as a writer of short fiction. In 'The Killers', two gangsters wait in a small-town diner for a Swedish boxer they have been hired to kill, while young Nick Adams tries to warn him; in 'Hills Like White Elephants', an American and a young woman wait for a train in Spain, talking around an operation neither of them names; 'The Undefeated' follows an aging bullfighter who refuses to give up; and 'In Another Country' is set among wounded soldiers in a Milan hospital.
context: Hemingway believed that a story's strength lies in what it leaves out, like an iceberg with most of its mass beneath the water, and these stories, with their spare dialogue, influenced writers everywhere. His novels [The Sun Also Rises](/book/61232?lang=en) and [A Farewell to Arms](/book/68678?lang=en) are also in the library.

about: A doctor tells Lord Peter Wimsey and his friend Inspector Parker about an elderly patient of his who was dying slowly of cancer but died suddenly, years before he expected, just when a change in the law might have affected who would inherit her money. There was no sign of poison and no apparent motive, and his suspicions ruined his practice. Wimsey decides to investigate a murder that may never have happened, helped by his inquisitive agent Miss Climpson, who is perfectly placed to gather gossip in a quiet country town.
context: Dorothy L. Sayers (1893–1957) published the novel in 1927, the third Lord Peter Wimsey mystery, and it is admired for its clever plot and its sharp picture of English society after the First World War; in the United States it was also published as The Dawson Pedigree. The first Wimsey novels are [Whose Body?](/book/53430?lang=en) and [Clouds of Witness](/book/64290?lang=en).

about: Before Jeeves and Blandings Castle, P. G. Wodehouse wrote romantic and comic stories for magazines, and this collection gathers nineteen of them. In the title story, a young woman composer in a London flat is driven mad by the noise of the painter upstairs; there are stories of shy young men and resourceful girls, golf, boxing, schoolboys, struggling artists and actors, and a clever butler who manipulates the romance of the family he serves, all told with the light, inventive humour that made Wodehouse famous.
context: Wodehouse (1881–1975) published the collection in 1914. It shows him finding the style and the comic characters he later perfected. For his best-loved creation, the valet who rescues his master from every scrape, read [My Man Jeeves](/book/8077?lang=en).

about: These five stories, written by the young Rudyard Kipling in India, deal with ghosts and terrors of many kinds. In 'The Phantom 'Rickshaw', an Englishman who cruelly ended an affair is haunted on the roads of Simla by the woman's ghost in her rickshaw; in 'The Strange Ride of Morrowbie Jukes', an engineer falls into a crater in the sand where people believed dead are trapped in a horrible community; 'The Man Who Would Be King' tells of two adventurers who make themselves kings in remote Kafiristan; and in 'The Finest Story in the World', a London clerk seems to remember his past lives.
context: Kipling published the collection in 1888 in a series of cheap paperbacks sold at Indian railway stations, when he was twenty-two. 'The Man Who Would Be King' also has its own page in the library: [The Man Who Would Be King](/book/8060?lang=en). His first stories of Anglo-Indian life are [Plain Tales from the Hills](/book/2057?lang=en).

about: Arthur Conan Doyle wrote many tales of horror and mystery besides his Sherlock Holmes stories, and this collection gathers thirteen of them. In 'The Horror of the Heights', a pilot climbing higher than anyone before discovers monstrous creatures living in the upper air; in 'The Terror of Blue John Gap', something huge lives in the caves of Derbyshire; 'The Leather Funnel' brings a dreamer back to a torture chamber of seventeenth-century France; and in 'The Lost Special', a whole train vanishes between two stations. There are also tales of a deadly Brazilian cat, a Jewish high priest's breastplate and a doctor's revenge.
context: Doyle published the collection in 1922, and its stories show his gift for building suspense from rational explanation. Holmes's own most frightening case is [The Hound of the Baskervilles](/book/55?lang=en), and Doyle's adventure among dinosaurs is [The Lost World](/book/61?lang=en).

about: Dr Cathcart, his young nephew Simpson, two guides and a cook set out to hunt moose in the vast, empty forests of northern Canada. One night by the fire the French-Canadian guide Défago grows terrified by a smell on the wind, and later, in their small tent in the dark, something calls his name and he rushes out into the snow. Simpson follows his tracks, which change in a way he cannot understand, and hears his voice crying from the sky about his feet of fire, as the hunting party discovers what the Native peoples of the region mean by the Wendigo.
context: Algernon Blackwood (1869–1951), who had himself camped and worked in the Canadian wilderness, published the story in 1910. It is one of the masterpieces of the supernatural tale, and H. P. Lovecraft greatly admired it. Blackwood's other great story of the wild is [The Willows](/book/10409?lang=en).

about: On Benefit Street in Providence, Rhode Island, stands an old house where, for generations, people have sickened and died. The narrator, who has been fascinated by the house since childhood, investigates its history with his scholarly uncle, Dr Elihu Whipple: the deaths of the families who lived there, the strange words spoken by the dying in French, a pale fungus in the cellar shaped like a doubled-up human figure. At last the two men decide to spend a night in the cellar with scientific instruments to confront whatever is there.
context: H. P. Lovecraft (1890–1937) wrote the story in 1924, based on a real house in his beloved Providence, and it was first published in a magazine only after his death. It is one of his finest tales of a horror rooted in history and place. His later cosmic horror includes [The Call of Cthulhu](/book/62316?lang=en) and [The Colour Out of Space](/book/62270?lang=en).

about: Conan, the barbarian adventurer who has become king of Aquilonia, is overthrown when his enemies bring back to life Xaltotun, a terrible sorcerer of a vanished empire, using a magic jewel called the Heart of Ahriman. Betrayed and imprisoned, Conan escapes from a dungeon full of horrors and sets out alone across the kingdoms of his world to recover the jewel, the only weapon that can defeat the wizard, from the pirate coasts to the pyramids of Stygia, and to win back his throne.
context: Robert E. Howard (1906–1936), a Texan writer who died at thirty, created Conan in 1932, and this, serialised in 1935 and 1936, is the only full-length Conan novel he wrote. It is a founding work of 'sword and sorcery' fantasy. Compare the earlier planetary adventures of Burroughs's [The Gods of Mars](/book/434?lang=en).

about: In 1918 a manuscript sealed in a thermos flask is found floating off the coast of Greenland. It is the story of Bowen Tyler, an American whose ship is sunk by a German submarine during the First World War. With a young woman, Lys La Rue, and a few British sailors, he captures the submarine, but sabotage leaves them lost at sea until they reach an unknown island surrounded by cliffs, Caprona, where dinosaurs still live and primitive human tribes seem to represent every stage of evolution.
context: Edgar Rice Burroughs, the creator of Tarzan, published the story in 1918; it is the first part of a trilogy about the island of Caspak. It belongs to the 'lost world' tradition of adventure. Compare Conan Doyle's [The Lost World](/book/61?lang=en) and Burroughs's own [A Princess of Mars](/book/432?lang=en).

about: In the future, old age has been cured, and to keep the population of the United States at forty million, a new life can begin only when someone volunteers to die. The Federal Bureau of Termination, whose telephone number is 2 B R 0 2 B, 'to be or not to be', handles the arrangements. In the waiting room of a Chicago hospital, where a painter is finishing a cheerful mural of the perfect society, Edward K. Wehling Jr. waits for the birth of triplets, knowing that his family can keep only one of them unless two people agree to die.
context: Kurt Vonnegut (1922–2007) published this short, darkly funny story in a science fiction magazine in 1962, and it shows in miniature the satire and humanity of his later novels. Its title plays on [Hamlet](/book/1?lang=en). Compare Zamyatin's earlier vision of a perfectly managed society, [We](/book/56360?lang=en).

about: Dick Jarvis, the chemist of the first expedition to Mars, crash-lands his small rocket far from the main ship and must walk hundreds of miles back across the desert. On the way he rescues a strange, ostrich-like Martian, Tweel, from a tentacled creature, and the two become friends, though they can barely understand each other. Together they meet other bizarre beings: a silicon creature that eats sand and builds pyramids of its own waste bricks, barrel-shaped creatures pushing carts, and a dream-beast that lures its prey with illusions of what they most desire.
context: Stanley G. Weinbaum (1902–1935) published the story in 1934, and its Martians, intelligent but truly alien rather than monsters, delighted readers and influenced writers such as Isaac Asimov; he died of cancer a year and a half later. Compare the hostile Martians of Wells's [The War of the Worlds](/book/180?lang=en).

about: On New Year's night, Captain Hector Servadac, a French officer stationed on the coast of Algeria, and his orderly Ben Zoof are thrown to the ground by a terrible shock. When they recover, the sun rises in the west, the days are shorter, the sea has changed and the Earth seems to have vanished: a comet has grazed the planet and carried away fragments of the Mediterranean region, with a handful of people, including British officers from Gibraltar, Spanish peasants and a Russian count with his yacht. Together they travel through the solar system on the comet Gallia, hoping to return.
context: Jules Verne published the novel, Hector Servadac, in 1877. It mixes astronomy with comedy, although its portrait of a Jewish merchant reflects the prejudices of the time. This English version is titled Off on a Comet! Verne's more famous voyage into space is [From the Earth to the Moon](/book/124?lang=en).

about: The descendants of a Protestant family persecuted in the seventeenth century are scattered across the world, each holding a bronze medal that summons them to a house in Paris on 13 February 1832, where an immense fortune, grown over a century and a half, will be divided among those present. A Jesuit, the cunning and patient Rodin, plots to keep them away so that the fortune will pass to his order, while the old soldier Dagobert travels from Siberia with twin orphan girls, an Indian prince arrives from the East, and the legendary Wandering Jew, condemned to walk the earth until the end of time, secretly protects them, as cholera sweeps through Paris.
context: Eugène Sue (1804–1857) published the novel in newspaper instalments in 1844 and 1845, and it was one of the most popular books of its century, fiercely hostile to the Jesuits. Its sprawling suspense rivals that of [The Count of Monte Cristo](/book/132?lang=en), and its picture of poverty anticipates [Les Misérables](/book/44?lang=en).

about: Left penniless after her father's death, Cytherea Graye takes a post as lady's companion to the wealthy, unmarried Miss Aldclyffe, who, it turns out, once loved Cytherea's father. Separated from Edward Springrove, the young architect she loves, Cytherea is pursued by Miss Aldclyffe's new steward, the handsome and mysterious Aeneas Manston, whose wife is believed to have died in a fire. Pressed by poverty and duty, she agrees to marry him, and only then do the secrets of the past begin to surface.
context: This was Thomas Hardy's first published novel, issued anonymously in 1871 at his own expense, and it is a complicated sensation novel in the manner of Wilkie Collins, full of coincidences, crimes and detection. It already shows Hardy's eye for the Dorset countryside. Compare Collins's [The Woman in White](/book/880?lang=en) and Hardy's next novel, [Under the Greenwood Tree](/book/2801?lang=en).

about: Dmitri Sanin, a lonely man of fifty-two, finds an old garnet cross in a drawer and remembers the summer of 1840, when, as a young Russian traveller in Frankfurt, he walked into an Italian sweet shop and helped revive a boy who had fainted. He fell in love with the boy's beautiful sister, Gemma, fought a duel for her honour, and became engaged to her. To raise money for their marriage, he went to sell his estate to the rich wife of a schoolfellow, the fascinating Maria Nikolaevna, and in a few days at the spa of Wiesbaden he lost everything.
context: Ivan Turgenev published the short novel in 1872, and it is one of his most beautiful and painful stories of first love and weakness. This translation is by Constance Garnett. Compare Turgenev's [First Love, and Other Stories](/book/51638?lang=en) and his great novel [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en).

about: Germinie Lacerteux is the devoted servant of an elderly spinster, Mademoiselle de Varandeuil, who loves her like a daughter and never suspects her secret. Lonely and passionate, Germinie falls in love with Jupillon, the selfish son of a dairywoman, gives him all her savings, steals to support him, drinks and sinks into misery, while by day she continues to serve her mistress faithfully, until illness brings her to the public hospital.
context: The brothers Edmond and Jules de Goncourt published the novel in 1865, after discovering, on the death of their own servant, the hidden double life she had led. In their preface they claimed for the poor the right to be the subject of serious novels, and the book paved the way for the naturalism of Zola's [L'Assommoir](/book/8312?lang=en). Compare George Moore's [Esther Waters](/book/8070?lang=en).

about: Robert Elsmere, a young, idealistic clergyman, marries the deeply religious Catherine Leyburn and takes up a parish in the Surrey countryside. There, through the library of the sceptical local squire and his own study of history, he comes to doubt the miracles of the Gospels and the divinity of Christ. Unable to remain a priest, he resigns, to his wife's anguish, moves to London and founds a 'New Brotherhood' to serve the working people of the East End, while their marriage is tested by the gulf between his new faith and hers.
context: Mrs Humphry Ward (1851–1920), a niece of the poet Matthew Arnold, published the novel in 1888, and it became a best seller on both sides of the Atlantic; the former prime minister Gladstone wrote a long review attacking its ideas. It captures the Victorian crisis of faith. Compare George Eliot's [Middlemarch](/book/490?lang=en) and Newman's account of a conversion in the opposite direction, [Apologia Pro Vita Sua](/book/17606?lang=en).

about: 'It was a dark and stormy night; the rain fell in torrents...' So begins the story of Paul Clifford, an orphan brought up in a London thieves' tavern. Wrongly sent to prison as a boy, he learns crime there, becomes the charming leader of a gang of highwaymen under the name of Captain Lovett, falls in love with the beautiful Lucy Brandon, and is finally tried before a stern judge, Lucy's uncle, who turns out to be connected to him in a way no one expected. Along the way the novel satirises politicians, lawyers and society as greater robbers than the highwaymen.
context: Edward Bulwer-Lytton published the novel in 1830. Its opening sentence has become famous as the classic example of overwritten prose, and a contest for the worst opening sentence is named after its author. His most famous novel is [The Last Days of Pompeii](/book/1787?lang=en); for an earlier satire on 'great' criminals, read Fielding's [Jonathan Wild](/book/5307?lang=en).

about: On the remote Shetland Islands in the early eighteenth century, young Mordaunt Mertoun, who lives with his gloomy father in a ruined house, saves a stranger from a shipwreck: Captain Cleveland, a dashing, mysterious seaman who is, in fact, a pirate. Cleveland wins the heart of Minna Troil, the romantic elder daughter of a rich Shetland landowner, while her sister Brenda loves Mordaunt, and the half-mad sibyl Norna of the Fitful Head, who claims to control the winds, guards a secret that binds them all.
context: Walter Scott published the novel in 1822, after visiting Shetland and Orkney on a voyage with the lighthouse engineer Robert Stevenson, the grandfather of Robert Louis Stevenson, and he based Cleveland partly on the real pirate John Gow. This edition was prepared by Andrew Lang. Scott's first novel is [Waverley](/book/2224?lang=en), and Stevenson's own pirates are in [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en).

about: In 1697 Charles Perrault published a small book of fairy tales that gave Europe some of its most famous stories in their classic form: Little Red Riding-Hood, Blue Beard and his forbidden room, the Sleeping Beauty in the Wood, the Master Cat or Puss-in-Boots, Cinderella and her little glass slipper, Riquet with the Tuft, Little Thumb and his brothers, The Fairies, The Ridiculous Wishes and Donkey-Skin. Each tale ends with a witty moral in verse, often addressed with irony to the adult readers of the French court.
context: Perrault (1628–1703), a member of the French Academy, wrote the tales from old folk stories, and they were later retold by the Brothers Grimm and by countless others. This edition, of 1922, is illustrated by the Irish artist Harry Clarke, with translations by Robert Samber and J. E. Mansion. Compare [Grimms' Fairy Tales](/book/317?lang=en).

about: This book introduces the myths and legends of China: how the giant Pangu shaped heaven and earth; the gods of the Taoist and Buddhist pantheons, from the Jade Emperor who rules heaven to the compassionate Guanyin; the Eight Immortals; the dragon kings of the seas; the gods of thunder, fire, wealth and the stars; and many folk tales of ghosts, fox spirits and heroes, including the adventures of Sun Wukong, the Monkey King. Werner also explains the beliefs and customs behind the stories.
context: E. T. C. Werner (1864–1954) spent many years in China as a British diplomat and published the book in 1922, with illustrations by Chinese artists. It remains a rich and readable introduction to Chinese mythology. For China's most famous ancient book of strategy, read [The Art of War](/book/256?lang=en).

about: Padraic Colum retells the myths of the Norse gods as one continuous story for young readers: the building of Asgard, Odin's sacrifice of an eye for wisdom at the well of Mimir, the thunder god Thor's adventures among the giants, the mischief of Loki, the binding of the wolf Fenrir, the death of the beautiful Baldur, and finally Ragnarok, the twilight of the gods. The book also tells the heroic story of Sigurd, the dragon-slayer, and the cursed gold of the Volsungs.
context: Colum (1881–1972), an Irish poet and playwright, published the book in 1920 with illustrations by Willy Pogány, and its clear, poetic prose has introduced generations of children to Norse mythology. Its sources are the Eddas, such as [The Younger Edda](/book/16965?lang=en), and [The Story of the Volsungs](/book/1391?lang=en).

about: In these comic verses, Hilaire Belloc offers 'cautionary tales' about children who come to terrible ends for small faults: Jim, who ran away from his nurse and was eaten by a lion; Henry King, who chewed bits of string and died of it; Matilda, who told lies and was burned to death because no one believed her cries of 'Fire!'; Rebecca, who slammed doors for fun and perished miserably; and Lord Lundy, who was too easily moved to tears and so was sent out to govern New South Wales.
context: Belloc (1870–1953) published the book in 1907 as a parody of the stern moral verses written for Victorian children, and its deadpan humour still makes children and adults laugh. The pictures are by his friend Basil Temple Blackwood. Its model is Heinrich Hoffmann's [Struwwelpeter](/book/10933?lang=en).

about: Benjamin Bunny, Peter Rabbit's cousin, finds Peter sitting sadly in a red handkerchief, because his clothes are still on the scarecrow in Mr McGregor's garden where he lost them. The two little rabbits slip back into the garden to fetch them, and Benjamin cheerfully fills the handkerchief with onions as a present for Peter's mother. But a cat appears and sits on the basket under which they are hiding, and only the arrival of old Mr Benjamin Bunny, Benjamin's fierce father, can save them.
context: Beatrix Potter published the story in 1904 as a sequel to [The Tale of Peter Rabbit](/book/12778?lang=en), and its pictures were drawn in the gardens of a house near Keswick, in the Lake District countryside she loved. It is one of the best-loved of her little books for small children.

about: On her way to visit relatives in California, Dorothy is caught in an earthquake, and with her cousin Zeb, a horse named Jim and her kitten Eureka she falls deep into the earth. They pass through underground lands: the country of the Mangaboos, cold vegetable people who grow on bushes, the Valley of Voe, where everyone is invisible, and the wooden land of the Gargoyles. There they meet an old friend, the Wizard, and with his help they find their way at last to the Emerald City, where Eureka is accused of a crime.
context: L. Frank Baum published the fourth Oz book in 1908 with illustrations by John R. Neill. Its strange underground adventures show Baum's endless invention. The series begins with [The Wonderful Wizard of Oz](/book/314?lang=en), and Dorothy's previous adventure is [Ozma of Oz](/book/786?lang=en).

about: In March 1711, Joseph Addison and Richard Steele began publishing The Spectator, a short essay that appeared every day except Sunday. Its imaginary author, Mr Spectator, a silent observer who watches London life from the coffee houses, writes about manners, fashion, marriage, the theatre and the opera, and introduces a club of characters, the most famous of whom is the old country gentleman Sir Roger de Coverley. Their aim, Addison wrote, was to enliven morality with wit and to temper wit with morality.
context: The Spectator, whose essays were read aloud in coffee houses across Britain, set a model for English prose and for journalism, and it was still read as a school classic in the nineteenth century. This first volume of Henry Morley's edition contains the opening numbers. The coffee houses where it was read are described in [All About Coffee](/book/25405?lang=en).

about: This first volume of Edmund Burke's works contains his early writings. In A Vindication of Natural Society (1756), he imitates and mocks the style of the philosopher Bolingbroke. In A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757), he argues that the sublime, the feeling we have before storms, mountains, vastness and darkness, springs from a kind of delightful terror, while beauty arises from smallness, smoothness and delicacy. The volume also contains political writings of the 1760s and 1770s, including Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents.
context: Burke (1729–1797), an Irish-born statesman, became the founder of modern conservatism with his Reflections on the Revolution in France, which provoked Thomas Paine's reply, [Rights of Man](/book/3831?lang=en). His Enquiry on the sublime deeply influenced Romantic art and the Gothic novel, such as [The Mysteries of Udolpho](/book/3390?lang=en).

about: In the winter of 1623 the poet John Donne, now Dean of St Paul's in London, fell dangerously ill, and as he lay in bed he wrote a series of twenty-three devotions, each made of a meditation, an expostulation and a prayer, following the stages of his sickness. In the seventeenth, hearing a church bell toll for a funeral, he writes the famous words: 'No man is an island, entire of itself... any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.' The volume adds Death's Duel, the sermon he preached shortly before his death.
context: Donne (1572–1631), the greatest of the Metaphysical poets, published the Devotions in 1624, and their passage on the bell has been quoted ever since; Ernest Hemingway took from it the title of a novel. Hemingway's stories in [Men Without Women](/book/63622?lang=en) are also in the library. For another great work of prayer, read [The Imitation of Christ](/book/1864?lang=en).

about: Brother Lawrence, a humble lay brother who worked for years in the kitchen of a Carmelite monastery in Paris, explains in conversations and letters his simple way of life with God. He did not find God more in church than in his kitchen, he says: whether cooking, washing pots or repairing sandals, he kept himself constantly aware of God's presence, speaking to him as a friend, and when he failed he simply turned back without anxiety. Prayer, for him, was not a special exercise but the habit of a whole day.
context: Brother Lawrence (about 1614–1691), born Nicolas Herman, had been a soldier and a footman before entering the monastery; his conversations and letters were gathered after his death by Abbé Joseph de Beaufort. The little book has been loved by readers of many Christian traditions. Compare [Revelations of Divine Love](/book/47985?lang=en) by Julian of Norwich and [The Imitation of Christ](/book/1864?lang=en).

about: The first word of the Rule is 'Listen'. It was written by Saint Benedict for the monks of his monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy in the sixth century. In seventy-three short chapters he sets out how a community should live: obedience to the abbot, who must govern with fatherly care; silence and humility, with its twelve steps; the hours of prayer through the day and night; manual work and reading, since idleness is the enemy of the soul; meals, clothing and sleep; and hospitality, for every guest should be received as Christ himself.
context: Benedict of Nursia (about 480–547) wrote the Rule with moderation and good sense, and it became the foundation of monastic life in Western Europe for over a thousand years; the monasteries it shaped preserved much of ancient learning. This translation is by Leonard J. Doyle. Compare [The Confessions of St. Augustine](/book/3417?lang=en).

about: In May 1373, a woman of thirty, believed to be dying, received a series of sixteen visions, or 'showings', of Christ's passion and of God's love. She recovered and spent years meditating on them as an anchoress, living alone in a cell attached to the church of St Julian in Norwich. Her Revelations explore the meaning of sin and suffering with great tenderness: God shows her the whole of creation as a little thing the size of a hazelnut, held in being by love, speaks of God as a mother, and assures her that 'all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well'.
context: Julian of Norwich (about 1343–after 1416) wrote what is believed to be the first book in English by a woman. This edition, by Grace Warrack, published in 1901, gives the longer version of the text in modernised English. Compare the gentler practical spirituality of Brother Lawrence's [The Practice of the Presence of God](/book/5701?lang=en).

about: 'As a man thinketh in his heart, so is he.' Taking this verse from the Book of Proverbs as his title, James Allen argues in seven short chapters that our thoughts shape our character, our circumstances, our health and our achievements. The mind, he says, is like a garden that will grow either flowers or weeds; circumstances do not make a person but reveal him; and calm, purposeful thinking brings strength and serenity.
context: Allen (1864–1912), an English writer who left business to live simply and write, published the essay in 1903, and it has been one of the most widely read books of self-improvement ever since. It can be read in an hour. Its Stoic ancestors include the [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en) of Marcus Aurelius and the [Discourses of Epictetus](/book/9776?lang=en).

about: Every morning, Arnold Bennett writes, you wake to find your purse magically filled with twenty-four hours, the same for rich and poor, and no one can take them from you. Yet most people, especially office workers who spend their days at dull jobs, waste the hours outside work. He offers practical advice: use the morning journey to concentrate the mind, set aside ninety minutes three evenings a week for serious reading or the arts, begin modestly, and never let the plan become a tyrant.
context: Bennett (1867–1931), a successful novelist, published the little book in 1908 for readers of a London newspaper, and its gentle, humorous advice still speaks to anyone who feels that life is slipping away. His great novel of ordinary lives is [The Old Wives' Tale](/book/5299?lang=en), and a sterner guide to the mind is James Allen's [As a Man Thinketh](/book/4588?lang=en).

about: How can an ordinary person learn to speak well in public? This practical guide begins with stage fright and how to master it, and then covers the techniques of effective speaking: avoiding monotony, emphasis, changing pitch and pace, the use of pauses, inflection, feeling and enthusiasm, gesture, the training of the voice, and the methods of argument, persuasion, description and narration. Each chapter ends with exercises and passages from famous speeches to practise.
context: The book, published in 1915, was written by the editor J. Berg Esenwein with Dale Carnegie, then a young teacher of public speaking in New York, who later became world famous with How to Win Friends and Influence People. The great speeches of Lincoln, often used as models, are in [The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln](/book/3375?lang=en).

about: José Raúl Capablanca, the Cuban world chess champion, explains the game from the ground up. Unusually, he begins not with openings but with the endgame, showing how to mate with few pieces and how to win with pawns, because, he argues, a player who understands the endgame understands the value of each piece. He then turns to the middle game, planning, attack and defence, and finally to the openings, illustrating his principles with annotated games, including some of his own victories.
context: Capablanca (1888–1942), famous for the clarity and ease of his play, published the book in 1921, the year he won the world championship from Emanuel Lasker, and it is still recommended to improving players. For puzzles of a different kind, many based on the chessboard, read Dudeney's [Amusements in Mathematics](/book/14865?lang=en).

about: Henry Ernest Dudeney, England's greatest maker of puzzles, gathers more than four hundred of them in this book, with full solutions. There are puzzles of arithmetic and money, of geometry and cutting shapes into pieces that form new shapes, of chessboards and the moves of the pieces, of magic squares, mazes, river crossings, measuring liquids, clocks, railways and unicursal routes, most of them wrapped in a short, amusing story. Some are easy, and some have challenged mathematicians for years.
context: Dudeney (1857–1930) published the collection in 1917, and many of his puzzles are still reprinted in books and newspapers around the world. It is a delightful way into mathematical thinking. For an equally friendly introduction to higher mathematics, read [Calculus Made Easy](/book/29748?lang=en).

about: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, one of the great masters of the orchestra, explains how to write for it. He describes each group of instruments, strings, woodwind, brass and percussion, with their ranges, colours and combinations, and then discusses how to orchestrate melody and harmony, how to balance the groups and how to create effects of light, shade and contrast. Every point is illustrated with examples drawn from his own works, such as the symphonic suite Scheherazade and his operas.
context: Rimsky-Korsakov (1844–1908) worked on the book for years, and it was completed after his death by his pupil and son-in-law Maximilian Steinberg; this English translation is by Edward Agate. It remains a classic textbook for composers. The stories behind his Scheherazade are in [The Thousand and One Nights](/book/30602?lang=en).

about: Harold Speed, an English painter, explains both the practice and the theory of drawing for students and amateurs. He distinguishes two ways of seeing and drawing: line drawing, which describes the edges and contours of forms, and mass drawing, which builds them from areas of light and shade, as a painter does. He discusses proportion, visual memory, rhythm, the academic and the personal approach, and the drawing of the great masters, illustrated with many of his own drawings and those of the old masters.
