context: Speed (1872–1957) published the book in 1913, and its common sense and clear teaching still make it a favourite with art students. For the notes of the greatest artist-scientist on the same subjects, read [The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci](/book/381?lang=en).

about: In the nineteenth century, flowers had meanings, and lovers could send messages with a bouquet: a red rose for love, ivy for fidelity, a yellow rose for jealousy, forget-me-nots for true love, rosemary for remembrance. This little book lists hundreds of flowers and plants alphabetically with the sentiment each one expresses, and it is decorated throughout with Kate Greenaway's charming drawings of children and flowers in her famous delicate style.
context: Kate Greenaway (1846–1901), one of the most popular illustrators of Victorian children's books, published it in 1884. It is a pretty record of a vanished language of courtship. A very different old book about plants is Culpeper's [Complete Herbal](/book/44709?lang=en).

about: Nicholas Culpeper, a London apothecary and physician, describes hundreds of English herbs: what each plant looks like, where it grows, when it flowers, which planet he believed governed it, and the illnesses it was thought to cure. He wrote in plain English, not Latin, so that ordinary people who could not afford doctors could treat themselves, and he combined traditional plant lore with the astrological medicine of his time. This edition adds a hundred more herbs and his guide to preparing remedies.
context: Culpeper (1616–1654) published the herbal in 1653, and it has hardly been out of print since; it is a fascinating document of the history of medicine and botany, but its remedies should not be used in place of modern medical advice. For a lighter Victorian book of flowers, read Greenaway's [Language of Flowers](/book/28175?lang=en).

about: Isabella Beeton's great book covers everything a Victorian household needed to know: how to manage servants and accounts, how to entertain and arrange a dinner, how to care for children and the sick, and, above all, how to cook, with nearly a thousand recipes for soups, fish, meat, puddings, preserves and drinks. Its recipes were among the first to list the ingredients first, with the cost, the time needed and the number of people served, a model still followed by cookbooks today.
context: Beeton (1836–1865) wrote it in her early twenties for the magazine published by her husband, and it appeared as a book in 1861; she died at twenty-eight, but her name became synonymous with domestic advice. It is a window into Victorian daily life. For manners at table and elsewhere, read Emily Post's [Etiquette](/book/12788?lang=en).

about: What should one say when introduced to a stranger, how should a dinner be served, who pays for a wedding, how long should mourning last, and how should a letter of condolence be written? Emily Post answers these and hundreds of other questions about manners in society, business and the home, from formal balls and country house visits to travel and conversation, insisting that the heart of good manners is not rules but consideration for others.
context: Post (1872–1960), a novelist from New York society, published the book in 1922, and it became the standard American guide to etiquette, revised through many editions. It is also a vivid portrait of social life in the 1920s. Compare the eighteenth-century advice of [Lord Chesterfield's Letters to His Son](/book/3481?lang=en).

about: Born in India in 1893, Mukunda Lal Ghosh tells how, as a boy, he longed for God, ran away towards the Himalayas, and at last found his master, Sri Yukteswar, who trained him in the discipline of Kriya Yoga and gave him the monastic name Yogananda. He describes the saints and holy people he met, many of the wonders attributed to them, his meetings with Rabindranath Tagore and Mahatma Gandhi, and his mission to the West, where he arrived in 1920 and founded a society to teach meditation.
context: Paramahansa Yogananda (1893–1952) published the book in 1946, and it became one of the most popular spiritual autobiographies of the twentieth century; Steve Jobs is said to have reread it every year. Readers may take its miracles as faith or as legend. Tagore's own spiritual thought is in [Sadhana](/book/361?lang=en) and [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en).

about: King Henry VIII of England wrote these seventeen love letters, some in French and some in English, to Anne Boleyn in the years around 1527 and 1528, while he was trying to have his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled so that he could marry her. They show the king as an impatient lover, pleading, complaining of her silence and of the slowness of the Pope, sending her gifts and meat from his hunting, and signing with his initials and a heart.
context: Anne became queen in 1533 and was executed three years later; the king's break with Rome over the marriage began the English Reformation. The originals are, curiously, in the Vatican Library, where they may have been taken as evidence. This edition adds notes on their history. The religious struggles that followed are told, from a Protestant point of view, in [Fox's Book of Martyrs](/book/19993?lang=en).

about: John A. Lomax travelled through the American West collecting the songs that cowboys sang on the long cattle drives, around campfires and in saloons. Among them are 'The Old Chisholm Trail', 'Whoopee Ti Yi Yo, Git Along, Little Dogies', 'The Cowboy's Lament', better known as 'The Streets of Laredo', 'Jesse James', 'Sam Bass' and 'Home on the Range', together with ballads of buffalo hunters, outlaws, miners and settlers, many of them never written down before.
context: Lomax (1867–1948), a Texan who later became one of America's greatest collectors of folk music, published the book in 1910 with a letter of encouragement from Theodore Roosevelt. It preserved a whole oral tradition just as the open range was disappearing. The history of that frontier is told in Turner's [The Frontier in American History](/book/20453?lang=en).

about: John Foxe tells the stories of Christians who died for their faith, from the martyrs of the Roman persecutions and the medieval reformers, such as John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, to the English Protestants burned at the stake under Queen Mary in the 1550s. Among the most famous scenes are the burning of the bishops Latimer and Ridley at Oxford, when Latimer told his friend to take comfort, for they would light such a candle in England as would never be put out, and the death of Archbishop Cranmer, who held his right hand in the flames first because it had signed his recantation.
context: Foxe (1516–1587) first published his huge Acts and Monuments in 1563, and it was placed in many English churches beside the Bible; it shaped English Protestant identity for centuries, though its view of Catholics is fiercely partisan. This popular edition is much shorter than the original. John Bunyan, author of [The Pilgrim's Progress](/book/481?lang=en), read it in prison.

about: What makes an action virtuous or vicious? David Hume argues that morality rests not on reason alone but on feeling: we call qualities virtuous when they arouse in us a sentiment of approval, and we approve of qualities that are useful or agreeable, either to the person who has them or to others. He examines benevolence, justice, which he says arises from its usefulness to society, and the qualities we admire in a person, from courage and cheerfulness to wit and good manners, and in an appendix he argues that reason alone can never move us to act.
context: Hume (1711–1776) published the book in 1751 as a new version of the moral part of his earlier [Treatise of Human Nature](/book/278?lang=en), and he considered it the best of all his writings. It is the companion to his [Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding](/book/277?lang=en).

about: Writing as Geoffrey Crayon, an American traveller in England, Washington Irving collects his impressions and stories: the voyage across the Atlantic, the quiet English countryside and its customs, Westminster Abbey, Shakespeare's Stratford, old country inns and a series of essays on an English Christmas, together with tales of ghosts and legends. Two of the stories, set among the Dutch settlers of the Hudson Valley, became the first classics of American fiction: 'Rip Van Winkle', who sleeps for twenty years, and 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow', with its Headless Horseman.
context: Irving published the book in parts in 1819 and 1820, and it was the first American book to win wide success in Britain; its Christmas essays influenced Dickens's [A Christmas Carol](/book/33?lang=en). Its two famous tales also have their own pages: [Rip Van Winkle](/book/55419?lang=en) and [The Legend of Sleepy Hollow](/book/417?lang=en).
